# Situation Model

> [!definition] **Situation Model** *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> In discourse comprehension theory (van Dijk & Kintsch, 1983), a representation of the *situation* described by a text — not merely a propositional encoding of the text's surface content but a multidimensional representation including spatial, temporal, causal, and intentional structure. Closely related to mental models theory but developed independently and with a stronger empirical tradition in comprehension research.

## Core Explanation

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The foundational monograph. Establishes the theoretical framework, the contrast with rule-based theories, the empirical program, and the connection to model-theoretic semantics. Essential reading — but note that subsequent work has substantially revised the theory.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The major empirical program. Systematic investigation of syllogistic, propositional, and relational reasoning from the mental models perspective. Contains the most complete presentation of the model-number predictions.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The primary theoretical alternative. Develops the mental logic account (PSYCOP) in detail. Essential for understanding what mental models theory is *contrasted against*; also contains important methodological critiques.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Comprehensive review of the empirical literature. Remains a standard reference for the difficulty effects, belief-bias findings, and comparative performance of models and rules.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Introduces pragmatic reasoning schemas — the main alternative that accommodates content effects within a rule-based framework. Directly challenges the interpretation of facilitation effects as evidence for mental models.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Establishes the probabilistic rational analysis framework for the Wason selection task. Argues that human performance is near-optimal under realistic probabilistic assumptions — the most important challenge to both mental models and mental logic accounts.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The canonical argument that apparent analog properties of mental imagery could be artifacts of tacit knowledge rather than evidence of a genuinely analog representational format. Applies directly to the analogical status of mental models.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Develops the situation model framework in discourse comprehension — the closest empirical tradition to mental models theory with stronger methodological development and broader empirical coverage.

> [!analytical-insight] Key Insight *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> When people reason — whether about spatial relations, conditional statements, syllogistic arguments, or causal sequences — they construct one or more mental models that represent possible states of the world described by the premises. A conclusion is endorsed if it holds in all constructed models. Reasoning errors occur not because inference rules are applied incorrectly, but because people typically construct an incomplete subset of the logically possible models, and a conclusion that seems to…

> [!analytical-insight] Key Insight *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-first-principles-report-2026-03-11]])*
> From the four axioms together, the following conclusion follows: human reasoning is a *constructive, resource-sensitive, content-sensitive process that produces systematic patterns of success and failure*. This conclusion is robust. What does *not* follow from the axioms is the representational format of the construction — whether the constructed representations are analogical mental models, propositional rule applications, probabilistic estimates, or some multi-format combination. The axioms…

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Johnson-Laird & Bara (1984) tested all 64 syllogistic figures and found that error rates correlated significantly with the number of distinct mental models required for each. One-model problems yielded nearly perfect performance; three-model problems yielded error rates exceeding 50% in some figures. This graded difficulty function — and its prediction from a model-multiplicity metric computed *before* testing — constitutes one of the strongest pieces of evidence for MMT over mental logic alternatives.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The foundational text establishing [[Mental-Models-Theory]] in its comprehensive form. Johnson-Laird develops the distinction between propositional representations, mental models, and mental images; proposes the three-stage inference cycle; demonstrates the model-multiplicity account of syllogistic reasoning difficulty; and extends the framework to spatial, relational, and modal reasoning. Essential primary reading for any serious engagement with the theory. Readers approaching without background in logic or cognitive science should be prepared for technical density in chapters 3–6.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Comprehensive experimental and theoretical treatment of deductive reasoning from the mental models perspective. Reports the systematic studies of all 64 syllogistic figures, proposes the principle of truth, and develops the computational model in detail. A key reference for the empirical evidence supporting MMT over mental logic alternatives.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Develops the application of the principle of truth to conditional ("if-then") reasoning — one of the most contested domains in the reasoning literature. The paper demonstrates how the principle predicts specific error patterns in conditional inference and engages directly with mental logic alternatives. Supports the Phase III discussion of the theoretical landscape and the Principle of Truth.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Extends MMT to counterfactual reasoning, developing the claim that people represent both the actual and the imagined alternative when thinking counterfactually. Contains extensive empirical support for the dual-model account of counterfactual cognition. Important for the Phase IV discussion of counterfactual mechanisms and for the planned expansion node on [[Counterfactual-Reasoning]].

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Proposes the Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension and introduces the situation model as the deepest level of text representation. Foundational for the extension of MMT to comprehension and for the planned expansion node on [[Situation-Models-in-Text-Comprehension]]. Kintsch's distinction among surface form, text-base, and situation model has become standard in discourse psychology.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Introduces the Event Indexing Model, specifying the five dimensions (space, time, causality, intentionality, protagonist) along which situation models are tracked during narrative comprehension. Reports reading-time studies showing that discontinuities along these dimensions slow comprehension — strong evidence that readers actively maintain and update multidimensional situation models.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Reports the classic study documenting children's synthetic mental models of the Earth's shape and how these models combine naive perceptual beliefs with partially absorbed scientific information. Essential for the Phase V discussion of science education applications. Demonstrates the coherence and persistence of misconception-as-model and the inadequacy of simple information presentation as a remediation strategy.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> The most comprehensive treatment of [[Multimedia-Learning|Multimedia Learning Theory]], integrating three decades of experimental research on instructional design. Mayer's theory is explicitly grounded in the mental model framework: his "generative theory of multimedia learning" proposes that learners build verbal models, pictorial models, and an integrated mental model, and that effective instruction supports this construction without overloading working memory channels. Directly relevant to Phase V applications.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[mental-models-johnson-laird-foundational-report-2026-03-11]])*
> Key empirical study demonstrating that mechanical reasoning depends on the construction and mental animation of spatial mental models. Readers who received only text were less able to reason about the mechanism than those receiving diagrams — not because the text was inadequate propositionally, but because the text made model construction more effortful. Supports the Phase IV discussion of spatial mental models and mental simulation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The error detection paradigm is often interpreted as demonstrating that readers have poor monitoring skills — that they lack the ability to detect comprehension failures. A more precise reading of the evidence suggests something subtler: readers have the *capacity* for monitoring but deploy it selectively and inconsistently. The critical variable is not capacity but the conditions under which monitoring is spontaneously activated. This reframing has direct implications for intervention: if the problem is selective deployment, then strategy instruction that provides strategies without addressing the conditions of deployment will have limited generalizability.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Garner's comprehensive review of metacognitive failures in reading identified a pattern she called "compile to understand" — the tendency of many readers to treat successful word-by-word processing as equivalent to successful comprehension. Readers who "compile" in this sense feel that they have understood a text if they have read all the words without stumbling, regardless of whether those words have been integrated into a coherent [[Situation-Model]]. This illusion — a specific variant of the [[Fluency-Illusion]] — is, Garner argues, the primary mechanism by which monitoring fails in most adult readers. The feeling of smooth, fluent reading suppresses the generation of monitoring signals that would otherwise be triggered by comprehension failure.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> A striking pattern emerges when the most effective reading interventions are examined structurally: they all *externalize* the monitoring process. Think-aloud protocols, self-explanation, reciprocal teaching, annotation — each works in part by moving metacognitive monitoring from an internal, invisible, easily-suppressed process to an external, visible, socially-consequential one. This is not incidental to their effectiveness: it is the mechanism. The implication is that the [[Monitoring-Gap]] is most reliably closed not by instructing readers to monitor internally more carefully, but by creating conditions in which monitoring must be expressed.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Foundational study establishing that readers can apply comprehension standards when explicitly instructed but rarely apply them spontaneously. Key evidence for the monitoring-regulation decoupling problem. Supports Phase III and the central analytical reframe.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The seminal review establishing comprehension monitoring as a core metacognitive skill in reading. Distinguished monitoring from other reading skills and provided the framework that subsequent decades of research built on. Cited in Phase III and throughout.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Classic study demonstrating schema-dependent comprehension — participants who read the "washing clothes" passage without a title showed severely impaired comprehension and recall. Used in Phase III to establish that comprehension failures are often invisible to the reader.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Established the self-explanation effect: readers who generate self-explanations during reading show dramatically superior comprehension and transfer compared to passive readers. Key evidence for the externalization principle in Phase III.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational paper establishing the metacognitive knowledge/regulation/experience trichotomy used throughout this analysis. Particularly important for the concept of metacognitive experience as the trigger layer for regulation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The most comprehensive treatment of metacognitive failures in reading. Identified the "compile to understand" illusion, documented the evidence on adult readers' poor monitoring, and provided the fix-up strategy taxonomy used in Phase IV. Core reference for the fluency trap mechanism.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The authoritative account of the construction-integration model of text comprehension, including the textbase/situation model distinction used throughout this analysis. Provides the cognitive architecture within which comprehension monitoring must be understood.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Established the automaticity account of skilled reading — the theoretical foundation for the fluency trap mechanism. The argument that decoding automatization frees resources for comprehension is here complicated by the insight that those resources are not automatically redirected to monitoring.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The monitoring-control model of metacognition used as the primary theoretical framework in Phase II and IV. The distinction between monitoring (upward) and control (downward) information flow provided the precise architecture for the decoupling analysis.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational reciprocal teaching study. Produced some of the largest effect sizes in comprehension instruction research. Analyzed here as evidence for the externalization principle: the social externalization of monitoring was the key architectural change.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Strong evidence for the self-explanation effect in instructional contexts, extending the Chi et al. findings. Supports the externalization principle and the claim that it is the monitoring-externalization component of self-explanation (not elaboration per se) that drives comprehension gains.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Comprehensive review of the situation model literature, establishing the five dimensions of situational coherence monitoring (temporal, causal, spatial, protagonist, intentional). Supports the three-tier monitoring model's Tier 3 specification.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Studies using self-paced reading paradigms (where readers control how long each unit is displayed) consistently show that reading times are longer at points that require bridging inferences — connecting information separated by many sentences. These slowing events are associated with better Situation Model quality. Silent reading naturally provides self-pacing; oral reading does not. The implication is that silent reading enables the reader to linger precisely at the points where critical comprehension events occur.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The evidence from the Matthew Effect literature suggests that there is a threshold effect in reading and critical analysis: below a certain vocabulary fluency level, silent reading cannot produce critical engagement regardless of the reader's intention, because all available working memory is consumed by decoding. This is not a deficit of motivation or strategy but a cognitive resource constraint. Pedagogically, this implies that developing critical readers requires sufficient vocabulary development before strategic reading interventions can be effective — a point frequently overlooked in curricula that attempt critical reading too early.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The evidence from comprehension monitoring research suggests that the [[Fluency-Illusion]] is not merely a nuisance — it is the primary mechanism by which silent reading fails to develop critical analysis even in experienced readers. When reading feels effortless, readers interpret the feeling of processing ease as evidence of understanding, and [[Metacognitive-Monitoring]] is suppressed. This creates a perverse dynamic: the better a reader's decoding skills, the more vulnerable they may be to passive engagement, because fluency itself produces a false signal of comprehension. Critical analysis development requires disrupting this dynamic — which is precisely what strategies like [[Elaborative-Interrogation]], annotation, and [[Self-Explanation-Effect|self-explanation]] do.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational paper establishing the Construction-Integration model of reading. Demonstrates that reading involves two phases — construction (activating a broad associative network) and integration (constraining to coherent representations) — and that the depth of Situation Model construction determines the quality of comprehension. Central to Phases II and IV.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The seminal demonstration of the Self-Explanation Effect. Shows that readers who explain texts to themselves during reading produce dramatically better comprehension and transfer than readers who read without self-explanation. The mechanism — forcing Constructive mode engagement — is central to this analysis's Phase III and IV arguments.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational paper establishing the Matthew Effect in reading. Documents the compounding mechanism by which early reading advantages accumulate and proposes the vocabulary-working memory link central to this analysis's account of why critical analysis development is uneven across readers.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational treatment of comprehension monitoring in reading. Establishes that many readers fail to detect text inconsistencies and that comprehension monitoring can be taught. Directly supports this analysis's fourth mechanism and the Illusion of Knowing argument.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> A comprehensive treatment of think-aloud protocols during reading, demonstrating the constructive and evaluative operations that skilled readers perform during silent reading. Provides empirical grounding for the inference hierarchy proposed in Phase IV.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The original levels-of-processing paper. Establishes that depth of semantic processing — not repetition or effort per se — determines retention and comprehension quality. Foundational to Phase II's framework and the distinction between elaborative and evaluative processing.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The paper establishing the ICAP Framework used as a central analytical tool in Phase II. Demonstrates that Constructive and Interactive engagement modes produce significantly better learning outcomes than Active and Passive modes, and that the mode of engagement is not determined by the activity but by the cognitive operations the learner performs.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational treatment of Desirable Difficulties. Establishes that processing conditions that feel more effortful produce better retention and transfer, and that fluency is a misleading guide to learning depth. Connected to the Fluency Illusion argument in Phase III.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The most comprehensive review of eye-tracking data on reading behavior, documenting regression patterns and their relationship to inference generation and complex text processing. Provides empirical grounding for the self-pacing mechanism in Phase III.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> An important empirical paper on actively open-minded thinking and myside bias. Documents the tendency for motivated reasoning to filter evidence in self-serving ways, directly relevant to Phase V's argument about the confirmation bias ceiling of solo silent reading and the necessity of social discourse.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The foundational working memory model paper, establishing the distinction between the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive. The phonological loop mechanism central to this analysis is rooted in this framework.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Keith Rayner's decades of eye movement research (summarized most comprehensively in Rayner et al., 2016) establish that skilled readers make approximately 4 fixations per second, with roughly 85% of content words receiving a direct fixation. High-frequency, short, predictable words are often skipped (approximately 30% of the time), but this skipping occurs because parafoveal preview has already partially processed them — not because they are being "seen" peripherally without fixation. Crucially, attempts to suppress fixations or reduce their duration consistently degrade comprehension for complex material.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The eye movement literature does not show that skilled readers have cracked a peripheral vision code that novices haven't. It shows the opposite: the difference between skilled and average readers is primarily in fixation efficiency (less rereading, faster individual fixation processing, better parafoveal preview use) — not in an ability to extract meaning from unfixated text. Claims that one can "read" at 1,000+ WPM by reducing sub-vocalization or using peripheral scanning are inconsistent with the perceptual span data. At those speeds, something is happening — perhaps selective extraction of key content words — but it is more accurately called skimming than reading.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Taken together, the evidence suggests that the most productive path to faster, higher-comprehension reading runs through vocabulary development, domain knowledge building, and comprehension monitoring training — not through eye movement mechanics, sub-vocalization suppression, or peripheral vision expansion. The strategies with the strongest evidence base are cognitively demanding but they produce genuine, durable gains. The strategies marketed as shortcuts tend to produce speed without comprehension, and often produce readers who don't notice the comprehension loss.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The most comprehensive scientific review of speed-reading claims against the eye movement evidence base. Systematically examines RSVP, peripheral vision claims, and sub-vocalization suppression. Supports Phases II and III. Essential reading for anyone evaluating commercial speed-reading products.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Presents the Lexical Quality Hypothesis — the theoretical foundation for the vocabulary automaticity argument in Phase IV. Argues that the quality of lexical representations (their precision, completeness, and consolidation) is the primary determinant of reading ability differences. Strongly supports the highest-leverage intervention recommendation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Original articulation of the distinction between propositional text base and situation model, foundational for Phase II's definition of comprehension. Provides the theoretical grounding for why surface-level reading metrics are insufficient as comprehension standards.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Comprehensive review of reading rate research establishing the empirical base rate of skilled adult reading speed. Introduces the concept of "rauding" (efficient reading at the optimal rate for comprehension), providing the theoretical foundation for the comprehension-indexed speed metric. Supports Phase III.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> The definitive summary of two decades of eye movement research in reading, establishing the perceptual span constraint and fixation duration norms. Foundational for Phase III's evidence review on the mechanics of skilled reading.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Updated working memory model including the episodic buffer, directly relevant to the situation model construction bottleneck. Provides theoretical grounding for Phase IV's treatment of working memory integration demands during reading.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Original advance organizer study, providing empirical grounding for the prior knowledge pre-activation strategy in Phase V. Demonstrably improves both comprehension and retention through schema pre-activation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Theoretical account of how experts use long-term memory structures to extend effective working memory capacity in their domain. Provides the mechanistic bridge between domain expertise and the reading speed advantage — supports the schema-as-inference-engine analysis in Phase IV.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Foundational for the [[Fluency-Illusion]] analysis — demonstrates that subjective ease of processing is negatively correlated with actual learning depth. Directly relevant to the speed-monitoring incompatibility and the risks of bandwidth compression training.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[silent-reading-fluency-speed-comprehension-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Comprehensive framework for the types of inferences generated during reading and their resource demands. Provides the inferential bridging analysis underpinning Bottleneck 3 in Phase II, and grounds the prior knowledge pre-activation argument of Phase V.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Primary Sources and Scholarly Works**
> 
> The research for this report synthesized information from multiple authoritative sources on ancient Stoicism and Hellenistic philosophy:
> 
> - [Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/stoicism/) — Comprehensive academic overview of Stoic philosophy, its historical development, and core doctrines
> - [Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Stoicism](https://iep.utm.edu/stoicism/) — Detailed treatment of Stoic metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics
> - [Ancient History Encyclopedia: Stoicism](https://www.worldhistory.org/stoicism/) — Historical context and biographical information on major Stoic figures
> - [Stanford Encyclopedia: Hellenistic Philosophy](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/hellenistic-philosophy/) — Broader context of Hellenistic philosophical movements
> - [Stanford Encyclopedia: Epictetus](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epictetus/) — Detailed analysis of Epictetus's life, works, and philosophy
> - [Stanford Encyclopedia: Marcus Aurelius](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/marcus-aurelius/) — Scholarly treatment of Marcus Aurelius's *Meditations* and philosophical contributions
> 
> For further study, the surviving texts themselves remain essential: Epictetus's *Discourses* and *Enchiridion* (translated by Robin Hard or Robert Dobbin), Seneca's *Letters from a Stoic* and *Moral Essays*, and Marcus Aurelius's *Meditations* (Gregory Hays translation recommended for accessibility, Robin Hard for scholarly accuracy). For comprehensive treatment of Stoic physics and logic largely absent from Roman sources, consult A.A. Long and D.N. Sedley's *The Hellenistic Philosophers* (Cambridge, 1987), the standard scholarly collection of fragments and testimonia with commentary.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Research into the neuroscience of journaling demonstrates that writing before sleep helps pre-organize experiences, making the brain's nighttime consolidation work more efficient, with consistent practice decreasing sleep onset time from 45 to approximately 15 minutes while improving self-reflection quality as internal dialogue shifts from harsh self-criticism toward curious and compassionate inquiry. This transformation occurs because regular writing strengthens connections between emotional and rational brain centers, effectively enhancing the prefrontal cortex's regulatory capacity over limbic emotional systems—precisely the neurobiological substrate of what Stoics conceptualized as "rational supremacy over passion."

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The popular synthesis of Dweck's research program, reaching the broad audience and generating the cultural penetration of the growth mindset concept. Primary source for the conventional account in Phase I.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The academic synthesis of Dweck's theoretical framework, providing the most rigorous statement of the implicit theories approach. Essential for understanding the technical distinctions between entity and incremental theories and their proposed effects.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The foundational paper establishing attribution theory's three-dimensional model (locus, stability, controllability) and its predictions for persistence and emotion. The empirical foundation for Axiom 1 of this report.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Large-scale meta-analysis finding that the relationship between mindset and academic achievement is very small (r ≈ .10), and that mindset interventions produce near-zero effects in general populations with potentially meaningful effects only in at-risk populations. Critical evidence against Assumption 6.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The largest preregistered mindset intervention study to date, reporting small but significant effects on challenge-seeking and GPA for lower-achieving students at under-resourced schools. Most favorable recent evidence for targeted mindset effects; used to establish the scope condition for intervention efficacy.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Foundational paper establishing self-efficacy theory and the primacy of mastery experiences as the source of efficacy beliefs. The empirical and theoretical foundation for Axiom 2 of this report.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The paper establishing the learning/performance goal distinction and demonstrating that goal orientation mediates the relationship between ability beliefs and behavioral responses to failure. Critical foundation for Axiom 3.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> A systematic methodological critique finding that the evidence base for mindset theory's core causal claims is significantly weaker than typically presented, identifying issues with operationalization, causal inference, and publication bias. Essential methodological context for the assumption audit.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Clinical Validation**
> Stoic-informed CBT techniques have demonstrated effectiveness for social anxiety, obsessive-compulsive disorder, major depressive disorder, personality disorders, and psychological aspects of stuttering. The neural circuits targeted—particularly those involved in [[Fear-Extinction]], [[Emotional-Regulation]], and [[Executive-Control]]—align with the psychological architecture Stoic practices engage.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The foundational empirical study demonstrating the undermining effect of external rewards on intrinsic motivation. Launched the SDT research programme by challenging behaviourist orthodoxy and establishing the importance of perceived locus of causality.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The first comprehensive theoretical statement of SDT, integrating CET, OIT, and the basic needs framework. Establishes the organismic-integration philosophical architecture and the three-need structure.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The definitive meta-analysis of the undermining effect, examining 128 studies. Finds that expected, tangible, contingent rewards undermine intrinsic motivation; unexpected, non-contingent, verbal rewards do not. Highly influential; also the subject of significant methodological debate (see Cameron & Pierce).

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The most-cited summary of SDT, accessible overview of the six mini-theories and key empirical findings. The best entry point for understanding the conventional SDT framework as intended by its architects.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The foundational paper distinguishing independent and interdependent self-construals and their implications for motivation, cognition, and affect. Essential context for evaluating SDT's cross-cultural universality claims, particularly regarding the autonomy need.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Develops the distinction between need satisfaction and need frustration as partially independent dimensions — a significant internal revision of the original SDT model. Demonstrates that need frustration predicts ill-being beyond what need satisfaction alone explains.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Proposes beneficence as a fourth candidate basic psychological need, independent of the three SDT needs, with empirical evidence for its contribution to well-being. Challenges the completeness claim of the three-need structure.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> Philosophical analysis of the concept of innateness and the evidential standards required to establish that a cognitive or motivational property is biologically grounded rather than universally acquired. Provides the philosophical framework for evaluating SDT's innateness claim rigorously.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The seminal paper in the philosophy of agency distinguishing first-order desires from second-order volitions and locating freedom of will in the alignment between these levels. Provides the philosophical benchmark against which SDT's autonomy construct can be measured — and found to fall short of full self-determination.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> The foundational text of attachment theory, establishing that affiliative bonds are a biological system that shapes developmental trajectories and internal working models. Provides the theoretical grounding for Axiom 4's claim that secure attachment is a precondition for autonomous motivation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The existence of specific comprehension difficulties — readers with intact decoding and impaired situation model construction — constitutes near-conclusive evidence that the received view is wrong about sufficiency. If sentence-level processing were sufficient for situation model construction, this population could not exist. The evidence forces a stronger conclusion than "decoding is necessary but not sufficient": it forces the conclusion that situation model construction is a **qualitatively distinct** cognitive process that requires resources and operations not involved in sentence-level processing, and that automatic bottom-up processing does not, by itself, initiate or sustain those operations.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> Studies on judgment of learning (Nelson & Narens, 1990; Koriat, 1997) demonstrate that readers' confidence in their comprehension is primarily predicted by processing fluency — how easily and smoothly the text was processed — rather than by the actual coherence of the situation model they constructed. This means that readers who construct poor situation models but process the text fluently will systematically rate their own comprehension as high. They will not spontaneously re-read, generate questions, or engage in monitoring strategies precisely because the fluency signal tells them everything is fine. The received view, by implying that fluent sentence-level processing leads to comprehension, reinforces and validates this monitoring failure. It provides a theoretical justification for the fluency illusion rather than a corrective against it.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> Studies consistently demonstrate that prior knowledge about a text's topic predicts situation model quality independently of, and often more strongly than, verbal ability, vocabulary, and reading fluency. Recht and Leslie (1988), in a landmark study, showed that low-verbal students with high baseball knowledge comprehended a baseball passage significantly better than high-verbal students with low baseball knowledge. The situation model — a coherent representation of *what is happening in the described world* — simply cannot be constructed by a reader who lacks the conceptual structures to interpret the events the text describes. This is not a motivational or strategic problem; it is a structural one. Prior knowledge is constitutive of situation model construction, not merely helpful for it.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The foundational source for the three-level model of text representation and the original statement of the situation model construct. Directly supports Phase II's framework section and provides the theoretical basis for the challenges in Phase III. The introduction and Chapter 1 are the most relevant sections for this report's argument.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The primary statement of the Construction-Integration model. Central to Phase IV's alternative framework treatment. This paper provides the mechanistic account of why integration fails and why prior knowledge is constitutive rather than merely facilitative of comprehension.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The full elaboration of the CI model with comprehensive empirical review. The most authoritative synthesis of the alternative framework offered in Phase IV. Chapter 4 on situation models and Chapter 6 on individual differences are most directly relevant.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The original statement of the Event Indexing Model. Provides the empirical basis for the five-dimension structure of situation models; supports the monitoring checklist recommendations in Phase V.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> Comprehensive review of situation model research. Directly supports Phase III's empirical challenge and Phase IV's alternative framework. The review's treatment of the five dimensions and their empirical evidence is the primary source for the Event Indexing Model discussion.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The original statement of the Simple View of Reading. Central to the steel-man construction in Phase I. Should be read to understand the best version of the received view's empirical support before engaging with the challenges.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> Key empirical source for the specific comprehender dissociation. Central to Phase III's empirical challenge. Demonstrates the dissociability of decoding and situation model construction in children.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The original Matthew Effect paper. Supports Phase III's critical lens and Phase VII's PKB connections discussion. Explains the compounding nature of situation model deficits over developmental time.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> A comprehensive review of the inference generation literature. Supports Phase III's empirical challenge regarding the non-automatic nature of elaborative inferences. The review's treatment of inference types and their generation conditions is the primary source for the inference discussion.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The baseball knowledge study. Direct empirical support for the prior-knowledge-as-constitutive claim in Phase III. Demonstrates that topic knowledge overrides verbal ability as a predictor of situation model quality.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> The foundational source for schema theory. Supports the philosophical challenge in Phase III regarding text-self-sufficiency; demonstrates experimentally that comprehension and memory are reconstructive processes that depend on schemas, not extractive processes that depend on texts. [[Frederic-Bartlett]]

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Kintsch and van Dijk (1978) and subsequent researchers showed that readers who were asked "inference questions" (questions requiring integration across text segments or combination with prior knowledge) performed dramatically worse than those asked "textbase questions" (questions answerable from explicit text statements) — but only when readers had read without strategic purpose. Readers given explicit instructions to construct an understanding of "how the described system works" showed dramatically improved inference question performance without losing textbase performance. This finding was replicated by Graesser, Singer, and Trabasso (1994) using longer, more complex texts.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The Kintsch/Graesser line of research consistently shows that the single greatest predictor of situation model quality is not reading ability, domain knowledge, or text difficulty — it is whether the reader is actively engaged in trying to understand *how* and *why*, rather than *what*. This is an orientation effect, not an ability effect. The implication is that most adults who "get lost in details" are not failing due to cognitive limitations; they are failing due to a suboptimal reading orientation that tracks textbase when it should be tracking situational coherence.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Karpicke and Roediger (2008) showed that students who re-read passages consistently rated their comprehension higher than students who attempted free recall of the same passages — yet performed significantly worse on subsequent tests. The re-reading students experienced *fluency* (the text felt easy to process on the second reading) and mistook this processing ease for understanding. The free recall students experienced *difficulty* (they could not retrieve much), which accurately reflected their incomplete situation models.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Maki and colleagues (1994–2000) conducted a series of studies on metacognitive accuracy in reading comprehension — the correlation between students' predicted comprehension and actual test performance. Across studies, the correlation was positive but surprisingly weak (typically around r = 0.30–0.40), particularly for inference questions. Crucially, the lowest metacognitive accuracy was found for students who had read most fluently — they were confident precisely because the reading had felt easy, not because they had built a situation model.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, and Glaser (1994) studied students learning from worked examples in physics. Students who spontaneously explained what they were reading — generating causal accounts, bridging gaps, relating examples to principles — showed dramatically superior performance on transfer tests compared to students who read without self-explaining, even when the latter group spent more time reading. The effect was not about time on task but about the qualitative nature of the processing. Self-explanation forces situation model construction because it requires the reader to produce causal inferences that passive reading does not demand.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Slamecka and Graf's original generation effect experiments showed that words generated by participants (from partial cues) were recalled significantly better than words read passively — even when the generated words were identical to the read words. Subsequent research by Jacoby (1978) and Roediger and colleagues established that the generation advantage extends to conceptual content: generating an explanation, a paraphrase, or an inference produces substantially stronger memory for the underlying concept than reading it passively.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Taken together, the self-explanation, generation effect, and retrieval practice literatures converge on a finding that is simple to state but radical in its implications: situation models cannot be *received*; they can only be *constructed*. The cognitive work required to build a situation model — generating causal inferences, bridging implicit gaps, integrating prior knowledge — is specifically the work that passive reading allows the reader to avoid. This is the deep reason why reading efficiency strategies that reduce cognitive effort during reading (faster reading, skimming, re-reading instead of recalling) consistently produce poor knowledge retention: they are optimizing against the very cognitive load that situation model construction requires.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Recht and Leslie (1988) studied students with high and low baseball knowledge reading a passage about a baseball game. They also divided students by reading ability. The result was stark: high-knowledge readers outperformed low-knowledge readers on comprehension regardless of reading ability. High-knowledge poor readers outperformed low-knowledge good readers. Prior knowledge provided the situational context — the partial situation model — into which text propositions could be placed, allowing high-knowledge readers to construct detailed, coherent models even when their linguistic processing was less efficient.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The definitive presentation of the Construction-Integration model, providing the computational framework for understanding how three levels of text representation are built. Phases II and IV of this report draw heavily on this source.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** The section on situation models (pp. 170–175) is the most directly relevant to this report's analytical framework.
> 
> **Historical Significance:** This paper transformed reading comprehension research from a description-level field into a mechanistically grounded computational science.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The foundational book-length treatment of discourse comprehension strategy, introducing the textbase/situation model distinction in its fully developed form and providing extensive evidence for the three-level architecture.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Chapter 2 (propositional representation), Chapter 5 (situation models), and Chapter 11 (individual differences in comprehension strategy).

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The definitive review of Event Indexing Model research, synthesizing experimental evidence for the five CATSM dimensions. Central to the Phase II framework and the Causal Spine Bottleneck analysis in Phase IV.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** The section on causal dimension tracking (pp. 171–175) is directly relevant to the Causal Spine Bottleneck analysis.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The landmark study establishing the self-explanation effect. Provides the primary empirical basis for the Generation Constraint argument in Phases III and IV.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** The analysis of "good" versus "poor" self-explanations (pp. 163–172) is particularly relevant.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The influential study documenting that retrieval practice (free recall) produces substantially better learning than re-reading, providing the evidence for the Fluency Illusion analysis and the post-reading recall intervention.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> A comprehensive review and theoretical synthesis of inference generation research during reading. Central to the Generation Deficit analysis in Phase IV.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Documents the interaction between prior knowledge and text coherence in situation model construction, providing evidence for the prior knowledge bootstrapping analysis.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The baseball knowledge study demonstrating that domain knowledge overrides reading ability in predicting comprehension performance. Essential evidence for the prior knowledge dimension of situation model construction.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The original generation effect study. Foundational to the generation constraint analysis.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> The original advance organizer study. Provides the empirical basis for the pre-reading frame protocol.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The moderating effect of prior knowledge on EI effectiveness is one of the most robust findings in the strategy literature. Studies consistently show:
> - Participants with domain-relevant knowledge benefit substantially more from EI than those without (Woloshyn et al., 1992; Martin & Pressley, 1991)
> - When learners are asked to elaborate on entirely novel facts (e.g., facts about a fictional African tribe, or made-up biological properties), EI effects are markedly reduced (Wood et al., 1990)
> - When prior knowledge is experimentally provided before EI (e.g., by having learners read a background passage), the EI benefit is partially restored (Pressley et al., 1992)
> - The relationship between prior knowledge and EI benefit is approximately continuous — modest prior knowledge produces modest EI benefits, rich prior knowledge produces rich EI benefits

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The prior knowledge moderator is typically discussed as a "limitation" or "boundary condition" of EI — the implication being that EI works in the normal case but fails when knowledge is absent. This framing is misleading. The more accurate reading of the evidence is that prior knowledge is not limiting an otherwise-functional process; it is a *required input* to the process. You cannot build a situation model without integration anchors, and prior knowledge provides those anchors. The evidence does not show EI becoming *less effective* when prior knowledge is absent — it shows EI becoming *impossible* in its proper sense, because the cognitive operation EI invokes (integration into a situation model) requires materials the learner doesn't have. This is a structural dependency, not a surface moderation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> If elaborative interrogation worked simply by increasing "depth of processing" in a generic sense, we would expect: (a) relatively uniform effects across knowledge levels, (b) relatively similar effects for good and bad "why" questions, and (c) roughly comparable advantages for recall and comprehension. The observed pattern — knowledge-dependent, question-quality-sensitive, comprehension-dominant effects — is precisely what a mechanism specifically targeting situation model construction would predict. The evidence thus provides converging support for the architectural specificity argument developed in Phase IV.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> This foundational study established the basic EI paradigm and demonstrated robust effects of why-question elaboration on both intentional and incidental memory. Critically introduces the manipulation of elaboration precision and the comparison of generated versus provided elaborations.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Experiments 1-3 for the core EI demonstration; Experiment 4 for the generation advantage.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The pivotal prior knowledge moderator study. Systematically manipulated learner background knowledge and demonstrated that EI's advantage over re-reading collapses when prior knowledge is absent. Essential reading for understanding the mechanism argument.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Experiments 1-3 for the prior knowledge manipulation; General Discussion for the theoretical interpretation.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The theoretical foundation from which EI research emerged. Introduces the depth-of-processing framework and the distinction between maintenance and elaborative rehearsal. Essential for understanding why EI is usually described as a "deep processing" strategy — and why that description requires upgrading.
> 
> **Historical Significance:** One of the most cited papers in cognitive psychology; initiated decades of research on encoding processes and replaced the structural models of memory with a processing-oriented framework.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The source of the three-level text representation model (surface form, textbase, situation model) that serves as the primary analytical framework in this report. The situation model / textbase distinction is the architectural foundation of the Comprehension Gateway Mechanism.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Chapters 3-5 for the theoretical architecture; Chapter 6 for the empirical grounding of the situation model construct.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The definitive statement of Kintsch's construction-integration model. Refines the three-level model extensively and provides the computational/process-level account of how situation models are constructed during reading.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The most comprehensive meta-analytic review of learning strategies. Rates EI as moderate utility, identifies the prior knowledge moderator as a key limitation, and situates EI within the broader strategy landscape. Essential for understanding EI's position relative to retrieval practice, distributed practice, and other high-utility strategies.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Section 3.2 on elaborative interrogation; the General Discussion for practical implications.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The foundational generation effect paper. Demonstrates that self-generated items are remembered better than read items across a variety of paradigms. Provides the theoretical backdrop for the EI generation advantage discussed in Phase III.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> The canonical statement of the desirable difficulties framework. Establishes that conditions that impair performance during acquisition often enhance long-term retention — the theoretical context in which EI's cognitive demand is understood as beneficial rather than merely taxing.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Extension of the EI research program to older children. Documents the generation advantage and provides evidence that EI's mechanism requires the active construction of causal connections, not merely the provision of additional information about the topic.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Directly demonstrates that EI effect magnitude varies with question type — a finding that presages the Dual Register Diagnostic. Questions requiring genuine causal reasoning produce larger effects than questions that can be answered by paraphrase or text retrieval.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. J. (1974).** Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), *The psychology of learning and motivation* (Vol. 8, pp. 47–89). Academic Press. — The founding paper of the multicomponent working memory model. Presents the dual-task experiments that challenged the unitary short-term memory concept and proposed the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Baddeley, A. D. (2000).** The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory? *Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4*(11), 417–423. — The paper introducing the episodic buffer as the fourth component of the model, motivating its theoretical necessity through empirical anomalies and connecting it to conscious awareness and episodic long-term memory.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Baddeley, A. D. (2012).** Working memory: Theories, models, and controversies. *Annual Review of Psychology, 63*, 1–29. — Baddeley's comprehensive review of the model's development, empirical status, and major theoretical controversies, including the competing models of Cowan and Ericsson; considered the definitive statement of the mature version of the theory.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Cowan, N. (2001).** The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. *Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24*(1), 87–114. — The primary statement of Cowan's embedded-processes model and his ~4-chunk capacity estimate for the focus of attention, challenging important assumptions of the Baddeley-Hitch model.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Miyake, A., Friedman, N. P., Emerson, M. J., Witzki, A. H., Howerter, A., & Wager, T. D. (2000).** The unity and diversity of executive functions and their contributions to complex "frontal lobe" tasks: A latent variable analysis. *Cognitive Psychology, 41*, 49–100. — The landmark latent variable study that fractionated executive functions into shifting, updating, and inhibition, providing a principled decomposition of Baddeley's central executive.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Sweller, J. (1988).** Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. *Cognitive Science, 12*, 257–285. — The founding paper of [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], explicitly drawing on Baddeley's working memory architecture to explain why problem-solving is often an inefficient instructional method compared to worked examples.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Mayer, R. E. (2009).** *Multimedia learning* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. — The comprehensive statement of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning with its twelve design principles, evidence base, moderating variables, and connections to Baddeley's working memory architecture.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980).** Individual differences in working memory and reading. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19*, 450–466. — The introduction of the Reading Span task and the first demonstration of the strong predictive relationship between working memory capacity and reading comprehension, launching the individual differences research programme.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Gathercole, S. E., & Alloway, T. P. (2008).** *Working memory and learning: A practical guide for teachers*. SAGE. — Applied translation of working memory research for educational practitioners, covering working memory assessment, implications for children with learning difficulties, and classroom strategies for working memory support.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Melby-Lervåg, M., & Hulme, C. (2013).** Is working memory training effective? A meta-analytic review. *Developmental Psychology, 49*(2), 270–291. — The most comprehensive meta-analysis of working memory training effects, finding robust near-transfer but no reliable far-transfer, significantly tempering earlier optimism about training-based cognitive enhancement.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Logie, R. H. (1995).** *Visuo-spatial working memory*. Erlbaum. — The primary statement of the distinction between visual cache and inner scribe within the visuospatial sketchpad, providing theoretical refinement and neuropsychological evidence for the sketchpad's internal architecture.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Norman, D. A., & Shallice, T. (1986).** Attention to action: Willed and automatic control of behavior. In R. J. Davidson, G. E. Schwartz, & D. Shapiro (Eds.), *Consciousness and self-regulation* (Vol. 4, pp. 1–18). Plenum. — The foundational paper for the Supervisory Attentional System (SAS), which Baddeley adopted as the theoretical model of the central executive.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Engle, R. W., Tuholski, S. W., Laughlin, J. E., & Conway, A. R. A. (1999).** Working memory, short-term memory, and general fluid intelligence: A latent-variable approach. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 128*(3), 309–331. — The latent variable study demonstrating that complex span (working memory capacity) and simple span are separable constructs, and that working memory capacity uniquely predicts fluid intelligence beyond short-term memory.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The foundational paper introducing the propositional theory of text comprehension that became the CI model. Introduces the textbase concept and the analysis of macro-structure construction. This report's theoretical core.
> **Recommended section:** Entire paper for foundations; Section 2 on macro-structure most directly relevant to academic reading.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The paper introducing the Construction-Integration model's two-phase cycle. Essential reading for understanding the spreading activation and constraint satisfaction mechanisms discussed throughout this report.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The original reciprocal teaching study, reporting both the theoretical rationale and the first experimental evidence. Effect sizes were large; this paper launched three decades of reciprocal teaching research and replication.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The definitive reference on vocabulary acquisition for reading comprehension, including the coverage threshold research establishing 98% as the functional minimum for adequate comprehension. Directly informs the vocabulary section of this report.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The primary reference for the Tier 1/2/3 vocabulary framework used throughout this report. Provides both theoretical framework and practical instructional guidance for academic vocabulary development.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The foundational study demonstrating large effects of self-explanation during text reading on comprehension and learning. The mechanism is identified as forced situation model construction through inference generation. Directly informs Section 6.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The seminal theoretical account of cumulative advantage and disadvantage in reading development. The Matthew Effect metaphor (from Matthew 25:29) is introduced here. This paper's influence on reading research has been enormous and continues to shape intervention priorities.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** Short theoretical paper introducing the metacognition construct in its mature form. Defines metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation in terms that remain standard. Critical background for this report's metacognition sections.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** Introduces the five-dimensional Event-Indexing Model of situation model construction. Compact paper with large empirical and theoretical impact. Informs Section 5 on inference generation and situation model dimensions.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** Accessible and elegant account of why background knowledge is the most powerful lever in reading comprehension development. Argues that reading comprehension "skill" is substantially a knowledge issue. Widely assigned in teacher education; directly relevant to the knowledge-building debate (Section 7).

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The key theoretical chapter developing modern schema theory as a computational-cognitive framework. Defines schemas, explains their activation and inheritance properties, and articulates the schema theory account of reading comprehension. Essential background for Section 4.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** Comprehensive synthesis of Ann Brown's metacognitive monitoring research in the context of reading comprehension. Key reference for the comprehension monitoring and self-regulation sections.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Annotation:** The constructionist theory paper distinguishing coherence from elaborative inferences and characterising the conditions under which each is generated. Informs Section 5's inference generation analysis.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The foundational review establishing schema theory as the dominant framework for reading comprehension research. Demonstrates comprehensively the relationship between prior knowledge and comprehension quality. Central framework for Section 6.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The foundational empirical demonstration that memory and comprehension are schema-driven and constructive, not reproductive. His cross-cultural folk tale experiments remain compelling evidence for schema-driven comprehension distortion.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The landmark study establishing the self-explanation effect. Documented that students who spontaneously self-explained during learning dramatically outperformed those who did not, launching a productive research program on elaborative learning strategies. Central to Section 5.3.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The most authoritative systematic review of the evidence base for learning strategies, classifying 10 techniques by utility based on literature review. Establishes retrieval practice and elaborative interrogation as high-utility strategies; re-reading and highlighting as low-utility. Essential practical reference for Section 5.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The definitive statement of the metacognition framework introducing the distinction between metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive experiences, and identifying metacognitive monitoring as a critical self-regulatory process. Foundational for Section 3.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* Kintsch's landmark theoretical paper articulating the Construction-Integration model and establishing the theoretical distinction between textbase and situation model construction. The foundational text for the entire multi-level comprehension framework discussed in Section 1.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* Establishes the monitoring-control framework that provides the formal computational model for metacognitive processes during reading and learning. Essential theoretical infrastructure for Section 3.2.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* The founding paper of Reciprocal Teaching, documenting the design rationale and initial research evidence for the four-strategy collaborative reading protocol. The most frequently cited paper in reading comprehension instruction research. Essential for Section 7.2.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* Landmark experimental demonstration of the testing effect showing that retrieval practice dramatically outperforms re-study for long-term retention, even when initial learning is equated. Central evidence for the strategy hierarchy in Section 5.4.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> *Annotation:* Establishes the three-phase self-regulated learning model (forethought, performance, self-reflection) that frames the metacognitive architecture of self-directed academic reading in Section 7.4.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> The foundational mechanistic analysis of elaborative interrogation, distinguishing EI from analogical encoding and specifying the conditions under which each produces learning advantages. Establishes the accuracy constraint and the distinctiveness hypothesis as central mechanisms. Essential primary source for Phase IV's mechanism analysis.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** The discussion section provides the most theoretically precise mechanistic account; the results section documents the prior knowledge moderation effect.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> One of the foundational studies establishing the EI effect for factual propositions. Documents the generation advantage (self-generated elaborations > read elaborations) and provides the initial framework for EI as a learnable study strategy.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** Experiment 2 provides the most direct test of the generation component; the general discussion situates EI within the elaborative strategies literature.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Directly addresses the prior knowledge moderator using cross-cultural comparisons (Canadian and German students studying German history and geography). Establishes that prior knowledge availability is the primary determinant of EI effectiveness, not learner age or general strategy knowledge.
> 
> **Recommended Sections:** The cross-cultural comparisons in Experiment 3 are particularly illuminating for the prior knowledge moderator; the discussion provides the clearest statement of the prior knowledge threshold problem.

> [!evidence] Supporting Evidence *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> The most comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation of ten major learning strategies, rating EI as "moderate utility." Provides the comparative framework situating EI relative to retrieval practice, distributed practice, self-explanation, and lower-utility strategies.
