> **The Stoic Reading**: This is not passive acceptance. Marcus continued to make decisions, to correct where correction was possible, to hold people accountable to their obligations. What Stoic practice prevented was the contamination of his judgment by resentment — the degradation of his own character that would follow from treating his frustrations as license for cruelty or unfairness.
> 
> **The Lesson**: The Meditations are a record of someone who genuinely practiced this. The practice did not produce a person who never felt frustration; it produced a person who could feel frustration and continue to act with justice and generosity anyway.

> [!example] **Untitled** *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Case: Navigating a Chronic Relational Difficulty**
> 
> **The Situation**: An adult child navigating a parent whose behavior is consistently undermining, delivered without apparent self-awareness.
> 
> **The Stoic Analysis**:
> 
> First — the *Dichotomy of Control*. Her father's behavior is not in her control. His character was formed over eight decades; she did not produce it and cannot now fundamentally alter it. What *is* within her control: her interpretation of his comments, her emotional response to them, what she chooses to say in reply, how long she remains in the conversation, and whether she allows his assessment of her choices to contaminate her own self-assessment.
> 
> Second — the *involuntary error principle*. Why does her father behave as he does? Most likely: he was raised in a cultural context where parental authority was expressed through critique rather than affirmation; he genuinely believes he is helping; he may be experiencing anxiety about his own diminishing influence and relevance, which his criticism is a distorted attempt to manage. None of this excuses the behavior. All of it makes it comprehensible — and comprehension is the prerequisite for a response that is proportionate and useful rather than reactive and escalating.
> 
> Third — the *kathêkon*. What does the role of an adult child genuinely require? Honesty when honesty serves connection. Patience with the limitations of an elderly person. Setting appropriate limits on interactions that have become destructive. Not requiring the relationship to be other than it is.
> 
> **The Response**: Mara can choose to gently name the pattern once ("Dad, when you say things like that, I notice it makes me want to avoid talking to you about what matters to me, which isn't what I want"). She can choose to not defend her decisions — because their worth is not determined by his assessment. She can choose a brief, kind response and then change the subject. She can choose to reduce the topics she raises.
> 
> **The Lesson**: None of this makes the relationship what she wished it were. Stoicism does not promise relational transformation. It offers something more reliably available: the capacity to engage with a difficult relationship without being diminished by it — to maintain one's own character and one's own self-assessment independent of whether the other person changes.

> [!example] **Untitled** *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Case: Virtue-Based Friendship in Action**
> 
> **The Situation**: A philosopher corresponding with a student/friend over several years on the deepest questions of how to live.
> 
> **The Distinctive Features**: The friendship Seneca enacts with Lucilius is characterized by several qualities that Stoic philosophy mandates: absolute honesty (Seneca does not flatter, and he does not hide his own failings); genuine concern for Lucilius's flourishing rather than his happiness (Seneca challenges Lucilius when challenge is what growth requires, not merely when it is comfortable); recognition of their shared enterprise (both are making their way toward wisdom, and the friendship is animated by this shared direction); and absence of utility calculation (Seneca does not present the friendship as useful to either party — its value is intrinsic, located in the mutual recognition of two people genuinely trying to live well).
> 
> **The Lesson**: Stoic friendship is not cold or theoretical. The letters pulse with genuine affection, humor, and the particular pleasure of intellectual companionship. What Stoicism adds to ordinary affection is an orientation: the best thing you can do for someone you love is to be honest with them, to take their growth seriously, and to relate to them as the rational and capable being they are rather than as a source of your emotional needs.

> [!example] **Untitled** *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Case: Seneca's Meditatio Paupertatis in Practice**
> 
> **The Situation**: In Letter XVIII of the *Epistulae Morales*, Seneca describes his practice of periodic voluntary simplicity, written with the self-aware irony of a very rich man telling a friend to be poor sometimes. He describes setting aside several days to live on minimal rations — coarse bread, water, no comfortable bed — not as penance but as philosophical calibration. "I am not setting this before you as a rule," he writes, "but as a test. Lay aside for a few days your usual comforts, and let yourself discover whether poverty frightens you as much as your habits have led you to believe."
> 
> **The Stoic Reading**: Seneca is not advocating permanent asceticism. He continues to live in considerable comfort for the rest of the year. What the periodic poverty accomplishes is twofold. First, it provides an empirical test of a philosophical claim: that one's genuine wellbeing does not depend on one's material standard of living. The test is designed to be failed (if poverty turns out to be as devastating as feared) or passed (if it turns out, as Seneca believed, that the fear of poverty was more painful than poverty itself). Second, it recalibrates appreciation: after several days on bread and water, the ordinary meals that Seneca returned to were experienced, he reports, with genuine gratitude rather than as mere background entitlements. Negative visualization (addressed elsewhere in the series — see [[Stoicism-in-Practice-Daily-Exercises-and-Mindset-Shifts]]) operates cognitively; meditatio paupertatis operates experientially.
> 
> **The Lesson**: The practice demonstrates that the felt sense of sufficiency — of having enough — is not a fixed quantity determined by one's material circumstances but a calibratable psychological state that can be maintained at a wide range of income levels through appropriate philosophical practice. The person who practices periodic simplicity is less vulnerable to the anxiety of potential loss, more capable of genuine appreciation for what they have, and less driven by the compulsive acquisition that the fear of insufficiency generates.

> [!example] **Untitled** *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Case: Marcus Aurelius — Simplicity Under the Purple**
> 
> **The Situation**: The *Meditations* were not written for publication. They are private philosophical exercises — reminders that Marcus wrote to himself during military campaigns, composed in the awareness that the emperor's life offered every opportunity for corruption through excess. He notes his own tendencies toward pleasure in food, entertainment, and ease with the clinical detachment of a physician monitoring symptoms. He reminds himself, repeatedly, that his role is to govern justly, that the purple robe does not change the nature of the man wearing it, and that the goods of power and wealth are real but of no ultimate significance.
> 
> **The Stoic Reading**: What Marcus practices is not the renunciation of imperial comfort but what we might call the psychological non-identification with it. He uses his position's resources as tools for governance and the common good while refusing to let his identity, his security, or his happiness become anchored to them. This is precisely the Stoic preferred indifferents doctrine applied to life at the extreme of material abundance: "I have all this, and I know it is not what I am." This stance, maintained across decades under the continuous pressure of absolute power, is perhaps the most demanding form of Stoic simplicity — not the simplicity of the person who lacks temptation because they lack resources, but the simplicity of the person who has every material good available and chooses daily to hold them as instruments rather than as the substance of a good life.
> 
> **The Lesson**: Stoic minimalism is equally applicable at every income level because its target is not the quantity of goods possessed but the quality of the relationship to possession. The millionaire who holds their wealth as a preferred indifferent is, in Stoic terms, living more simply than the person of modest means who is chronically anxious about the possibility of poverty and whose wellbeing is contingent on maintaining their financial position. The psychological discipline, not the material condition, determines the quality of the Stoic life.

> [!example] **Untitled** *(from [[stoicism-codebase-pack]])*
> **Case: Voluntary Simplicity in Contemporary Life**
> 
> **The Situation**: Potts's argument — developed without direct reference to Stoicism but with remarkable convergence — is that most people are time-poor and thing-rich in a way that inverts the actual conditions of a good life. The things that constitute genuine wellbeing (deep engagement with meaningful activities, rich relationships, the experience of novelty and growth) are time-intensive and materially cheap. The things that modern culture treats as constitutive of success (large homes, new vehicles, luxury goods) are materially expensive and time-consuming to maintain, and their wellbeing returns are subject to rapid hedonic adaptation. His prescription — reduce material complexity to create temporal and psychological space for intrinsically meaningful activity — is structurally identical to the Stoic framework.
> 
> **The Stoic Reading**: What Potts describes as a practical lifestyle discovery, the Stoics articulated as philosophical argument backed by psychological reasoning: the confusion between the instruments of a good life and its substance is the primary generator of both unnecessary suffering and the compulsive accumulation that crowds out genuine wellbeing. The [[Discipline-of-Desire]] directed toward what self-determination theorists call intrinsic goods — meaningful experience, competence, authentic connection — rather than toward the material goods that generate hedonic adaptation, is the practical expression of the Stoic preferred indifferents doctrine.
> 
> **The Lesson**: The Stoic framework gives contemporary minimalism its deepest philosophical grounding. The minimalist practices most people find most valuable — owning fewer but better-considered possessions, creating space for meaningful activity rather than maintenance of complexity, evaluating purchases by contribution to genuine wellbeing rather than by hedonic anticipation — are implementations of the Stoic philosophical position that only [[Virtue-Ethics|virtue and reason-aligned activity]] constitute genuine goods, and that material goods beyond sufficiency should be evaluated by whether they serve or undermine those genuine goods.

> [!example] **The Cascade in Concrete Terms** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Imagine reading a cognitive psychology chapter on the relationship between working memory capacity and reading comprehension. The text presents: (1) working memory capacity research, (2) reading comprehension research, (3) a correlation finding, (4) a proposal about the mechanism. A reader in the failure cascade will successfully build a textbase: "Working memory capacity correlates with reading comprehension. The mechanism might involve..." But the situation model requires the reader to actively generate: *Why* would working memory capacity matter for reading comprehension specifically? *What is the actual process by which WM supports comprehension?* *What would this mean for how to help low-WM readers?* These are inference questions. The cascade reader never asks them. They finish the chapter able to recall the correlation finding and unable to explain anything about the underlying process.

> [!example] **The Working Memory in Arithmetic** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> Consider mental arithmetic: 37 × 8. To solve this, you must hold "37" and "8" in mind simultaneously, retrieve multiplication facts from [[Long-Term-Memory]], compute 30 × 8 = 240 while holding this partial result, then compute 7 × 8 = 56 while retaining 240, then add 240 + 56 = 296 while holding both results. This task demands not just passive storage but active coordination between temporary storage buffers and an attentional-executive controller that sequences operations, retrieves long-term knowledge, and integrates partial results. A single unitary buffer cannot explain the distinct functional demands of holding partial results versus executing retrieval and computation operations.

> [!example] **Phonological Loop in Language Learning** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> The phonological loop's role in foreign language acquisition illustrates its developmental importance. When learning a new word in a second language, the learner must temporarily hold the phonological form of the new word in the phonological store long enough to establish a stable long-term phonological representation. Research by Papagno, Valentine, and Baddeley demonstrated that patients with articulatory suppression showed dramatically impaired foreign vocabulary learning but relatively normal first-language associative learning. Children with good phonological working memory show superior foreign language acquisition. This suggests that the phonological loop is not merely a temporary storage mechanism but plays a critical role in establishing long-term [[Declarative-Memory]] representations for novel phonological forms — bridging the gap between temporary storage and permanent linguistic knowledge.

> [!example] **The Visuospatial Sketchpad in Navigation and Design** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> Consider a familiar example: mentally navigating from your home to a local landmark without physically moving. To perform this task, you must maintain and update a spatial representation of your environment, tracking your simulated position relative to landmarks, turns, and distances. This task draws heavily on the inner scribe component of the visuospatial sketchpad. Now consider a different task: imaging what your friend's face looks like when she is laughing. This task invokes the visual object cache rather than the inner scribe. The fact that an experienced navigator can simultaneously recall a facial expression while planning a route (with some mutual cost) is consistent with the partial independence of the visual and spatial sub-components: they share the broader attentional resources of the [[Central-Executive]] but have some degree of independent storage capacity.

> [!example] **The Central Executive Under Cognitive Overload** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> Consider the experience of attempting to follow a complex lecture while simultaneously taking detailed notes. Note-taking loads the phonological loop (processing the lecturer's speech) and the motor system (producing written output). The central executive must simultaneously monitor comprehension (flagging gaps or contradictions), decide which information is worth recording, coordinate the allocation of attention between listening and writing, and retrieve relevant prior knowledge to contextualize new information. When the lecture becomes too information-dense, the central executive cannot simultaneously manage all these demands. A common result is that note-taking degrades — the learner shifts to near-verbatim transcription (minimizing executive involvement) or comprehension monitoring fails as full attention is devoted to the act of writing. This experience of "losing the thread while writing furiously" is precisely the kind of central executive overload that the working memory model predicts from its architecture.

> [!example] **The Episodic Buffer in Reading Comprehension** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> Consider reading a complex passage describing a spatial scene: "The large oak table occupied the center of the room. To the left, three arched windows admitted afternoon light. Against the far wall, an oak bookcase reached the ceiling, its lower shelves crowded with thick volumes. A figure in a blue coat stood before it, reading." Comprehending this passage and holding its content in mind requires more than either the phonological loop (which stores the sounds of the words) or the visuospatial sketchpad (which maintains spatial images) can accomplish individually. The integrated scene — including spatial layout, lighting quality, the human figure, and the narrative implication of someone reading from the bookcase — requires the episodic buffer's ability to temporarily bind phonological, visual, spatial, and semantic information into a unified situational representation. This is the construct of the [[Mental-Model|situation model]] in text comprehension research, and the episodic buffer provides its working memory foundation.

> [!example] **The Split-Attention Effect in Chemistry Instruction** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> A chemistry textbook presents a diagram of a molecular structure on one page and its accompanying explanation on the facing page. A student must look back and forth between the diagram and the text, using working memory to maintain the partial diagram while reading the explanation, then reverting to the diagram to verify understanding. This split-attention configuration imposes extraneous cognitive load because the mental integration of diagram and text competes with the learning of the chemistry itself. CLT-based redesign would embed the explanatory text directly in the diagram, or present the labeled diagram as a single integrated source, eliminating the need for working-memory-intensive mental integration. The [[Split-Attention-Effect]] predicts that the integrated-format group will learn more from the same content because their working memory executive resources are freed for schema construction rather than format integration.

> [!example] **The Matthew Effect in a University Cohort** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> Consider two students entering a biology degree programme. Student A has read extensively about science during secondary school — popular science books, science journalism, Wikipedia-level biology — accumulating broad domain vocabulary and conceptual schema. Student B has read minimally, despite equivalent intelligence, arriving with standard curriculum biology exposure only. In the first semester, Student A reads a cell biology textbook with 70% of its vocabulary already in their mental lexicon; Student B encounters 50% unfamiliar vocabulary per page. Student A's comprehension proceeds fluently; Student B's comprehension is effortful, slow, and less complete. Student A learns from reading; Student B reads without learning. By year two, the knowledge gap has widened substantially, and the difference is mistaken for a difference in intelligence or ability.

> [!example] **The Coxhead Academic Word List in Practice** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> Consider the word *reiterate*. A student who knows it means "to say again" has Tier 1 recognition. A student who knows it in academic prose typically signals that an author is emphasising a point they consider at risk of being misread, and that the re-statement typically carries a slight shift in emphasis or register from the original, has deep Tier 2 knowledge. The first student reads the paragraph and moves on; the second student pauses to consider *why* the author chose to re-emphasise at this juncture — a metacognitive act embedded in vocabulary depth.

> [!example] **Bridging Inference Failure in Academic Reading** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> A developing reader encounters: "Critics argued that the methodology confounded self-selection with treatment effects. Subsequent meta-analyses revealed effect sizes substantially below initial estimates." A skilled academic reader immediately generates the implicit bridge: the confounding undermined causal inference, inflating effect sizes, which meta-analysis corrected by aggregating better-controlled studies. A developing reader without the methodological schema for confounding and selection bias reads two facts without a connecting argument — the passage yields a textbase but not a situation model.
> 
> **Teaching implication:** Explicit instruction in the typical inferential structures of academic genres — what kinds of inferences different academic text types routinely require — is as important as vocabulary instruction and schema activation.

> [!example] **Reciprocal Teaching in an Academic Text Context** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> A group of university students reads a challenging economics paper. The "teacher" for that passage asks a prediction: "Based on the section heading *Adverse Selection in Insurance Markets*, what do you expect the argument to claim?" Students generate predictions drawing on prior knowledge schemas. During reading, strategy roles rotate: the questioner asks "What assumption does the author make about information symmetry?" The clarifier notes: "I don't know what 'moral hazard' means in this context." The summariser synthesises: "So the argument is that when buyers know more than sellers, markets can fail — this is what the author means by market failure."
> 
> This four-strategy cycle makes situation model construction a *visible, social, strategic* process rather than a solitary, invisible, tacit one.




































## Spaced Repetition Seeds

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three levels of text representation in van Dijk & Kintsch's model, and which one constitutes genuine comprehension?
> 
> **A:** Surface code (exact wording, fades rapidly), propositional text base (explicit semantic content, supports recognition), and situation model (mental representation of the described world, supports inference and application). The situation model is the gold standard — the level at which genuine, transferable comprehension occurs.
> 
> **Source:** Phase II, Perspectival Framework
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Type:** Definition
> **Tags:** #situation-model #reading-comprehension #van-Dijk-Kintsch

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2
> **A:** **Q:** What are the five dimensions of the Event Indexing Model, and why do they matter for reading?
> 
> **A:** Temporal (when), spatial (where), causal (why), intentional (what agents are trying to achieve), and entity (who and their current state). Skilled readers continuously monitor all five dimensions as they read, updating their situation model when any shifts. The dimensions matter because situation model failure often maps to failure in a *specific* dimension — naming the dimension of confusion allows targeted intervention rather than indiscriminate re-reading.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Event Indexing Model
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Definition
> **Tags:** #situation-model #event-indexing-model #reading-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Automatic-Assembly Fallacy, and what evidence falsifies it in reading comprehension?
> 
> **A:** The Automatic-Assembly Fallacy is the mistaken belief that adequate processing at a lower level automatically produces coherent integration at a higher level. In reading, it is the belief that understanding sentences automatically produces a coherent situation model. It is falsified by the specific comprehender dissociation: readers with intact word-level decoding and sentence-level processing who nevertheless construct severely impaired situation models. If the automatic-assembly claim were correct, this population could not exist.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Reconstructive Synthesis
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Distinction
> **Tags:** #automatic-assembly-fallacy #situation-model #specific-comprehenders

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4
> **A:** **Q:** Why is the fluency illusion a monitoring failure, and why does the received view reinforce rather than correct it?
> 
> **A:** The fluency illusion is a monitoring failure because smooth, effortless processing of surface code and text base generates subjective comprehension confidence that does not accurately reflect situation model quality. Readers feel like they understand when they don't, because the processing that produces the fluency feeling (decoding, syntactic parsing, local semantic integration) succeeds even when situation model construction fails. The received view reinforces it by teaching readers that fluent sentence-level processing is the goal — which validates the fluency signal as a comprehension indicator rather than flagging it as a potentially misleading proxy.
> 
> **Source:** Phase III, Practical Challenge
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #fluency-illusion #metacognitive-monitoring #text-base-trap

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5
> **A:** **Q:** How does the received view survive dialectical scrutiny, and what specifically does it claim that proves false?
> 
> **A:** What survives: decoding automaticity is necessary for proficient reading, frees working memory for higher-level processing, and is the binding constraint for early readers and those with genuine decoding deficits. What collapses: the claim that comprehension of the whole follows automatically from comprehension of the parts — the Automatic-Assembly Fallacy. Decoding is necessary but not sufficient; situation model construction requires dedicated inference-generation and model-monitoring operations not derived from sentence-level processing.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Survival Assessment
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Distinction
> **Tags:** #simple-view-of-reading #situation-model #reconstruction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6
> **A:** **Q:** What does the Recht & Leslie (1988) baseball study demonstrate about prior knowledge in reading comprehension?
> 
> **A:** It demonstrates that topic-relevant prior knowledge predicts situation model quality more strongly than verbal ability. Low-verbal students with high baseball knowledge comprehended a baseball passage significantly better than high-verbal students with low baseball knowledge. This supports the claim that prior knowledge is constitutive of situation model construction — not merely helpful but necessary for executing the inferential operations that bridge the text base to a coherent world-representation.
> 
> **Source:** Phase III, Critical Challenge
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Application
> **Tags:** #prior-knowledge #situation-model #matthew-effect

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Text-Base Trap, and why is it "stable"?
> 
> **A:** The Text-Base Trap is a stable cognitive equilibrium in which a reader successfully processes the propositional text base, experiences processing fluency, interprets that fluency as comprehension, and therefore generates no monitoring responses that would initiate the additional operations required for situation model construction. It is stable because it produces no negative feedback signal — the reader feels fine, the text is processing smoothly, and there is no phenomenological marker for the absence of a situation model. It persists until an external comprehension test specifically targeting the situation model reveals the gap.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Reconstructive Synthesis
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #text-base-trap #fluency-illusion #metacognitive-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Construction-Integration model's account of why poor situation models form?
> 
> **A:** In the CI model, comprehension proceeds through cycling construction phases (building a network of propositions from text plus activated prior knowledge) and integration phases (refining the network through spreading activation to produce coherence). Poor situation models form when the integration phase fails — when the spreading-activation convergence that should produce a coherent situation model does not reach a coherent outcome. This failure is most commonly caused by inadequate prior knowledge (insufficient integration constraints) or failure to generate the elaborative inferences that bridge propositions to a world-representation.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Alternative Framework 1
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #construction-integration #situation-model #inference-generation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Automatic-Assembly Fallacy transfer to software architecture?
> 
> **A:** In software engineering, individually well-written functions do not automatically produce well-designed system architecture. Architecture requires dedicated architectural attention — a global-level perspective that cannot be derived from reviewing each function in isolation. An engineer who checks each function for correctness and concludes the system is well-designed is committing the Automatic-Assembly Fallacy. The transfer encoding: satisfaction with local quality (clean functions, correct syntax) should always be accompanied by a dedicated global-coherence check (separation of concerns, dependency structure, maintainability).
> 
> **Source:** Phase VI, FAR Transfer
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Connection
> **Tags:** #automatic-assembly-fallacy #far-transfer #software-architecture

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10
> **A:** **Q:** What specific monitoring practice does the reconstructed understanding recommend that the received view never recommends?
> 
> **A:** The reconstructed understanding requires situation-model-level monitoring even in the *absence* of confusion — a proactive global coherence check that does not wait for a negative monitoring signal. Specifically: periodically closing or looking away from the text and attempting to reconstruct the situation model (who is involved, what is happening, why it is happening, how it is happening, and where/when it takes place). This is the opposite of the received view's implicit guidance, which treats the absence of confusion as evidence of comprehension. The metacognitive inversion required: felt comprehension (fluency) is evidence of text-base success, not situation model success.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Metacognitive Inversion section
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Application
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-monitoring #situation-model #reading-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between a textbase and a situation model?
> 
> **A:** A textbase is a propositional representation of *what the text said* — the ideas expressed in the text, stripped of their exact wording. A situation model is a representation of *what the text is about* — the state of affairs, system, or argument described, integrated with prior knowledge. The textbase represents the text; the situation model represents the world the text describes.
> 
> **Source:** Phase II, Three-Level Architecture
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Type:** Distinction
> **Tags:** #situation-model #textbase #reading-comprehension

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What are the five dimensions of the Event Indexing Model (CATSM), and which is most vulnerable to disruption in academic expository text?
> 
> **A:** Causality, Agency, Time, Space, Motivation. Causality is most vulnerable in academic text because causal relations are frequently implicit — the text presents X and Y without explicitly marking the causal connection, requiring the reader to generate bridging inferences using prior knowledge. When prior knowledge is insufficient, the causal dimension collapses, disrupting all other dimensions.
> 
> **Source:** Phase II, Event Indexing Model; Phase IV, Mechanism 3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #CATSM #event-indexing-model #causal-inference #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Fluency Illusion, and why is it specifically dangerous for situation model construction?
> 
> **A:** The Fluency Illusion is the metacognitive error in which ease of processing (fluency) is mistaken for depth of understanding. It is specifically dangerous for situation model construction because it produces a false comprehension signal that terminates comprehension effort before the situation model is built. A reader can fluently build a textbase, experience the ease of processing as understanding, and never engage the active inference generation that situation model construction requires.
> 
> **Source:** Phase III, Evidence Area 2; Phase IV, Mechanism 2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Definition
> **Tags:** #fluency-illusion #textbase-trap #metacognition #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What distinguishes comprehension failure from the Textbase Trap from comprehension failure from cognitive overload?
> 
> **A:** Cognitive overload failure (Mechanism 1) is experienced as difficulty — the reader knows they are struggling. The Textbase Trap (Mechanism 2) is experienced as confidence — the reader feels they understood. This is the critical diagnostic distinction: a reader who feels confused after reading may have an overload problem; a reader who feels confident but cannot answer inference questions has a Textbase Trap problem. The Textbase Trap produces "confident incomprehension."
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Mechanisms 1 and 2
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Distinction
> **Tags:** #textbase-trap #cognitive-load #comprehension-failure #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Generation Constraint on situation model construction?
> 
> **A:** The Generation Constraint states that situation models cannot be received through passive reading — they can only be produced through active construction. The cognitive work of generating causal inferences, bridging implicit gaps, and integrating prior knowledge is specifically the work that passive reading allows readers to avoid. This is why re-reading fails to repair comprehension and why post-reading free recall significantly outperforms re-reading for retention: retrieval practice forces the generative work that passive reading bypasses.
> 
> **Source:** Phase III, Evidence Area 3; Phase IV, Mechanism 4
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #generation-effect #generation-constraint #active-reading #retrieval-practice

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Frame-Before-Fill Asymmetry, and what practical reading intervention does it most directly support?
> 
> **A:** The Frame-Before-Fill Asymmetry states that situation model construction is directionally one-way: a structural frame can accept and organize details, but an accumulation of unframed details cannot generate a structural frame. This directly supports pre-reading scaffolding as a prerequisite (not merely a helpful addition) to content reading. Scanning structure, writing a prediction sentence, and formulating a purpose question before reading build the partial structural frame into which content-level propositions can attach. Without this frame, proposition accumulation produces a textbase but not a situation model.
> 
> **Source:** Phase VI, Original Synthesis; Phase V, Practical Applications
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Application
> **Tags:** #frame-before-fill #advance-organizer #pre-reading #situation-model-construction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the generation effect in memory research (Slamecka & Graf, 1978) relate to the self-explanation effect in reading comprehension (Chi et al., 1989)?
> 
> **A:** Both establish the same structural principle — the Generation Constraint — from different methodological directions. Slamecka & Graf showed that words actively generated by participants were remembered better than identical words passively read, demonstrating the memory advantage of active production over passive reception. Chi et al. showed that students who explained worked examples during study — generating causal accounts rather than reading passively — built substantially better knowledge representations. Both converge on the claim that generation (producing new content from partial cues) is the mechanism that forces active encoding and model construction.
> 
> **Source:** Phase III, Evidence Areas 3 and 4
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Connection
> **Tags:** #generation-effect #self-explanation #generation-constraint #learning-science

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Basic
> **A:** **Q:** What is the correct diagnostic question to ask when you feel "lost in details" during reading?
> 
> **A:** Not "which detail did I miss?" but "where did I lose the causal chain?" The experience of getting lost in details is the reader's awareness of CATSM incoherence — not a loss of any specific detail, but a loss of the causal spine that would give details their structural positions. The corrective is to locate the specific gap where an implicit causal inference was not generated, generate a tentative bridging inference, and allow the other CATSM dimensions to re-cohere around the reconstructed causal spine.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Mechanism 3
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Type:** Application
> **Tags:** #causal-spine #CATSM #reading-strategy #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Describe the Failure Cascade in situation model construction.
> 
> **A:** Working memory load from dense text reduces available resources for inference generation (Mechanism 1). Automatic textbase building proceeds fluently, producing a false comprehension signal (Mechanism 2, Textbase Trap). The false signal terminates active monitoring and inference generation before the causal spine is established (Mechanism 3). Without active inference generation, the CATSM dimensions remain incoherent (Mechanism 4). The reader progresses through the text building a rich textbase and a deficient situation model, confident throughout.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Dynamic Interaction section
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Type:** Process
> **Tags:** #failure-cascade #situation-model #mechanism #reading-comprehension

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Frame-Before-Fill principle operate in software architecture design, and what does this analogy illuminate about reading comprehension?
> 
> **A:** In software architecture, developers who begin implementing components without first establishing a system-level architecture face the software equivalent of the textbase trap: working components that don't cohere into a working system. The architectural frame (system diagram, dependency map) gives component implementations a structural position — just as a pre-reading structural frame gives text propositions a structural position. The analogy illuminates that Frame-Before-Fill is a domain-independent cognitive construction principle, not a reading-specific technique. It applies wherever complex mental models must be built from detailed inputs.
> 
> **Source:** Phase VII, FAR Transfer
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Type:** Connection
> **Tags:** #frame-before-fill #far-transfer #software-architecture #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is elaborative interrogation, and what is the specific question format it uses?
> 
> **A:** Elaborative interrogation is a study strategy in which the learner generates answers to "why" questions about factual material being studied — specifically, "Why is it true that [fact]?" The defining feature is the causal-explanatory demand, which distinguishes EI from other question-asking strategies that use "what" or "when" formats.
> 
> **Source:** Phase I / Lexicon A
> 
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> 
> **Type:** Definition
> 
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #reading-strategies, #learning-science

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between a textbase and a situation model? Give a concrete reading example.
> 
> **A:** A textbase is the propositional representation of what the text asserts, stripped of exact wording — it supports verbatim recall and close-paraphrase recognition. A situation model is the integrated representation of the subject matter itself, constructed by fusing textbase propositions with prior knowledge schemas — it supports inference, transfer, and novel application. Example: a reader who can recall that "photosynthesis converts light into glucose" has a textbase; one who can explain why plants use glucose as an energy carrier rather than storing ATP directly has a situation model.
> 
> **Source:** Phase II
> 
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> 
> **Type:** Distinction
> 
> **Tags:** #situation-model, #textbase, #text-comprehension, #van-dijk-kintsch

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Comprehension Gateway Mechanism, and what are its three structural components?
> 
> **A:** The Comprehension Gateway Mechanism is the process by which EI produces comprehension benefits: a Register 2 "why" question makes textbase-level retrieval insufficient, forcing situation model construction. Its three components are: (1) Demand-Exceeds-Textbase Structure — the question cannot be answered from the text; (2) Integration Anchor Requirement — construction requires connecting text propositions to prior knowledge schemas; (3) Construction Premium — generating the connection produces richer encoding than receiving it.
> 
> **Source:** Phase VI, Synthesis
> 
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> 
> **Type:** Process
> 
> **Tags:** #comprehension-gateway, #elaborative-interrogation, #situation-model, #original-construct

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** Why does prior knowledge moderate elaborative interrogation effectiveness, and is this moderation peripheral or structural?
> 
> **A:** Prior knowledge moderation is structural, not peripheral. Situation model construction — the process EI invokes — requires prior knowledge schemas as integration anchors: points of connection to which new text propositions can be attached within a causal-relational framework. A learner without relevant prior knowledge cannot execute the gateway mechanism because they lack the integration anchors that construction requires. This is why EI effects collapse (not merely diminish) when prior knowledge is absent, and why providing background reading before EI instruction partially restores EI benefits.
> 
> **Source:** Phases III-IV
> 
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> 
> **Type:** Connection
> 
> **Tags:** #prior-knowledge, #elaborative-interrogation, #integration-anchor, #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Dual Register Diagnostic, and how is a Register 1 question distinguished from a Register 2 question?
> 
> **A:** The Dual Register Diagnostic classifies EI questions by their answer level: Register 1 questions can be answered by someone who knows only the text (textbase-satisfiable); Register 2 questions require world knowledge not in the text (situation model-requiring). The diagnostic test is: "Could a reader with only this text, and no other knowledge, answer this question?" If yes: Register 1. If no: Register 2. Register 1 questions do not function as comprehension gateways and produce weak EI effects.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.2
> 
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> 
> **Type:** Distinction
> 
> **Tags:** #dual-register, #elaborative-interrogation, #question-design, #original-construct

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the generation advantage in EI, and why does it specifically arise in elaborative interrogation rather than from the generic generation effect alone?
> 
> **A:** The generation advantage is the finding that self-produced elaborations outperform experimenter-provided elaborations in EI. While the generic generation effect (Slamecka & Graf, 1978) contributes, EI's generation advantage also includes a specific construction premium: generating a causal connection requires actively traversing the conceptual path from text proposition to prior knowledge schema, reinforcing both the path and the endpoint. Provided elaborations allow recognition of a connection; generated elaborations require its construction — and the construction is the learning.
> 
> **Source:** Phases III and IV
> 
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> 
> **Type:** Process
> 
> **Tags:** #generation-effect, #elaborative-interrogation, #construction-premium

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** How should elaborative interrogation be integrated into PKB note-building practice, and what is the key design criterion for EI-style note prompts?
> 
> **A:** In PKB practice, EI should be applied by: (1) formulating Register 2 "why" questions as you read — ones whose answers require constructing causal connections, not locating sentences; (2) generating answers before consulting other sources; (3) writing notes at the situation model level ("X causes Y because [mechanism]") rather than the textbase level ("X causes Y"); (4) tagging unanswerable questions as prior knowledge gaps requiring background reading. The key design criterion for note prompts is the Dual Register Diagnostic: a prompt should be answerable only by constructing a causal-functional account, not by paraphrasing the source.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Best Practice callout
> 
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> 
> **Type:** Application
> 
> **Tags:** #pkb-practice, #elaborative-interrogation, #note-design, #reading-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Demand-Architecture Isomorphism, and what does it predict about the relationship between task design and learning depth?
> 
> **A:** The Demand-Architecture Isomorphism is the principle that the level of cognitive architecture engaged in processing is isomorphic to the level required to satisfy the task's demand structure. It predicts that: the level of understanding produced by a learning activity is determined by the minimum representational level needed to answer the task, not by the learner's subjective effort. A textbase-satisfiable question produces textbase encoding regardless of effort; a situation-model-requiring question forces situation model encoding. This implies that the most important instructional design decision is not "how difficult" but "what level of architecture does answering this demand?"
> 
> **Source:** Phase VI
> 
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> 
> **Type:** Definition
> 
> **Tags:** #demand-architecture, #instructional-design, #situation-model, #original-construct

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does elaborative interrogation connect to the desirable difficulties framework, and what specifically is "desirable" about EI's difficulty?
> 
> **A:** EI is a desirable difficulty (Bjork, 1994) because the cognitive demand it imposes is precisely the demand of situation model construction — the load that produces durable, transferable understanding. But EI's difficulty is not generically desirable; it is specifically targeted: the question format structurally blocks the textbase shortcut and requires exactly the kind of cognitive work (integration of text propositions with prior schemas) that produces rich encoding. The difficulty is desirable because it *is* the mechanism of the benefit — not an unfortunate cost of a useful technique but the productive struggle of construction itself.
> 
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.4
> 
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> 
> **Type:** Connection
> 
> **Tags:** #desirable-difficulties, #elaborative-interrogation, #productive-struggle

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the expertise reversal effect for EI, and why does the Comprehension Gateway Mechanism predict it?
> 
> **A:** The expertise reversal effect for EI is the finding that EI benefit diminishes as learners become expert in a domain — eventually becoming redundant or counterproductive. The Comprehension Gateway Mechanism predicts this: experts already construct situation models automatically during reading because their prior knowledge schemas are rich and activated rapidly. The gateway mechanism is no longer needed — the door is already open. Requiring experts to generate elaborations for material they already have situation models for produces redundancy effects (wasted processing resources on unnecessary elaboration), not learning benefits.
> 
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.2
> 
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> 
> **Type:** Process
> 
> **Tags:** #expertise-reversal, #elaborative-interrogation, #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition: Working Memory
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between working memory and short-term memory, and why does the distinction matter?
> **A:** Short-term memory refers to any passive temporary storage of information; working memory additionally involves active manipulation as well as multiple specialized components (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, central executive, episodic buffer). The distinction matters because simple digit-span measures of short-term memory fail to predict higher cognitive functioning, while complex span measures of working memory (which engage executive attention) strongly predict reasoning, comprehension, and learning outcomes.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition: Phonological Loop Phenomena
> **A:** **Q:** Name and briefly explain the four core phenomena demonstrating the phonological loop's architecture.
> **A:** (1) *Phonological similarity effect*: phonologically similar sequences are harder to recall (shows phonological coding). (2) *Word-length effect*: fewer long words recalled than short words (shows rehearsal buffer time-limited). (3) *Irrelevant speech effect*: background speech impairs verbal recall even when ignored (shows automatic access to phonological store). (4) *Articulatory suppression*: speaking concurrently eliminates word-length effect and disrupts phonological coding (shows rehearsal's dependence on articulatory motor programming).

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Distinction: Slave Systems vs. Central Executive
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fundamental distinction between the slave systems (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad) and the central executive in Baddeley's model?
> **A:** Slave systems are dedicated storage and maintenance buffers for specific representational formats (phonological/verbal; visuospatial). They operate with relative automaticity once activated. The central executive is a domain-general, limited-capacity attentional control system with no dedicated storage — it manages attention, coordinates slave systems, inhibits irrelevant information, and interfaces with long-term memory. It is the executive control that makes working memory "working."

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Process: Cognitive Load Reduction
> **A:** **Q:** According to Cognitive Load Theory, what is the primary goal of instructional design, and what is the mechanism linking it to learning?
> **A:** The primary goal is to reduce *extraneous cognitive load* (load imposed by poor instructional format) while preserving *germane cognitive load* (effort invested in schema construction). When extraneous load is reduced, working memory executive resources are freed for the active integration and elaboration of new information into long-term schemas — which is the mechanism of learning. Without freed executive capacity, the learner processes the material but cannot invest cognitive effort in schema formation.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Application: Split-Attention Effect
> **A:** **Q:** What is the split-attention effect and what instructional design principle does it motivate?
> **A:** The split-attention effect is the finding that learners who must mentally integrate information from physically or temporally separated sources perform worse than those who process the same information in an integrated format. The mechanism is that mental integration itself consumes working memory executive resources, leaving less capacity for learning. The design principle is *spatial and temporal contiguity*: place related text and diagrams physically adjacent (spatial contiguity) and present complementary narration and animation simultaneously rather than sequentially (temporal contiguity).

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Distinction: Near vs. Far Transfer in WM Training
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between near and far transfer in the context of working memory training, and what does the evidence show?
> **A:** *Near transfer*: improvement on tasks similar to the trained tasks (e.g., train on one working memory span task, improve on other span tasks). *Far transfer*: improvement on untrained, conceptually distinct cognitive abilities (reading comprehension, mathematics, fluid intelligence). Evidence: near transfer is consistently found in WM training studies; far transfer is generally *not* found in well-controlled conditions (Melby-Lervåg & Hulme, 2013). The implication: WM training improves WM task performance without expanding the broader cognitive capacity associated with WM.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Connection: Episodic Buffer and Reading Comprehension
> **A:** **Q:** How does the episodic buffer explain the comprehension of complex narratives that exceed the capacity of the phonological loop or visuospatial sketchpad alone?
> **A:** Complex narrative comprehension requires integrating verbal content (phonological loop), physical scene descriptions (visuospatial sketchpad), semantic knowledge (long-term memory), and temporal/causal structure into a unified situation model. The episodic buffer provides the temporary multimodal integration workspace where this binding occurs — it can hold approximately 4 chunks of integrated multimodal information, where each "chunk" is a rich episodic representation combining verbal, visual, spatial, and semantic features. Without the episodic buffer, the model cannot explain how working memory maintains complex situation models during reading.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Application: Working Memory in ADHD vs. Dyslexia
> **A:** **Q:** How do the working memory profiles in ADHD and dyslexia differ, and what does this selectivity reveal about working memory architecture?
> **A:** ADHD: selective impairment in central executive functions (controlled attention, updating, inhibition, task-switching) with relatively preserved simple phonological span. Dyslexia: selective impairment in phonological loop capacity (reduced digit span, impaired non-word repetition, low phonological awareness) with relatively preserved visuospatial and executive functions. The selectivity demonstrates the independence of working memory components: ADHD implicates prefrontal executive systems; dyslexia implicates left inferior parietal/Broca's area phonological systems. Each disorder validates the model's architectural distinctions.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Definition: Expertise Reversal Effect
> **A:** **Q:** What is the expertise reversal effect and why does it challenge the universal application of CLT instructional principles?
> **A:** The expertise reversal effect: instructional guidance that helps novices learn can actually impair learning in more advanced learners. As expertise grows, long-term schemas reduce the intrinsic load of the material, and scaffolding becomes redundant and forces processing of information the expert already knows — imposing extraneous load without benefit. This challenges universal application of CLT principles because the optimal instructional format depends on learner expertise: worked examples for novices; problem-solving for experts; faded guidance for learners transitioning between these stages.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Distinction: Baddeley vs. Cowan Models
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fundamental architectural difference between Baddeley's multicomponent model and Cowan's embedded-processes model?
> **A:** Baddeley: proposes specialized short-term storage subsystems (phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad) that are structurally distinct from long-term memory, with capacity determined by modality-specific mechanisms. Cowan: proposes working memory is simply activated long-term memory — a subset of activated representations held in a limited focus of attention (~3-4 chunks, modality-independent). No specialized short-term stores; just different activation levels of long-term memory. Key difference: Baddeley predicts modality-specific capacity limits; Cowan predicts a single modality-independent capacity limit for the focus of attention.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Process: Central Executive Functions
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four principal functions of the central executive in Baddeley's model?
> **A:** (1) *Focusing attention*: selecting relevant information from competing inputs and maintaining goal-relevant representations. (2) *Dividing attention*: distributing attentional resources across multiple concurrent tasks. (3) *Switching attention*: flexibly shifting between task sets, retrieval strategies, or mental representations (with associated switching costs). (4) *Interfacing with long-term memory*: selectively activating relevant long-term knowledge to support current working memory operations, enabling reasoning and comprehension tasks that require integration of stored knowledge with new information.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Q:** Application: Modality Effect in Multimedia Learning
> **A:** **Q:** What is the modality effect in multimedia learning, how does Baddeley's model explain it, and what is its design implication?
> **A:** The modality effect: learning is better when complex visual material is accompanied by spoken narration rather than on-screen text. Baddeley's explanation: text and diagram compete for the same visuospatial processing channel, causing bottleneck. Narration and diagram use separate channels (phonological loop for narration; visuospatial sketchpad for diagram), allowing parallel processing and more total information capacity. Design implication: for complex animated or diagrammatic material, use spoken narration rather than on-screen explanatory text to exploit the dual-channel architecture of working memory.

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three representational levels in Kintsch's Construction-Integration model?
> **A:** (1) Surface structure — verbatim wording; (2) Textbase — the propositional content stripped of wording; (3) Situation model — the mental representation of the denoted state of affairs (what the text is about, not the text itself).
> **Source:** § Section 1 / Conceptual Foundations
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** CI-model, reading-comprehension, kintsch

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Verbal Efficiency Theory prediction about word-level processing and comprehension?
> **A:** Readers whose word recognition is effortful (not automatic) consume working memory resources on decoding, leaving fewer cognitive resources for higher-order processes: inference generation, coherence monitoring, and situation model construction. Individual differences in reading comprehension are substantially explained by this cognitive bottleneck.
> **Source:** § Section 2 / Word-Level Processing
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** verbal-efficiency, working-memory, perfetti, fluency

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the vocabulary coverage threshold for functional comprehension of academic texts, and what proportion of texts' academic vocabulary must a reader know?
> **A:** Nation (2001): approximately 98% of running words in a text must be known for adequate comprehension. Below 95% coverage, comprehension breaks down due to accumulated inferential gaps. For academic texts, this requires 5,000–8,000 general word families PLUS ~2,000–5,000 specialised academic word families.
> **Source:** § Section 3 / Vocabulary Knowledge
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** vocabulary, coverage-threshold, nation, academic-vocabulary

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** Distinguish schema assimilation from schema accommodation in the context of academic reading.
> **A:** *Assimilation*: new textual information is incorporated into an existing schema without modifying the schema — efficient when the schema is accurate. *Accommodation*: the schema is modified or a new schema is created in response to information that cannot be correctly assimilated. Misconception-based interference occurs when faulty schemas assimilate information that should require accommodation, producing apparent but distorted understanding.
> **Source:** § Section 4 / Schema and Prior Knowledge
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** schema-theory, assimilation, accommodation, conceptual-change

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What distinction does Graesser et al.'s constructionist theory make between coherence inferences and elaborative inferences?
> **A:** *Coherence (bridging) inferences* are generated automatically to maintain local and global coherence between text segments — they fill the logical gaps between adjacent propositions. *Elaborative inferences* are generated selectively to enrich the situation model with relevant world knowledge beyond coherence requirements. Academic texts are dense with coherence inferences requiring disciplinary knowledge; comprehension failure often involves missing coherence inferences.
> **Source:** § Section 5 / Inference Generation
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** inference, CI-model, graesser, constructionist-theory

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the "illusion of knowing" (fluency illusion) in academic reading, and why does it obstruct comprehension development?
> **A:** The fluency illusion (Bjork, 1994) is the systematic overestimation of one's comprehension quality when text is processed fluently and confirms existing beliefs. It decouples subjective certainty from actual situation model accuracy. It obstructs comprehension development because it prevents metacognitive monitoring from triggering fix-up strategies — if you believe you understand, you don't deploy repair, and comprehension gaps persist unaddressed.
> **Source:** § Section 6 / Metacognitive Monitoring
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** metacognition, fluency-illusion, bjork, comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Matthew Effect in reading comprehension, and what mechanisms drive it?
> **A:** Stanovich (1986): vocabulary and schema advantages in early reading produce greater comprehension success, which produces greater reading motivation and volume, which produces greater incidental vocabulary acquisition and schema development, which compounds the advantage. Simultaneously, early difficulties reduce reading motivation and volume, compounding the disadvantage. The result is systematic, cumulative divergence between high and low readers over schooling. The name references Matthew 25:29 ("to him who has, more will be given").
> **Source:** § Section 2 (Matthew Effect), Section 7 (interventions)
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** matthew-effect, stanovich, reading-development, vocabulary

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four strategies in Reciprocal Teaching, and what comprehension function does each serve?
> **A:** 1. *Prediction* — activates prior knowledge schemas and generates textual expectations (schema activation). 2. *Questioning* — requires integrating text propositions into comprehension-checkpoint questions (textbase and situation model). 3. *Clarifying* — identifies and addresses vocabulary, coherence, and structural failures (comprehension monitoring + fix-up). 4. *Summarising* — requires integrating the passage into a coherent whole at the situation model level (integration and coherence checking).
> **Source:** § Section 7 / Instructional Principles
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** reciprocal-teaching, palincsar, brown, reading-strategy

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What does the VSI Triad synthesis claim about individual-component reading instruction?
> **A:** The Vocabulary-Schema-Inference Triad claims that the three primary components of academic reading comprehension interact *multiplicatively* rather than additively: deficiency in any one cascades into failure across the others. This implies that isolated vocabulary instruction, isolated schema-building, or isolated inference strategy instruction each produces narrow, non-transferring gains — effective academic reading instruction must address all three components concurrently and with metacognitive monitoring as the regulatory overlay.
> **Source:** § Synthesis / VSI Triad
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** VSI-triad, synthesis, integrated-instruction, reading-comprehension

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** Name and describe the five dimensions of Zwaan's Event-Indexing Model.
> **A:** Readers continuously track: (1) *Time* — temporal ordering and sequence of events; (2) *Space* — spatial location and relationship of entities; (3) *Causality* — cause-effect and reason-consequence chains; (4) *Intentionality* — goals, motivations, and actions of agents; (5) *Entity identity* — stable tracking of who/what across mentions and pronoun chains. Academic texts make differential demands on these dimensions depending on genre and discipline.
> **Source:** § Section 5 / Inference Generation and Situation Model
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** event-indexing, zwaan, situation-model, inference

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the difference between a textbase and a situation model in reading comprehension?
> **A:** **A:** A *textbase* is a propositional semantic representation of what the text explicitly says — a network of propositions derived from the text's surface content. A *situation model* is a richer mental model of the actual situation, event, or concept described by the text, incorporating prior knowledge, inferences, spatial relationships, and causal structure. Situation models support transfer and problem-solving; textbase representations support paraphrase and recognition.
> **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #reading-comprehension #cognitive-science

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Fluency Illusion, and why does it undermine metacognitive monitoring?
> **A:** **A:** The Fluency Illusion is the systematic tendency to interpret *ease of text processing* (perceptual fluency) as evidence of *comprehension depth*, when fluency and comprehension are not reliably related. Re-reading increases fluency without necessarily improving situation model quality — but the increased fluency feels like improved understanding. This creates false metacognitive confidence and is a primary driver of the passive re-reading trap.
> **Source:** Section 8.2 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #metacognition #fluency-illusion

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What are the three sub-types of metacognitive knowledge, and which is most predictive of strategic reading proficiency?
> **A:** **A:** (1) *Declarative* — knowing *what* strategies exist; (2) *Procedural* — knowing *how* to execute strategies; (3) *Conditional* — knowing *when* and *why* to use which strategy. Conditional metacognitive knowledge is most predictive of advanced reading proficiency and hardest to develop through instruction.
> **Source:** Section 3.1 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #metacognition #self-regulated-learning

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Matthew Effect in reading, and what does this report claim about its interaction with metacognitive monitoring?
> **A:** **A:** The Matthew Effect describes how early reading advantages (vocabulary, comprehension) compound over time — rich get richer, poor get poorer in literacy development. This report's synthesis argues that the Matthew Effect creates a *double failure trap*: poor domain knowledge simultaneously degrades comprehension (less effective schema application) and degrades metacognitive monitoring accuracy (schemas needed for monitoring failures are absent). Both deficits compound each other.
> **Source:** Section 6.4 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #matthew-effect #metacognition #prior-knowledge

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** According to Dunlosky et al. (2013), which learning strategies have high utility? Which have low utility?
> **A:** **A:** **High utility:** retrieval practice (practice testing) and spaced repetition. **Moderate utility:** elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaving. **Low utility:** re-reading and highlighting. The high-utility strategies are underused by most students despite being most effective; the low-utility strategies are overused because they feel effective (due to Fluency Illusion).
> **Source:** Section 5.2 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #learning-strategies #retrieval-practice

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is Reciprocal Teaching, and what four strategies does it involve?
> **A:** **A:** Reciprocal Teaching (Palincsar & Brown, 1984) is a scaffolded reading comprehension intervention involving small groups rotating through four metacognitive strategies: (1) **Summarizing** — capturing main points to check integration; (2) **Question generating** — formulating key questions to promote elaboration; (3) **Clarifying** — addressing confusing terms or passages; (4) **Predicting** — using text structure to anticipate upcoming content. Each strategy constitutes a component of the metacognitive monitoring-and-control cycle.
> **Source:** Section 7.2 | **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #reciprocal-teaching #reading-instruction #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Zone of Proximal Development, and how does it apply to reading comprehension instruction?
> **A:** **A:** Vygotsky's ZPD defines the range of tasks a learner cannot manage independently but can manage with appropriate support. In reading instruction, the ZPD identifies texts and tasks where comprehension is possible with scaffolding but would fail without it. Optimal instruction targets the ZPD — neither too easy (no challenge) nor too difficult (incomprehensible even with support). Scaffolding is gradually reduced as the learner's independent competence develops (I-We-You progression).
> **Difficulty:** Basic | **Tags:** #vygotsky #scaffolding #zone-of-proximal-development

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is conditional metacognitive knowledge, and why is it more powerful than declarative or procedural metacognitive knowledge for reading?
> **A:** **A:** Conditional metacognitive knowledge is knowing *when* and *why* to apply specific reading strategies — understanding the match between strategy type, text type, and comprehension goal. It is more powerful than declarative knowledge (knowing strategies exist) or procedural knowledge (knowing how to execute them) because it enables strategic flexibility: deploying the right strategy in the right context rather than applying favorite strategies indiscriminately. This strategy-selection capacity is the metacognitive master skill.
> **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #metacognitive-knowledge #conditional-knowledge #strategy-selection

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is elaborative interrogation, and what mechanism explains its effectiveness?
> **A:** **A:** Elaborative interrogation is a reading strategy involving self-generated "Why is this true?" questions after encountering factual or explanatory claims. Its effectiveness is explained by multiple converging mechanisms: (1) prior knowledge activation (retrieving related schemas); (2) semantic elaboration (connecting the claim to a knowledge network, creating multiple retrieval pathways); (3) inference generation (producing causal inferences beyond text information); (4) comprehension monitoring (inability to generate a plausible "why" signals comprehension failure).
> **Source:** Section 5.2 | **Difficulty:** Intermediate | **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation #deep-processing
