> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Q:** Q:** What is the Nelson-Narens monitoring-control model, and what is the key distinction it draws?
> **A:** **A:** The Nelson-Narens (1990) model describes metacognitive functioning as a two-level system: the *object level* (the actual cognitive reading processes — word recognition, sentence parsing, situation model construction) and the *meta level* (the monitoring and control system operating on object-level processes). *Monitoring* = information flow from object to meta level (the meta system's observation of comprehension state). *Control* = information flow from meta to object level (executive regulation of reading behavior in response to monitoring). Key insight: monitoring and control are distinct — readers can monitor failures without deploying appropriate control responses.
> **Source:** Section 3.2 | **Difficulty:** Advanced | **Tags:** #metacognition #nelson-narens #monitoring-control

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is elaborative interrogation, and what distinguishes it from simply re-reading or questioning a text?
> **A:** EI is a generative learning strategy in which the learner answers "why is this true?" questions about specific factual propositions, drawing on prior knowledge to produce causal-explanatory accounts. It is distinguished by its generative character (answers must be produced, not read), its why-format constraint (causal-explanatory, not just reflective), and its prior knowledge activation requirement.
> **Source:** Phase II
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #learning-strategy, #definition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** How does elaborative interrogation differ from self-explanation in content target and mechanism?
> **A:** EI targets factual-relational propositions ("X has property Y") and produces causal accounts of why facts hold; self-explanation targets procedural or causal content and produces accounts of how processes work. The mechanisms partially overlap (both involve generative processing) but EI more directly depends on prior semantic knowledge for answer generation.
> **Source:** Phase II
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #self-explanation, #distinction

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Mechanism
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three components of the mechanism chain linking EI execution to superior retention?
> **A:** (1) Cued prior knowledge retrieval: the why-question activates relevant prior knowledge networks; (2) elaborative integration: the retrieved prior knowledge is connected to the target proposition, forming a causal account; (3) networked encoding: the target proposition is stored within the activated knowledge network, providing multiple retrieval pathways.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #mechanism, #encoding

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Theory Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does levels-of-processing theory explain EI's effectiveness? What specifically does EI guarantee that passive re-reading does not?
> **A:** LOP theory holds that encoding durability is a function of semantic depth and elaborative richness. EI structurally guarantees semantic-level processing: generating a why-answer necessarily engages with relational, causal, meaningful features of the proposition. Passive re-reading can remain at the surface-feature level, producing the fluency illusion without deep encoding.
> **Source:** Phase III
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #levels-of-processing, #elaborative-interrogation, #deep-processing

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Prior Knowledge Moderator
> **A:** **Q:** Why does elaborative interrogation fail (or backfire) when prior knowledge is insufficient? What is the specific risk?
> **A:** When prior knowledge is insufficient, learners cannot generate accurate elaborations. If they generate inaccurate causal accounts with confidence, these accounts may be encoded alongside or instead of the target fact, creating misconceptions. The accuracy constraint means EI's effectiveness depends on the quality, not merely the quantity, of generated elaborations.
> **Source:** Phases III, IV
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #prior-knowledge, #accuracy-constraint, #elaborative-interrogation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What are Dunlosky et al.'s (2013) utility ratings for EI relative to retrieval practice and re-reading?
> **A:** EI received "moderate utility" — above re-reading and highlighting (low utility), but below retrieval practice and distributed practice (high utility). The moderate rating reflects genuine but conditioned efficacy: EI is reliably effective when prior knowledge supports accurate elaboration generation, but not universally effective.
> **Source:** Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #dunlosky, #learning-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Mechanism
> **A:** **Q:** What is the distinctiveness hypothesis in EI research, and how does it complement the integration mechanism?
> **A:** The distinctiveness hypothesis (McDaniel & Donnelly, 1996) holds that EI generates distinctive memory traces — encoded with a unique constellation of semantic features — that are resistant to interference. Distinctiveness accounts for why EI items resist intrusion from similar information; integration (connecting to prior knowledge networks) accounts for why they have multiple retrieval pathways. Together they produce both resistance to interference and enhanced cue-based retrieval.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #distinctiveness, #elaborative-interrogation, #mechanism

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What is the "accuracy-activation dialectic" and why does it matter for expert use of EI?
> **A:** The accuracy-activation dialectic (original synthesis) names the tension between two facts: (1) EI is most powerful when prior knowledge is richest; but (2) rich prior knowledge creates the risk that fluent but inaccurate schemata will distort encoding of genuinely discrepant new information. Expert EI use requires maintaining calibrated skepticism toward self-generated elaborations — neither assuming accuracy because elaboration felt fluent nor abandoning elaboration because the domain is difficult.
> **Source:** Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #accuracy-constraint, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** How does EI contribute specifically to situation model construction during reading?
> **A:** Situation models have multiple dimensions (spatial, temporal, causal, referential). EI contributes specifically to the causal dimension: by generating why-answers, the reader explicitly constructs the causal network linking text propositions. This produces a more causally coherent mental model of the described state of affairs, enabling inference and transfer beyond verbatim text recall.
> **Source:** Phase IV
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #situation-model, #elaborative-interrogation, #comprehension

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** Why is EI described as complementary rather than competitive with retrieval practice? At what points in the learning cycle does each strategy operate?
> **A:** EI primarily operates during *initial encoding* — it deepens and enriches the quality of the initial memory trace by integrating new propositions into the prior knowledge network. Retrieval practice primarily operates during *consolidation* — strengthening already-encoded information through active reconstruction against resistance. Combining EI (for deep initial encoding) with subsequent spaced retrieval practice (for consolidation) should outperform either strategy alone.
> **Source:** Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #retrieval-practice, #elaborative-interrogation, #learning-sequence

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 11 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fluency illusion, and why is elaborative interrogation structurally resistant to it?
> **A:** The fluency illusion is the metacognitive error of mistaking the subjective ease of re-processing familiar-seeming material for genuine comprehension or retention. Re-reading produces fluency without encoding depth, generating a false sense of understanding. EI is resistant to the fluency illusion because the generative demand — producing a causal answer — exposes the gap between fluency and genuine comprehension: a learner cannot feel fluent about a why-answer they cannot actually produce.
> **Source:** Phase III, V
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fluency-illusion, #elaborative-interrogation, #metacognitive-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 12 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** In the PKB context, what distinguishes a note produced through EI (a "synthesis artifact") from a transcription note? Why does this matter?
> **A:** A transcription note records what the source said; a synthesis artifact (EI note) records *why the source's claim is true*, connecting the new proposition to existing PKB nodes through generated causal accounts. The difference is epistemic: synthesis artifacts are integrated into the knowledge graph (with wiki-links to activated prior knowledge nodes), while transcription artifacts are isolated. EI notes add both a memory advantage (networked encoding) and a knowledge graph advantage (new edges between existing nodes).
> **Source:** Phase V, Appendix 6
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #pkb, #elaborative-interrogation, #synthesis

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 13 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What does the ICAP framework predict about EI's effectiveness, and why?
> **A:** ICAP predicts that constructive activities (which EI exemplifies) produce superior learning to active, passive, or interactive activities, because constructive activities require the learner to generate knowledge outputs that go beyond the presented information. EI specifically involves generating a causal explanation not contained in the text, placing it squarely in the constructive category. ICAP's constructive engagement hypothesis directly predicts EI's moderate-to-high utility rating.
> **Source:** Phase II
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #ICAP-framework, #elaborative-interrogation, #constructive-learning

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> **Q:** Seed 14 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What does the Matthew Effect imply for the pedagogical deployment of elaborative interrogation?
> **A:** The Matthew Effect describes cumulative advantage: those who have more knowledge gain more from EI (richer prior knowledge → better elaborations → deeper encoding), while those who have less gain less and risk misconception formation. This means EI functions as a *knowledge amplifier* rather than a knowledge equalizer: deploying it without prerequisite knowledge-building may widen the gap between learners with strong and weak domain backgrounds. Equitable deployment requires knowledge-building scaffolding before EI introduction in any domain.
> **Source:** Phase V
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #matthew-effect, #prior-knowledge, #elaborative-interrogation, #equity

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 1 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is comprehension monitoring, and at what levels does it operate?
> **A:** The continuous metacognitive evaluation of text representation adequacy against multiple standards (lexical, propositional, coherence, situation-model). Failures at any level constitute candidate triggers for regulatory response. Most poor comprehenders monitor at lexical/surface levels but neglect coherence and situation-model levels.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.1; Phase IV, Section 4.1
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #reading, #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 2 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between the textbase and the situation model, and why does the distinction matter for reading comprehension?
> **A:** The textbase is a propositional representation of what the text explicitly states; the situation model is the reader's integrated mental representation of the state of affairs described, enriched by inference and prior knowledge. Only situation-model construction constitutes deep comprehension; textbase representation supports only surface paraphrasing.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #reading, #situation-model, #textbase

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 3 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fluency illusion and what cognitive mechanism produces it?
> **A:** The misattribution of surface-reading fluency (decoding ease, lexical retrieval speed) to comprehension depth. Produced by the monitoring system's reliance on processing ease as a comprehension signal — but fluency carries information about surface-level processing, not situation-model construction. Cause: monitoring operates at the wrong level of text representation.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #fluency-illusion, #monitoring-failure

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 4 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** Describe the Nelson-Narens monitoring-control architecture as applied to reading.
> **A:** Object level = direct text processing (decoding, parsing, semantic integration). Meta level = metacognitive monitoring of object-level processes. Monitoring flows upward: represents state of comprehension. Control flows downward: adjusts object-level strategy in response. Effective comprehension monitoring requires: (1) accurate monitoring signals, (2) reliable monitoring-control coupling, (3) appropriate control responses.
> **Source:** Phase II, Section 2.3
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #nelson-narens, #metacognitive-monitoring, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 5 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What is the difference between metacognitive monitoring failure and motivational disengagement in the context of reading comprehension deficits?
> **A:** Monitoring failure = the reader genuinely does not detect comprehension breakdown (cognitive deficit in the detection mechanism). Motivational disengagement = the reader detects failure but suppresses regulatory response (motivationally driven suppression, often to protect self-efficacy). These two pathways require different instructional responses.
> **Source:** Phase VII, Section 3 (Tensions)
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #metacognition, #motivation, #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 6 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What are declarative, procedural, and conditional metacognitive knowledge, and how do they apply to reading strategy instruction?
> **A:** Declarative = knowing *that* (strategy names, self-knowledge); Procedural = knowing *how* (strategy execution); Conditional = knowing *when and why* (appropriateness conditions). Reading strategy instruction most commonly develops only declarative and procedural knowledge; conditional knowledge — the most critical for transfer — is most commonly neglected.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognitive-knowledge, #strategy-instruction, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 7 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four strategies in reciprocal teaching and what metacognitive function does each perform?
> **A:** (1) Predicting — activates prior knowledge, establishes comprehension goals; (2) Questioning — enforces self-monitoring via explicit comprehension question generation; (3) Clarifying — comprehension monitoring and fix-up strategy deployment for detected failures; (4) Summarizing — coherence evaluation at the discourse level, tests situation model construction.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #reciprocal-teaching, #metacognitive-strategies, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 8 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does Verbose Efficiency Theory connect decoding fluency to reading comprehension via the working memory mechanism?
> **A:** Inefficient decoding (non-automatic lexical access) consumes working memory resources with lexical-phonological retrieval, leaving insufficient capacity for comprehension processes (coherence monitoring, inference generation, situation-model construction). Therefore, reading fluency is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for metacognitive comprehension monitoring in demanding texts.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.5
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #verbal-efficiency-theory, #working-memory, #reading-fluency

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 9 — Distinction
> **A:** **Q:** What distinguishes effective annotation strategies from passive highlighting in terms of metacognitive engagement?
> **A:** Passive highlighting = topographic marking of verbatim text; associated with fluency illusion rather than comprehension monitoring. Effective annotation = content-transforming marks (questions, summaries, connections, evaluations) that require comprehension evaluation, inference generation, and prior-knowledge integration. Effective annotation externalizes the metacognitive regulatory dialogue; passive highlighting does not.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.4
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #annotation, #metacognition, #reading-strategies

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 10 — Process
> **A:** **Q:** What are the four stages of effective fix-up strategy deployment during reading?
> **A:** (1) Signal detection — monitoring detects comprehension failure; (2) Failure diagnosis — reader identifies the level/type of failure (lexical, propositional, coherence, situation-model); (3) Strategy selection — conditional metacognitive knowledge guides response selection; (4) Strategy execution and evaluation — strategy deployed and monitoring re-evaluates whether failure is resolved.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #fix-up-strategy, #comprehension-monitoring, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 11 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the Matthew Effect in reading relate to metacognitive monitoring capacity?
> **A:** Poor readers have reduced metacognitive monitoring capacity because demanding decoding exhausts working memory; reduced monitoring leads to reduced comprehension; reduced comprehension means less schema building and vocabulary growth, which keeps decoding demanding and keeps monitoring capacity suppressed. The failure cycle is: poor decoding → high cognitive load → suppressed monitoring → comprehension failure → reduced vocabulary and schema growth → continued poor decoding.
> **Source:** Phase IV, Section 4.5
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #matthew-effect, #metacognition, #reading, #cognitive-load

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 12 — Definition
> **A:** **Q:** What does "self-regulated reading" mean and how does it relate to Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model?
> **A:** Self-regulated reading is metacognitive, goal-directed, and strategically enacted text comprehension. Maps onto Zimmerman's three phases: (1) Forethought = goal-setting, prior knowledge activation, strategy planning; (2) Performance = comprehension monitoring, strategy deployment, attention regulation; (3) Self-reflection = outcome evaluation, attribution, strategy adaptation. Distinguishes reading as self-directed enterprise from externally regulated strategy use.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.4; Phase II, Section 2.1
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #self-regulated-learning, #reading, #metacognition

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 13 — Application
> **A:** **Q:** What is the KWL strategy, and which metacognitive reading functions does each component serve?
> **A:** K (What do I *Know*?) = prior knowledge activation and establishing comprehension baseline; W (What do I *Want* to know?) = goal-setting and directing monitoring attention; L (What have I *Learned*?) = comprehension evaluation, gap detection, and situation model assessment. Collectively: the KWL sequence operationalizes the forethought-monitoring-self-reflection SRL cycle for a single reading session.
> **Source:** Phase V, Section 5.3
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #KWL-strategy, #metacognition, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> **Q:** Seed 14 — Connection
> **A:** **Q:** How does the elaborative interrogation strategy operationalize the depth-of-processing principle in reading?
> **A:** Depth-of-processing principle: semantic/elaborative processing produces more durable encoding than surface processing. Elaborative interrogation operationalizes deep processing by requiring the reader to generate *why/how* explanations for text propositions, thereby enforcing semantic elaboration and prior-knowledge integration. The strategy converts passive proposition reception into active inferential construction — the functional equivalent of forced deep processing.
> **Source:** Phase III, Section 3.5; Phase VII, Lexicon
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #elaborative-interrogation, #levels-of-processing, #reading

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the distinction between textbase and situation model in Kintsch's reading comprehension model?
> **A:** The textbase is a coherent propositional representation of *what the text says* — the literal semantic content of the text's sentences. The situation model is a mental representation of *what the text describes* — the state of affairs in the world or domain the text refers to. Genuine comprehension requires situation model construction; textbase representation alone supports recognition but not transfer or integration.
> **Source:** Section 2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #comprehension #reading-theory #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the fluency illusion and why is it motivationally significant?
> **A:** The fluency illusion is the metacognitive error of mistaking the ease of text processing (reading fluency) for depth of comprehension (situation model construction). It is motivationally significant because it prevents deployment of deeper processing strategies (if the reader believes they understand, they stop working to understand), produces false assessment confidence, and when assessment performance fails, this failure is misattributed to ability rather than monitoring — reinforcing entity theories and performance-avoidance goals.
> **Source:** Sections 2 & 7
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #metacognition #fluency-illusion #comprehension-monitoring

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What are the three basic psychological needs in SDT, and how does each apply specifically to academic reading?
> **A:** (1) **Autonomy** — the need to experience reading as self-initiated and volitionally chosen. In reading: supporting autonomy means providing genuine rationales, meaningful choice within required content, and framing reading for personal understanding rather than external compliance. (2) **Competence** — the need to experience efficacy and mastery. In reading: satisfied by successful comprehension experiences, progressive difficulty calibration, and strategy training that produces genuine understanding. (3) **Relatedness** — the need for connection with others. In reading: satisfied by shared reading practices, discussion communities, and meaningful connection of reading content to valued relationships and communities.
> **Source:** Section 4
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #SDT #basic-psychological-needs #reading-motivation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** Distinguish mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals in the context of academic reading.
> **A:** **Mastery-approach:** Reading to develop genuine understanding; predicts deep processing, persistence, positive affect. **Mastery-avoidance:** Reading to avoid failure-to-understand, driven by comprehension anxiety; predicts self-monitoring and persistence from fear. **Performance-approach:** Reading to demonstrate superior comprehension relative to others; predicts adequate assessed performance but surface strategic reading. **Performance-avoidance:** Reading to avoid appearing incompetent; predicts avoidance, surface processing, learned helplessness — most consistently negative outcome profile.
> **Source:** Section 5
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #achievement-goal-theory #goal-orientation #reading-motivation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the logic of the three-tier strategy hierarchy and what does it mean to "start at the wrong tier"?
> **A:** The hierarchy sequences strategies according to prerequisite logic: Tier 1 (cognitive foundation) creates conditions Tier 2 presupposes; Tier 2 (comprehension strategies) creates conditions Tier 3 presupposes. Starting at the wrong tier means applying strategies that require conditions not yet in place. Example: teaching elaborative interrogation (Tier 2) to a reader with profound vocabulary gaps (Tier 1 deficit) will fail because the reader cannot generate meaningful elaborations when basic comprehension is blocked by unknown vocabulary. The diagnostic must precede the prescription.
> **Source:** Section 6
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #strategy-hierarchy #reading-motivation #intervention-design

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is self-explanation as a reading strategy and why is it more effective than summarization?
> **A:** Self-explanation involves generating explanatory verbalizations or written articulations of what a passage means in the reader's own words, how it relates to prior content and knowledge, and what gaps remain. It is more effective than summarization because it requires construction of causal relationships and inferential connections that the text may not state explicitly — forcing situation model construction rather than accurate textbase restatement. Summarization can be achieved at the textbase level; genuine self-explanation requires situation model access.
> **Source:** Section 6.3
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #self-explanation #comprehension-strategy #situation-model

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is Zimmerman's cyclical SRL model and what are the three phases applied to academic reading?
> **A:** **Forethought phase:** Before reading — goal setting (what do I want to genuinely understand?), strategic planning (which strategies are appropriate for this text?), motivational self-management (intrinsic goal activation, prior knowledge preparation). **Performance phase:** During reading — strategy deployment, comprehension monitoring, fix-up strategy selection and execution when failures are detected. **Self-reflection phase:** After reading — self-evaluation of comprehension quality, causal attribution of successes and failures, adaptive planning for the next reading session. The cycle makes self-regulated reading self-improving rather than repetitively consistent.
> **Source:** Section 7.2
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #self-regulated-learning #metacognition #reading-self-regulation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is interest theory's four-phase model and what distinguishes situational from individual interest?
> **A:** Four phases: (1) Triggered situational interest — externally triggered by environmental features; (2) Maintained situational interest — sustained by engaging content value; (3) Emerging individual interest — beginning of stored value and re-engagement tendency; (4) Well-developed individual interest — stable, self-sustaining predisposition to engage. **Situational interest** is triggered by specific contextual features (an engaging text, a surprising demonstration) and dissipates when those features are absent. **Individual interest** is a relatively stable personal predisposition that motivates seeking out domain-relevant content across contexts, independent of specific environmental triggers.
> **Source:** Section 3.3
> **Difficulty:** Intermediate
> **Tags:** #interest-theory #situational-interest #individual-interest #reading-motivation

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** Why is retrieval practice more effective than re-reading for long-term retention, and how should it be applied during academic reading?
> **A:** Retrieval practice is more effective because the act of retrieving strengthens the memory trace through effortful reconstruction (a desirable difficulty that enhances encoding), whereas re-reading produces recognition familiarity (high processing fluency) without effortful retrieval — it improves performance on immediate tests but not long-term retention. **Application during reading:** After completing a section, close or cover the text and write from memory the main points and key arguments. Check accuracy against the text. The gaps identified during retrieval attempts are precisely the content requiring focused re-reading or further elaboration.
> **Source:** Sections 6.3 and 7.3
> **Difficulty:** Basic
> **Tags:** #retrieval-practice #spaced-repetition #desirable-difficulties #reading-strategy

> [!flashcard] **Spaced Repetition** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> **Q:** Untitled
> **A:** **Q:** What is the Motivational-Cognitive Reading Stack and what diagnostic implication does it carry?
> **A:** The Stack integrates four systems that must each meet threshold development for motivated academic reading to be self-sustaining: **Layer 1** (Cognitive Pre-Conditions: fluency, vocabulary, working memory management, prior knowledge), **Layer 2** (Comprehension-Generating Strategies: self-explanation, elaborative interrogation, retrieval practice), **Layer 3** (Motivation Architecture: autonomous regulation, mastery goals, intrinsic goal framing, individual interest). **Diagnostic implication:** Identify the lowest layer where the system is failing. A reader who cannot sustain motivation despite good comprehension skills needs Layer 3 work. A reader who is motivated but comprehends shallowly needs Layer 2 strategy training. A reader whose strategies fail needs Layer 1 development. Starting intervention at the correct layer is essential.
> **Source:** Section 6.4 original synthesis
> **Difficulty:** Advanced
> **Tags:** #motivational-cognitive-stack #original-synthesis #reading-motivation #diagnostic





































































































## Key Figures & Intellectual Lineage

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch (1932–present)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Core Contribution:** Developed the Construction-Integration model of text comprehension with Teun van Dijk; distinguished the three levels of text representation (surface code, text base, situation model); provided the most rigorous computational account of how comprehension works.
> 
> **Role in the Dialectical Arc:** Primary developer of the alternative framework that displaces the received view; the CI model is both the theoretical ground for the challenges in Phase III and the foundation of the reconstruction in Phase V.
> 
> **Relationship to Other Figures/Frameworks:** Built on van Dijk's discourse structure analysis; extended and formalized by Zwaan & Radvansky's Event Indexing Model; related to Bartlett's schema theory as a successor framework.
> 
> **Key Works:** *Cognition and Text* (1974); *The Representation of Meaning in Memory* (1974); with van Dijk, "Toward a Model of Text Comprehension and Production" (1978); *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition* (1998).
> 
> **Relevance to This Analysis:** The three-level model is the primary theoretical weapon against the received view; the CI model explains the mechanism of situation model failure.

> [!person] **Rolf Zwaan (active 1990s–present)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Core Contribution:** Developed the Event Indexing Model (with Radvansky and Langston), identifying the five dimensions along which situation models are structured and updated during reading.
> 
> **Role in the Dialectical Arc:** Contributor to the challenge phases; the Event Indexing Model provides the structural description of what situation model construction requires and what fails in poor comprehenders.
> 
> **Key Works:** With Langston & Graesser, "The Construction of Situation Models in Narrative Comprehension" (1995); with Radvansky, "Situation Models in Language Comprehension and Memory" (1998).
> 
> **Relevance to This Analysis:** The five dimensions of the Event Indexing Model provide the operational monitoring checklist in the reconstructed understanding.

> [!person] **Philip Gough (1934–2007)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Core Contribution:** Co-developed (with William Tunmer) the Simple View of Reading, which formalized the decomposition of reading comprehension into decoding and linguistic comprehension components.
> 
> **Role in the Dialectical Arc:** Primary theoretical resource for the steel-manned received view; the Simple View correctly identifies decoding as necessary and is preserved in the reconstruction while being supplemented.
> 
> **Key Works:** With Tunmer, "Decoding, Reading, and Reading Disability" (1986); with Hoover, "The Simple View of Reading" (1990).
> 
> **Relevance to This Analysis:** The Simple View's empirical validity for early readers is the core of what survives dialectical scrutiny in the received view.

> [!person] **Keith Stanovich (1950–present)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-dialectical-re-examination-2026-03-29]])*
> **Core Contribution:** Identified the Matthew Effect in reading, showing that reading development is self-amplifying — advantages and disadvantages compound over time through the mechanism of vocabulary and prior knowledge development.
> 
> **Role in the Dialectical Arc:** Central to the critical lens challenge in Phase III; the Matthew Effect describes the population-level consequence of the situation model being prior-knowledge-dependent.
> 
> **Key Works:** "Matthew Effects in Reading" (1986); *Progress in Understanding Reading* (2000).
> 
> **Cross-References:** [[Keith-Stanovich]], [[Matthew-Effect-in-Reading]]

> [!person] **Teun A. van Dijk (b. 1943) & Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Van Dijk (University of Amsterdam) and Kintsch (University of Colorado) are the co-developers of the Construction-Integration model and the textbase/situation model distinction. Van Dijk's early work focused on discourse grammar and macro-structural analysis; Kintsch brought computational modeling and experimental psychology. Their collaboration produced *Strategies in Discourse Comprehension* (1983), the foundational text for the three-level architecture analyzed in this report.
> 
> **Key Works:** van Dijk & Kintsch (1983), *Strategies in Discourse Comprehension*; Kintsch (1988), "The Role of Knowledge in Discourse Comprehension: A Construction-Integration Model"; Kintsch (1998), *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*.
> 
> **Lineage:** Built on Bartlett's schema theory (1932), Fillmore's case grammar (1968), and propositional theories of meaning. Their work was extended by Zwaan & Radvansky (situation model dimensions), Graesser et al. (inference generation), and Mayer (multimedia learning).
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The three-level architecture (surface code/textbase/situation model) and the Construction-Integration model are the primary theoretical framework for this entire analysis.

> [!person] **Rolf Zwaan (b. 1961) & Gabriel Radvansky (b. 1963)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Zwaan (Erasmus University Rotterdam) and Radvansky (University of Notre Dame) developed the Event Indexing Model of situation model construction. Their work systematically identified the five dimensions (CATSM) along which readers track situational coherence.
> 
> **Key Works:** Zwaan, Langston & Graesser (1995), "The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension"; Zwaan & Radvansky (1998), "Situation models in language comprehension and memory."
> 
> **Lineage:** Extended van Dijk & Kintsch's framework by specifying the internal structure of the situation model; influenced by research on mental simulation (Barsalou) and mental models (Johnson-Laird).
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The CATSM dimensions framework, the Causal Spine Bottleneck analysis, and the diagnostic use of dimension-specific comprehension failures all build directly on Zwaan & Radvansky.

> [!person] **Michelene Chi (b. 1950)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Chi (Arizona State University, previously University of Pittsburgh) is the primary researcher behind the self-explanation effect. Her studies of expert-novice differences in physics problem solving revealed that spontaneous self-explanation — generating causal accounts of worked examples — is the primary mechanism distinguishing experts from novices during learning.
> 
> **Key Works:** Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann & Glaser (1989), "Self-Explanations: How Students Study and Use Examples in Learning to Solve Problems"; Chi et al. (1994).
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by expertise research (Ericsson, Simon) and constructivist learning theory; her work grounded in think-aloud protocol analysis.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Chi's self-explanation research provides the primary empirical evidence for the Generation Constraint and its role in situation model construction.

> [!person] **Frederic C. Bartlett (1886–1969)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Bartlett (Cambridge University) developed schema theory in his landmark work *Remembering* (1932), demonstrating that memory is reconstructive rather than reproductive — that people remember schematized, interpreted versions of events, not verbatim records.
> 
> **Key Works:** Bartlett (1932), *Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology*.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Gestalt psychology and James's functionalism; anticipated by Peirce and Dewey; extended by Rumelhart, Minsky (frames), and Schank & Abelson (scripts).
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Schema theory provides the theoretical foundation for the prior knowledge dimension of situation model construction — specifically why prior knowledge is not merely helpful but structurally necessary.

> [!person] **John D. Karpicke (b. 1981)** *(from [[situation-model-construction-focused-analysis-2026-03-29]])*
> Karpicke (Purdue University) is a leading researcher on retrieval practice and the testing effect, whose studies have most directly documented the Fluency Illusion in academic reading contexts.
> 
> **Key Works:** Karpicke & Roediger (2008), "The Critical Importance of Retrieval for Learning"; Karpicke & Blunt (2011), "Retrieval Practice Produces More Learning than Elaborative Studying."
> 
> **Lineage:** Extends Ebbinghaus's memory research and Roediger's retrieval practice work; provides the experimental basis for retrieval-based learning interventions.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Karpicke's research provides the evidence for the Fluency Illusion and the basis for the post-reading free recall intervention.

> [!person] **Fergus I. M. Craik (b. 1935) and Robert S. Lockhart (b. 1939)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Craik and Lockhart, working together at the University of Toronto, published the foundational [[Craik-and-Lockhart's-1972-paper|Levels of Processing paper]] in 1972, proposing that memory retention is a function of the depth of encoding rather than the structural rehearsal system postulated by Atkinson and Shiffrin. Their framework established the theoretical context within which EI research emerged and is most commonly interpreted.
> 
> **Key Works:** Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior*, 11(6), 671-684.
> 
> **Lineage:** Craik and Lockhart built on the information-processing tradition (Atkinson & Shiffrin) and provided the theoretical architecture that Pressley and colleagues later applied to EI. The LOP framework was subsequently extended and critiqued extensively; van Dijk and Kintsch's three-level model provides a more architecturally specific account of what "depth" means in text comprehension.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The LOP framework is the standard explanation for EI that this report critiques as insufficiently specific. Craik and Lockhart's contribution is honored — deep processing is genuinely what EI produces — but the report argues that "situation model construction" specifies the mechanism more precisely than "depth of processing" does.

> [!person] **Teun van Dijk (b. 1943) and Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Van Dijk and Kintsch, working in discourse psychology through the 1970s-1990s, developed the construction-integration model of text comprehension that introduced the critical three-level distinction (surface form, textbase, situation model). Kintsch's subsequent work refined the model extensively, making it the dominant theoretical framework in reading comprehension research.
> 
> **Key Works:** van Dijk, T. A., & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies of discourse comprehension.* New York: Academic Press. Kintsch, W. (1998). *Comprehension: A paradigm for cognition.* Cambridge University Press.
> 
> **Lineage:** Van Dijk built on the text grammar tradition; Kintsch brought propositional analysis and later connectionist mechanisms into the model. Their framework is the most widely used theoretical account of reading comprehension in cognitive science.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The three-level model is the primary analytical framework. The situation model / textbase distinction is the architectural foundation of the Comprehension Gateway Mechanism.

> [!person] **Michael Pressley (1951–2006)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Pressley, working primarily at the University of Maryland and later the University at Albany, was the most productive researcher in the EI tradition and contributed more than any other individual to establishing EI as a validated learning strategy. His research program systematically explored EI's boundary conditions, the prior knowledge moderator, and the generation advantage.
> 
> **Key Works:** Pressley, M., McDaniel, M. A., Turnure, J. E., Wood, E., & Ahmad, M. (1987). Generation and precision of elaboration: Effects on intentional and incidental learning. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition*, 13(2), 291-300.
> 
> **Lineage:** Pressley built on the LOP framework and the broader cognitive strategies research tradition (Flavell on metacognition, Palincsar and Brown on reciprocal teaching). His research is the primary empirical foundation for this report.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The empirical evidence base is primarily the Pressley research program. The analysis develops a mechanistic account that explains why Pressley's empirical patterns — prior knowledge moderation, generation advantage — look the way they do.

> [!person] **John Dunlosky (b. 1963 est.)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-30]])*
> Dunlosky, working at Kent State University, has been the most influential synthesizer of the learning strategies literature, conducting the most comprehensive meta-analytic review (Dunlosky et al., 2013) that assessed EI's utility alongside nine other major strategies.
> 
> **Key Works:** Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest*, 14(1), 4-58.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Dunlosky et al. meta-analysis provides the evidence synthesis and the framework for evaluating EI's utility rating and boundary conditions.

> [!person] **Alan D. Baddeley (1934– )** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Alan Baddeley** is the founder and primary architect of the multicomponent working memory model. His 2000 review in *Nature Reviews Neuroscience* remains one of the most cited papers in cognitive psychology. Baddeley's work spans the entire developmental arc of the model from 1974 through the 2000 episodic buffer addition and subsequent empirical work. He served as Director of the Medical Research Council's Applied Psychology Unit (APU) in Cambridge, which produced many of the key empirical studies supporting the model. His broader research programme addresses amnesia, prospective memory, and the relationship between working memory and long-term memory consolidation.

> [!person] **Graham Hitch (1945– )** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Graham Hitch** co-developed the multicomponent model with Baddeley in the landmark 1974 paper. His sustained contributions to the empirical investigation of working memory — particularly the phonological loop's role in cognitive development and mathematical cognition — extended the model's scope across the lifespan. His later work with Christopher Jarrold on working memory and developmental disability has influenced understanding of intellectual developmental disorders.

> [!person] **Nelson Cowan (1951– )** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Nelson Cowan** developed the embedded-processes model of working memory as the primary theoretical alternative to Baddeley's multicomponent framework. His 2001 capacity estimate of ~4 chunks in the focus of attention has become a widely cited marker of working memory's fundamental limit. His work on the development of working memory in childhood (alongside colleagues including Candice Morey and Christopher Jarrold) has been particularly influential on developmental cognitive psychology.

> [!person] **John Sweller** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **John Sweller** developed [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]] explicitly from Baddeley's working memory architecture, first articulating the theory in his 1988 paper on cognitive load during problem-solving. His programme of research identified the split-attention effect, the worked-example effect, the modality effect, and many other instructional phenomena predicted by CLT, and his collaborations with Fred Paas, Paul Chandler, and others produced the extensive meta-analytic evidence base that CLT now rests on.

> [!person] **Richard Mayer (1947– )** *(from [[baddeley-model-of-working-memory-foundational-report-2026-04-03]])*
> **Richard Mayer** developed the [[Cognitive-Theory-of-Multimedia-Learning]] in parallel with CLT, drawing on Baddeley's dual-channel architecture to produce twelve multimedia design principles supported by a large body of controlled experimental evidence. His textbook *Multimedia Learning* (2001; 2nd ed. 2009) is one of the most widely used educational psychology references internationally. His research on the modality effect, coherence principle, and segmenting principle has directly informed e-learning design worldwide.

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** — University of Colorado Boulder** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Core contribution:** Development of the Construction-Integration model of text comprehension (with Teun van Dijk, 1978; independently, 1988), the single most influential computational-cognitive theory of reading comprehension. Also developed the textbase/situation model distinction that transformed how comprehension researchers operationalise "understanding."
> 
> **Key works cited:** Kintsch & van Dijk (1978); Kintsch (1988) *Learning from Text, Levels of Comprehension*; Kintsch (1998) *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*
> 
> **Intellectual relationship:** Built on van Dijk's discourse analysis; the CI model responded to Bartlett's schema theory by providing a computational mechanism; influenced by information processing theory and parallel distributed processing models.
> 
> **See also:** [[Walter-Kintsch]]

> [!person] **Ann Brown (1943–1999)** — UC Berkeley** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Core contribution:** Applied metacognition theory to reading comprehension, developing both the theoretical framework for comprehension monitoring and the empirical methodology for studying it. Co-developed Reciprocal Teaching (with [[Reciprocal-Teaching|Annemarie Palincsar]]) — the most extensively validated reading comprehension intervention in educational research.
> 
> **Key works:** Brown (1978) *Knowing when, where, and how to remember: A problem of metacognition*; Palincsar & Brown (1984) *Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities*
> 
> **Intellectual relationship:** Extension of Flavell's metacognition framework into reading; influenced by Lev Vygotsky's zone of proximal development in the design of Reciprocal Teaching.
> 
> **See also:** [[Ann-Brown]], [[Metacognition]], [[Comprehension-Monitoring]]

> [!person] **Rolf Zwaan (b. 1961)** — Erasmus University Rotterdam** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Core contribution:** Development of the Event-Indexing Model of situation model construction (with Langston & Graesser, 1995), which specified the five dimensions (time, space, causality, intentionality, entity identity) along which readers track discourse-denoted situations. Also major contributions to the embodied cognition account of language and text comprehension.
> 
> **Key works:** Zwaan, Langston & Graesser (1995) *The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension*; Zwaan & Madden (2004) *Updating situation models*
> 
> **Intellectual relationship:** Extended Kintsch and van Dijk's situation model concept into a detailed multi-dimensional processing model; influenced by Johnson-Laird's mental model theory.
> 
> **See also:** [[Rolf-Zwaan]], [[Situation-Model]], [[Situation-Models-in-Text-Comprehension]]

> [!person] **Patricia Alexander** — University of Maryland** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> **Core contribution:** The Model of Domain Learning (MDL) — a developmental model of how domain knowledge and reading interest interact across three stages (acclimation, competence, proficiency) to shape academic reading comprehension. Alexander's research demonstrates that reading strategies interact differently with domain knowledge depending on which stage the reader occupies.
> 
> **Key works:** Alexander (1997) *Mapping the multidimensional nature of domain learning*; Alexander, Kulikowich & Schulze (1994) *How subject-matter knowledge affects recall and interest*
> 
> **Intellectual relationship:** Integrates schema theory, interest theory, and strategy research in a developmental frame; compatible with the CI model but adds a longitudinal, motivational dimension.
> 
> **See also:** [[Patricia-Alexander]]

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> Austrian-American cognitive psychologist and originator of the Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension. His decades-long research program at the University of Colorado produced the most comprehensive and empirically validated theory of reading comprehension in cognitive science.
> 
> *Core contribution:* The three-level text representation model (surface code → textbase → situation model) and the Construction-Integration computational model that describes how meaning is constructed from text through spreading activation and integration cycles.
> 
> *Relationship to other figures:* Extended and formalized insights from Bartlett's schema theory; his situation model concept integrates with Johnson-Laird's mental models; his CI model provides computational grounding for the psychological work of Graesser and Zwaan.
> 
> *Key work:* Kintsch (1988); van Dijk & Kintsch (1983)

> [!person] **John H. Flavell (b. 1928)** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> American developmental psychologist at Stanford, credited with establishing metacognition as a formal scientific construct. His research on children's memory monitoring in the 1970s initiated four decades of metacognition research.
> 
> *Core contribution:* The metacognition framework distinguishing metacognitive knowledge (person, task, and strategy knowledge) from metacognitive experiences, and the formal definition of metacognition as cognition about cognition with self-regulatory functions.
> 
> *Relationship to other figures:* His framework was extended by Ann Brown to reading comprehension contexts; Schraw & Moshman refined his knowledge taxonomy; Nelson & Narens formalized his monitoring-control distinction.
> 
> *Key work:* Flavell (1976, 1979)

> [!person] **Ann Leslie Brown (1943–1999)** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> British-American educational psychologist at UC Berkeley, whose research translated metacognition into reading comprehension instruction. She developed Reciprocal Teaching with Annemarie Palincsar, the most validated reading comprehension intervention in the literature.
> 
> *Core contribution:* Application of Flavell's metacognitive framework to reading comprehension in children; identification of comprehension monitoring as the critical trainable metacognitive process; development of Reciprocal Teaching as a systematic instructional approach.
> 
> *Key work:* Brown (1978, 1980); Palincsar & Brown (1984)

> [!person] **Thomas Nelson & Louis Narens (1990s)** *(from [[developing-reading-comprehension-and-metacognition-for-academic-texts-foundational-report-2026-04-08]])*
> Cognitive psychologists who formalized the monitoring-control distinction in metacognition into the influential two-level (object-level / meta-level) computational model. Their framework provided theoretical rigor to the mechanism by which metacognitive monitoring and regulation operate.
> 
> *Core contribution:* The formal monitoring-control model with bidirectional information flow between object level and meta level; the distinguishing of monitoring (meta → object information about cognitive state) from control (meta → object regulation of cognitive processes).
> 
> *Key work:* Nelson & Narens (1990, 1994)

> [!person] **Michael Pressley (1951–2006)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Professor of Educational Psychology and co-director of the Cognitive Strategy Instruction Research Group; among the most influential educational psychologists of the late 20th century in the study of learning strategies. Pressley's research program on cognitive strategies — beginning in the 1970s and extending through the 1990s — established the empirical foundations for EI, keyword mnemonics, reciprocal teaching, and self-regulated reading comprehension. His collaborative work with colleagues including [[Woloshyn,-Pressley-&-Schneider-1992|Woloshyn and Schneider]] directly established the prior knowledge moderator in the EI literature.
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in cognitive developmental psychology; influenced by [[Jean-Piaget|Piagetian]] constructivism, the information processing tradition, and John Flavell's metacognition research.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Provides the foundational empirical program for EI; the prior knowledge moderator he documented is the central empirical finding this report analyses.

> [!person] **Mark McDaniel (Contemporary)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Professor at Washington University in St. Louis; co-developer (with Carol Donnelly) of the definitive mechanistic account of elaborative interrogation. McDaniel's research integrates cognitive experimental psychology with educational application, and his work on the generation effect, desirable difficulties, and EI provides the most theoretically rigorous account of when and why EI works. The 2013 Dunlosky et al. meta-analysis, in which McDaniel is a co-author, provides the most comprehensive comparative evaluation of learning strategies.
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in the experimental cognitive tradition; influenced by Fergus Craik's levels-of-processing framework and Robert Bjork's desirable difficulties research.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** McDaniel & Donnelly (1996) is the central primary source for the mechanism analysis in Phase IV.

> [!person] **John Dunlosky (Contemporary)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Professor at Kent State University; director of the Center for Research in Applied Cognition. His 2013 paper with Rawson, Marsh, Nathan, and Willingham — "Improving Students' Learning with Effective Learning Techniques" — constitutes the most influential and comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation of study strategies and directly establishes EI's "moderate utility" rating in the broader strategy landscape.
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in cognitive experimental psychology; central figure in translational cognitive science linking laboratory memory research to educational practice.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Dunlosky et al. (2013) framework provides the comparative context for EI's effectiveness relative to the full landscape of study strategies.

> [!person] **Fergus Craik (Contemporary)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Emeritus Professor at the Rotman Research Institute, Toronto; co-author with Robert Lockhart of the 1972 levels-of-processing paper that established the theoretical framework within which EI is most naturally understood. Craik's subsequent work on elaboration within processing depth directly informs the distinction between sparse and rich elaborations that is central to this report's mechanism analysis.
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in the Bartlettian cognitive tradition; influenced by William James's account of attention and memory. [[Fergus-I.-M.-Craik|Fergus I. M. Craik]] represents the bridge between classic verbal memory research and contemporary cognitive neuroscience.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** LOP theory is one of the three theoretical pillars of the EI mechanism account; Craik's framework is referenced throughout Phase III and IV.

> [!person] **Merlin Wittrock (1931–2007)** *(from [[elaborative-interrogation-foundational-report-2026-03-30]])*
> Professor at UCLA; originator of generative learning theory (1974, 1990). Wittrock's work established that learning is fundamentally a constructive process and that instructional interventions should maximise active knowledge construction rather than passive reception. His generative model anticipates EI's design and provides the broader theoretical home in which EI's specific mechanism is situated.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Ausubel's meaningful learning theory and Piaget's constructivism; represents the educational psychology bridge between cognitive theory and instructional design.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Generative learning theory is the second theoretical pillar of the mechanism analysis and directly predicts EI's design requirements.

> [!person] **John H. Flavell (b. 1928)** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Developmental psychologist, Stanford University. Coined the term "metacognition" and developed the foundational tripartite taxonomy distinguishing metacognitive knowledge, metacognitive experiences, and metacognitive regulation. His 1979 paper "Metacognition and Cognitive Monitoring" in *American Psychologist* established the field's conceptual architecture and launched the empirical program that would produce the reading comprehension monitoring literature.
> 
> **Lineage:** Drew on Piaget's developmental tradition; influenced Ann Brown, who applied the framework to reading. Influenced by the information-processing revolution; influenced virtually the entire metacognition field.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Provides the foundational conceptual taxonomy; essentially all reading metacognition research derives from or responds to his framework.

> [!person] **Ann L. Brown (1943–1999)** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Developmental and educational psychologist, University of California, Berkeley. Brown's contributions to metacognitive reading research were twin-tracked: empirical (demonstrating comprehension monitoring deficits in poor readers and younger students) and pedagogical (co-developing Reciprocal Teaching with Palincsar). Her synthesis of Flavell's framework with Vygotsky's Zone of Proximal Development produced the social-constructivist metacognitive pedagogy that reciprocal teaching instantiates.
> 
> **Lineage:** Student of the Flavellian tradition; collaborator with [[Anneliese-Palincsar]] on instructional applications; influenced by Vygotsky via the Zone of Proximal Development.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Central to Phases III and V; her distinction between monitoring (evaluation) and regulation (fix-up) anchors the mechanistic treatment in Phase IV.

> [!person] **Gregory Schraw** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Educational psychologist; developed the Schraw-Moshman bipartite metacognitive framework and the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory (MAI), the most widely used self-report measure of metacognition in educational research. His theoretical contribution clarified the separability of knowledge-of-cognition from regulation-of-cognition as empirically distinct constructs with different developmental trajectories and instructional implications.
> 
> **Lineage:** Works within the Flavellian tradition; extended by Paris's declarative/procedural/conditional taxonomy; influenced by information-processing theories of self-regulation.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Schraw-Moshman framework anchors the conceptual foundations in Phase II and the theoretical landscape in Phase III.

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Cognitive psychologist, University of Colorado at Boulder. Kintsch's Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension provides the foundational architecture for understanding text representation at multiple levels, distinguishing surface code, textbase, and situation model. This three-level architecture is the theoretical ground on which monitoring-level distinctions are built in this report.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by propositional representation theories; developed the situation model concept with Teun van Dijk; foundational influence on all subsequent reading comprehension research.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The textbase/situation model distinction in Phase II and the four-layer monitoring architecture in Phase VI derive directly from his theoretical framework.

> [!person] **Paul Pintrich (1952–2003)** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Educational psychologist, University of Michigan. Pintrich's integrative framework for self-regulated learning — particularly his 4×4 matrix identifying both phases and domains of self-regulation — provided the motivational-cognitive integration that the purely cognitive metacognitive reading literature required. His Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ) operationalized metacognitive reading regulation as a measurable, motivationally embedded construct.
> 
> **Lineage:** Worked in the intersection of motivation theory and cognitive strategy research; collaborated extensively with Zimmerman and was deeply influenced by Bandura's Social Cognitive Theory.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Phase III's SRL section draws directly on Pintrich's framework; the motivational dimension of self-regulated reading in Phase III.4 reflects his contribution.

> [!person] **Barry Zimmerman (b. 1942)** *(from [[metacognition-and-reading-foundational-report-2026-03-31]])*
> Educational psychologist, CUNY Graduate Center. Zimmerman's cyclical model of self-regulated learning — with its three-phase forethought-performance-self-reflection architecture — provides the temporal scaffolding within which metacognitive reading regulation operates. His work on self-efficacy and reading strategy use established the motivational boundary conditions for strategic reading.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Bandura's self-efficacy theory; independently developed a self-regulation framework convergent with but distinct from Pintrich's; collaborated with Schunk on academic self-regulation.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Phase III.4 and the synthesis in Phase VI draw on his cyclical SRL model.

> [!person] **Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi (1934–2021)** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Hungarian-American psychologist; Primary contributor: [[Flow-Theory|Flow theory]] as applied to optimal experience in cognitively demanding activities. Flow's relevance to motivated academic reading: the flow channel (difficulty-to-skill ratio) provides the theoretical basis for text difficulty calibration as a motivational strategy. Key connection to this report: the optimal reading challenge zone specification derives directly from flow theory's challenge-skill balance principle.

> [!person] **Edward Deci and Richard Ryan** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Developers of [[Self-Determination-Theory]] (SDT); primary contribution: the distinction between autonomous and controlled motivation, the three basic psychological needs framework (autonomy, competence, relatedness), and the internalization continuum. Central to this report's Section 4, Tier 3 strategies, and the SDT-applied framework for reading environment design.

> [!person] **Sanna Hidi and K. Ann Renninger** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Developers of the four-phase [[Interest-Theory]] model; primary contribution: the developmental taxonomy of situational and individual interest and the mechanisms through which interest transitions across phases. Central to this report's Section 3 and the interest-building reading program strategy.

> [!person] **Thomas O. Nelson and Louis Narens** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Developers of the monitoring-control metacognitive framework; primary contribution: the distinction between meta-level monitoring and object-level control as the foundational architecture of metacognitive self-regulation. Central to this report's Section 7 and the comprehension monitoring analysis.

> [!person] **Barry Zimmerman (1942–2017)** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Developer of the cyclical [[Self-Regulated-Learning]] model; primary contribution: the forethought-performance-self-reflection cycle as the structural template for self-regulated academic performance. Central to this report's Section 7 and the reading self-regulation architecture.

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch** *(from [[motivated-academic-reading-foundational-report-2026-04-10]])*
> Cognitive psychologist; primary contributor with Teun van Dijk: the construction-integration model of reading comprehension and the three-level text representation framework (surface code → textbase → situation model). Foundational to this report's Section 2 and the entire cognitive architecture analysis.

> [!person] **Teun van Dijk (b. 1943)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> Dutch discourse analyst; Professor Emeritus, Universitat Pompeu Fabra (Barcelona). With Walter Kintsch, developed the tripartite text representation framework in *Strategies in Discourse Comprehension* (1983), introducing the situation model concept. Van Dijk's primary contribution was the discourse-analytical architecture: macrostructure, superstructure, and the situational dimension of comprehension.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Chomskyan linguistics and European structuralism; influenced later work in critical discourse analysis and sociolinguistic approaches to reading.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Co-originator of the three-level representation architecture that is this report's foundational theoretical commitment.

> [!person] **Walter Kintsch (b. 1932)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> Austrian-American cognitive psychologist; Professor Emeritus, University of Colorado Boulder. Developed propositional analysis methodology (with van Dijk, 1978), formalized the Construction-Integration model (1988), and produced the comprehensive synthesis *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition* (1998). Among the most influential psycholinguists of the 20th century.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by information processing psychology, cognitive science, and connectionist modeling; influenced Zwaan, van den Broek, and the subsequent generation of discourse psychologists.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The C-I model is the primary process account of situation model construction throughout this report.

> [!person] **Rolf Zwaan (b. ~1963)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> Dutch cognitive scientist; Professor, Erasmus University Rotterdam. Developed the Event Indexing Model (with Langston & Graesser, 1995; with Radvansky, 1998) and the embodied simulation account of language comprehension. His situation change paradigm provided the primary empirical methodology for testing the five-dimension account.
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in the Kintsch tradition; influenced by Perky's mental imagery research and Barsalou's perceptual symbol systems theory.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Event Indexing Model provides the structural account of what situation models contain, and is the theoretical basis for the DIME annotation protocol.

> [!person] **Morton Ann Gernsbacher (b. ~1955)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> American cognitive psychologist; Professor, University of Wisconsin–Madison. Developed the Structure Building Framework (1990) and the suppression hypothesis. Her research on individual differences in suppression efficiency provided the most direct evidence that comprehension skill is substantially determined by inhibitory capacity.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Kintsch and by associative memory research; influenced work on comprehension differences in autism spectrum conditions.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Structure Building Framework's suppression mechanism is incorporated into Phase IV's account of situation model failure modes and individual differences in comprehension.

> [!person] **Arthur Graesser (b. ~1945)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> American cognitive psychologist; Professor, University of Memphis. Co-developer of Constructionist Theory (with Singer & Trabasso, 1994) and prolific contributor to discourse processing and intelligent tutoring research. Principal author of *Handbook of Discourse Processes* (2003).
> 
> **Lineage:** Trained in experimental cognitive psychology; influenced by Kintsch, van Dijk, and Schank's conceptual dependency theory.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Constructionist Theory provides the specification of which inference types are automatic versus strategic — the theoretical foundation for this report's prescriptive reading strategies.

> [!person] **Paul van den Broek (b. ~1955)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> Dutch cognitive psychologist; Professor, Leiden University. Developer of the Landscape Model of reading (with Risden & Husebye-Hartmann, 1995) and the standards of coherence framework. His developmental work has extended situation model theory into reading development and individual differences contexts.
> 
> **Lineage:** Influenced by Kintsch, Trabasso, and the causal inference research tradition.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** The Landscape Model provides the dynamic account of situation model activation and decay that underlies the foregrounding effect and the discussion of model updating.

> [!person] **Meredyth Daneman (active 1970s–2000s)** *(from [[situation-models-text-comprehension-foundational-report-2026-03-29]])*
> Canadian cognitive psychologist, University of Toronto. Co-developed (with Patricia Carpenter) the reading span task as a measure of working memory capacity (1980), establishing the foundational empirical link between WMC and reading comprehension.
> 
> **Relationship to Report:** Daneman & Carpenter (1980) is the foundational study for Phase IV's account of working memory constraints on situation model construction.



















































## Conceptual Tensions

> [!tension] **Fluency as Both Resource and Liability** *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Fluency in word recognition and decoding is a demonstrably necessary condition for skilled reading comprehension — readers who must allocate working memory to word decoding have fewer cognitive resources for comprehension monitoring (LaBerge & Samuels, 1974; Perfetti, 1985). This is the "simple view of reading" logic: decode fluently, and cognitive resources are freed for comprehension. Yet the evidence on the [[Fluency-Illusion]] — reviewed in Phase IV — demonstrates that *too much* fluency paradoxically suppresses the monitoring signals that comprehension requires. The reader who decodes effortlessly is, in some sense, *less* likely to notice when comprehension is failing than the reader who struggles slightly. This is not a trivial finding: it suggests that the solution to reading comprehension difficulties is not simply increased fluency practice, and that as students become more fluent, monitoring instruction becomes *more* rather than less important.

> [!tension] **The Instructional Attribution Problem** *(from [[metacognition-silent-reading-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Comprehension monitoring interventions typically target one of these three mechanisms. But researchers and practitioners frequently attribute comprehension monitoring failures to the wrong mechanism — for instance, attributing effort abandonment to strategy ignorance and responding with more strategy instruction that doesn't change the effort-cost calculus. Or attributing signal threshold failure to strategy activation failure and responding with explicit strategy selection guides that don't address the signal's weakness in the first place. The field's inconsistent results may partly reflect this attribution confusion: interventions are often well-designed for the mechanism they target but misassigned to readers whose monitoring failures arise from different mechanisms.

> [!tension] **The Self-Explanation Paradox** *(from [[silent-reading-critical-analysis-focused-analysis-2026-03-21]])*
> Here is a genuine tension: the self-explanation effect depends on the reader verbalizing internally — using inner speech to construct explanations.
