Longmans.**: The seminal review establishing comprehension monitoring as a core metacognitive skill in reading. Distinguished monitoring from other reading skills and provided the framework that subsequent decades of research built on. Cited in Phase III and throughout.

- **Bransford, J. D. & Johnson, M. K. (1972). Contextual prerequisites for understanding: Some investigations of comprehension and recall. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior*, 11, 717–726.**: Classic study demonstrating schema-dependent comprehension — participants who read the "washing clothes" passage without a title showed severely impaired comprehension and recall. Used in Phase III to establish that comprehension failures are often invisible to the reader.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M. H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science*, 18, 439–477.**: Established the self-explanation effect: readers who generate self-explanations during reading show dramatically superior comprehension and transfer compared to passive readers. Key evidence for the externalization principle in Phase III.

- **Flavell, J. H. (1979). Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry. *American Psychologist*, 34, 906–911.**: The foundational paper establishing the metacognitive knowledge/regulation/experience trichotomy used throughout this analysis. Particularly important for the concept of metacognitive experience as the trigger layer for regulation.

- **Garner, R. (1987). *Metacognition and Reading Comprehension*. Ablex.**: The most comprehensive treatment of metacognitive failures in reading. Identified the "compile to understand" illusion, documented the evidence on adult readers' poor monitoring, and provided the fix-up strategy taxonomy used in Phase IV. Core reference for the fluency trap mechanism.

- **Kintsch, W. (1998). *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*. Cambridge University Press.**: The authoritative account of the construction-integration model of text comprehension, including the textbase/situation model distinction used throughout this analysis. Provides the cognitive architecture within which comprehension monitoring must be understood.

- **LaBerge, D. & Samuels, S. J. (1974). Toward a theory of automatic information processing in reading. *Cognitive Psychology*, 6, 293–323.**: Established the automaticity account of skilled reading — the theoretical foundation for the fluency trap mechanism. The argument that decoding automatization frees resources for comprehension is here complicated by the insight that those resources are not automatically redirected to monitoring.

- **Nelson, T. O. & Narens, L. (1990). Metamemory: A theoretical framework and new findings. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), *The Psychology of Learning and Motivation* (Vol. 26, pp. 125–173). Academic Press.**: The monitoring-control model of metacognition used as the primary theoretical framework in Phase II and IV. The distinction between monitoring (upward) and control (downward) information flow provided the precise architecture for the decoupling analysis.

- **Palincsar, A. S. & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction*, 1, 117–175.**: The foundational reciprocal teaching study. Produced some of the largest effect sizes in comprehension instruction research. Analyzed here as evidence for the externalization principle: the social externalization of monitoring was the key architectural change.

- **Renkl, A. (2002). Worked-out examples: Instructional explanations support learning by self-explanations. *Learning and Instruction*, 12, 529–556.**: Strong evidence for the self-explanation effect in instructional contexts, extending the Chi et al. findings. Supports the externalization principle and the claim that it is the monitoring-externalization component of self-explanation (not elaboration per se) that drives comprehension gains.

- **Zwaan, R. A. & Radvansky, G. A. (1998). Situation models in language comprehension and memory. *Psychological Bulletin*, 123, 162–185.**: Comprehensive review of the situation model literature, establishing the five dimensions of situational coherence monitoring (temporal, causal, spatial, protagonist, intentional). Supports the three-tier monitoring model's Tier 3 specification.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 163–182.**: The foundational paper establishing the Construction-Integration model of reading. Demonstrates that reading involves two phases — construction (activating a broad associative network) and integration (constraining to coherent representations) — and that the depth of Situation Model construction determines the quality of comprehension. Central to Phases II and IV.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M.-H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: The seminal demonstration of the Self-Explanation Effect. Shows that readers who explain texts to themselves during reading produce dramatically better comprehension and transfer than readers who read without self-explanation. The mechanism — forcing Constructive mode engagement — is central to this analysis's Phase III and IV arguments.

- **Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading: Some consequences of individual differences in the acquisition of literacy. *Reading Research Quarterly, 21*(4), 360–407.**: The foundational paper establishing the Matthew Effect in reading. Documents the compounding mechanism by which early reading advantages accumulate and proposes the vocabulary-working memory link central to this analysis's account of why critical analysis development is uneven across readers.

- **Baker, L., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Metacognitive skills and reading. In P. D. Pearson (Ed.), *Handbook of Reading Research* (pp. 353–394). Longman.**: The foundational treatment of comprehension monitoring in reading. Establishes that many readers fail to detect text inconsistencies and that comprehension monitoring can be taught. Directly supports this analysis's fourth mechanism and the Illusion of Knowing argument.

- **Pressley, M., & Afflerbach, P. (1995). *Verbal Protocols of Reading: The Nature of Constructively Responsive Reading.* Lawrence Erlbaum.**: A comprehensive treatment of think-aloud protocols during reading, demonstrating the constructive and evaluative operations that skilled readers perform during silent reading. Provides empirical grounding for the inference hierarchy proposed in Phase IV.

- **Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 11*(6), 671–684.**: The original levels-of-processing paper. Establishes that depth of semantic processing — not repetition or effort per se — determines retention and comprehension quality. Foundational to Phase II's framework and the distinction between elaborative and evaluative processing.

- **Chi, M. T. H., & Wylie, R. (2014). The ICAP framework: Linking cognitive engagement to active learning outcomes. *Educational Psychologist, 49*(4), 219–243.**: The paper establishing the ICAP Framework used as a central analytical tool in Phase II. Demonstrates that Constructive and Interactive engagement modes produce significantly better learning outcomes than Active and Passive modes, and that the mode of engagement is not determined by the activity but by the cognitive operations the learner performs.

- **Bjork, R. A. (1994). Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings. In J. Metcalfe & A. Shimamura (Eds.), *Metacognition: Knowing about Knowing* (pp. 185–205). MIT Press.**: The foundational treatment of Desirable Difficulties. Establishes that processing conditions that feel more effortful produce better retention and transfer, and that fluency is a misleading guide to learning depth. Connected to the Fluency Illusion argument in Phase III.

- **Rayner, K. (1998). Eye movements in reading and information processing: 20 years of research. *Psychological Bulletin, 124*(3), 372–422.**: The most comprehensive review of eye-tracking data on reading behavior, documenting regression patterns and their relationship to inference generation and complex text processing. Provides empirical grounding for the self-pacing mechanism in Phase III.

- **Baron, J. (1995). Myside bias in thinking about abortion. *Thinking and Reasoning, 1*(3), 221–235.**: An important empirical paper on actively open-minded thinking and myside bias. Documents the tendency for motivated reasoning to filter evidence in self-serving ways, directly relevant to Phase V's argument about the confirmation bias ceiling of solo silent reading and the necessity of social discourse.

- **Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), *The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, Vol. 8* (pp. 47–89). Academic Press.**: The foundational working memory model paper, establishing the distinction between the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive. The phonological loop mechanism central to this analysis is rooted in this framework.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 163–182.**: The foundational paper establishing the Construction-Integration model of reading. Demonstrates that reading involves two phases — construction (activating a broad associative network) and integration (constraining to coherent representations) — and that the depth of Situation Model construction determines the quality of comprehension. Central to Phases II and IV.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M.-H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: The seminal demonstration of the Self-Explanation Effect. Shows that readers who explain texts to themselves during reading produce dramatically better comprehension and transfer than readers who read without self-explanation. The mechanism — forcing Constructive mode engagement — is central to this analysis's Phase III and IV arguments.

- **Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading: Some consequences of individual differences in the acquisition of literacy. *Reading Research Quarterly, 21*(4), 360–407.**: The foundational paper establishing the Matthew Effect in reading. Documents the compounding mechanism by which early reading advantages accumulate and proposes the vocabulary-working memory link central to this analysis's account of why critical analysis development is uneven across readers.

- **Baker, L., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Metacognitive skills and reading. In P. D. Pearson (Ed.), *Handbook of Reading Research* (pp. 353–394). Longman.**: The foundational treatment of comprehension monitoring in reading. Establishes that many readers fail to detect text inconsistencies and that comprehension monitoring can be taught. Directly supports this analysis's fourth mechanism and the Illusion of Knowing argument.

- **Pressley, M., & Afflerbach, P. (1995). *Verbal Protocols of Reading: The Nature of Constructively Responsive Reading.* Lawrence Erlbaum.**: A comprehensive treatment of think-aloud protocols during reading, demonstrating the constructive and evaluative operations that skilled readers perform during silent reading. Provides empirical grounding for the inference hierarchy proposed in Phase IV.

- **Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 11*(6), 671–684.**: The original levels-of-processing paper. Establishes that depth of semantic processing — not repetition or effort per se — determines retention and comprehension quality. Foundational to Phase II's framework and the distinction between elaborative and evaluative processing.

- **Chi, M. T. H., & Wylie, R. (2014). The ICAP framework: Linking cognitive engagement to active learning outcomes. *Educational Psychologist, 49*(4), 219–243.**: The paper establishing the ICAP Framework used as a central analytical tool in Phase II. Demonstrates that Constructive and Interactive engagement modes produce significantly better learning outcomes than Active and Passive modes, and that the mode of engagement is not determined by the activity but by the cognitive operations the learner performs.

- **Bjork, R. A. (1994). Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings. In J. Metcalfe & A. Shimamura (Eds.), *Metacognition: Knowing about Knowing* (pp. 185–205). MIT Press.**: The foundational treatment of Desirable Difficulties. Establishes that processing conditions that feel more effortful produce better retention and transfer, and that fluency is a misleading guide to learning depth. Connected to the Fluency Illusion argument in Phase III.

- **Rayner, K. (1998). Eye movements in reading and information processing: 20 years of research. *Psychological Bulletin, 124*(3), 372–422.**: The most comprehensive review of eye-tracking data on reading behavior, documenting regression patterns and their relationship to inference generation and complex text processing. Provides empirical grounding for the self-pacing mechanism in Phase III.

- **Baron, J. (1995). Myside bias in thinking about abortion. *Thinking and Reasoning, 1*(3), 221–235.**: An important empirical paper on actively open-minded thinking and myside bias. Documents the tendency for motivated reasoning to filter evidence in self-serving ways, directly relevant to Phase V's argument about the confirmation bias ceiling of solo silent reading and the necessity of social discourse.

- **Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. (1974). Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), *The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, Vol. 8* (pp. 47–89). Academic Press.**: The foundational working memory model paper, establishing the distinction between the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive. The phonological loop mechanism central to this analysis is rooted in this framework.

- **Rayner, K., Schotter, E. R., Masson, M. E. J., Potter, M. C., & Treiman, R. (2016). So Much to Read, So Little Time: How Do We Read, and Can Speed Reading Help? *Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 17*(1), 4–34.**: The most comprehensive scientific review of speed-reading claims against the eye movement evidence base. Systematically examines RSVP, peripheral vision claims, and sub-vocalization suppression. Supports Phases II and III. Essential reading for anyone evaluating commercial speed-reading products.

- **Perfetti, C. A. (2007). Reading Ability: Lexical Quality to Comprehension. *Scientific Studies of Reading, 11*(4), 357–383.**: Presents the Lexical Quality Hypothesis — the theoretical foundation for the vocabulary automaticity argument in Phase IV. Argues that the quality of lexical representations (their precision, completeness, and consolidation) is the primary determinant of reading ability differences. Strongly supports the highest-leverage intervention recommendation.

- **Kintsch, W., & van Dijk, T. A. (1978). Toward a Model of Text Comprehension and Production. *Psychological Review, 85*(5), 363–394.**: Original articulation of the distinction between propositional text base and situation model, foundational for Phase II's definition of comprehension. Provides the theoretical grounding for why surface-level reading metrics are insufficient as comprehension standards.

- **Carver, R. P. (1990). *Reading Rate: A Review of Research and Theory*. Academic Press.**: Comprehensive review of reading rate research establishing the empirical base rate of skilled adult reading speed. Introduces the concept of "rauding" (efficient reading at the optimal rate for comprehension), providing the theoretical foundation for the comprehension-indexed speed metric. Supports Phase III.

- **Rayner, K. (1998). Eye Movements in Reading and Information Processing: 20 Years of Research. *Psychological Bulletin, 124*(3), 372–422.**: The definitive summary of two decades of eye movement research in reading, establishing the perceptual span constraint and fixation duration norms. Foundational for Phase III's evidence review on the mechanics of skilled reading.

- **Baddeley, A. D. (2000). The Episodic Buffer: A New Component of Working Memory? *Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4*(11), 417–423.**: Updated working memory model including the episodic buffer, directly relevant to the situation model construction bottleneck. Provides theoretical grounding for Phase IV's treatment of working memory integration demands during reading.

- **Ausubel, D. P. (1960). The Use of Advance Organizers in the Learning and Retention of Meaningful Verbal Material. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 51*(5), 267–272.**: Original advance organizer study, providing empirical grounding for the prior knowledge pre-activation strategy in Phase V. Demonstrably improves both comprehension and retention through schema pre-activation.

- **Ericsson, K. A., & Kintsch, W. (1995). Long-Term Working Memory. *Psychological Review, 102*(2), 211–245.**: Theoretical account of how experts use long-term memory structures to extend effective working memory capacity in their domain. Provides the mechanistic bridge between domain expertise and the reading speed advantage — supports the schema-as-inference-engine analysis in Phase IV.

- **Bjork, R. A., & Bjork, E. L. (2011). Making Things Hard on Yourself, but in a Good Way: Creating Desirable Difficulties to Enhance Learning. In M. A. Gernsbacher et al. (Eds.), *Psychology and the Real World*. Worth Publishers.**: Foundational for the [[Fluency-Illusion]] analysis — demonstrates that subjective ease of processing is negatively correlated with actual learning depth. Directly relevant to the speed-monitoring incompatibility and the risks of bandwidth compression training.

- **Graesser, A. C., Singer, M., & Trabasso, T. (1994). Constructing Inferences During Narrative Text Comprehension. *Psychological Review, 101*(3), 371–395.**: Comprehensive framework for the types of inferences generated during reading and their resource demands. Provides the inferential bridging analysis underpinning Bottleneck 3 in Phase II, and grounds the prior knowledge pre-activation argument of Phase V.

- **Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. J. (1974)**: **Baddeley, A. D., & Hitch, G. J. (1974).** Working memory. In G. H. Bower (Ed.), *The psychology of learning and motivation* (Vol. 8, pp. 47–89). Academic Press. — The founding paper of the multicomponent working memory model. Presents the dual-task experiments that challenged the unitary short-term memory concept and proposed the phonological loop, visuospatial sketchpad, and central executive.

- **Baddeley, A. D. (2000)**: **Baddeley, A. D. (2000).** The episodic buffer: A new component of working memory? *Trends in Cognitive Sciences, 4*(11), 417–423. — The paper introducing the episodic buffer as the fourth component of the model, motivating its theoretical necessity through empirical anomalies and connecting it to conscious awareness and episodic long-term memory.

- **Baddeley, A. D. (2012)**: **Baddeley, A. D. (2012).** Working memory: Theories, models, and controversies. *Annual Review of Psychology, 63*, 1–29. — Baddeley's comprehensive review of the model's development, empirical status, and major theoretical controversies, including the competing models of Cowan and Ericsson; considered the definitive statement of the mature version of the theory.

- **Cowan, N. (2001)**: **Cowan, N. (2001).** The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity. *Behavioral and Brain Sciences, 24*(1), 87–114. — The primary statement of Cowan's embedded-processes model and his ~4-chunk capacity estimate for the focus of attention, challenging important assumptions of the Baddeley-Hitch model.

- **Miyake, A., et al. (2000)**: **Miyake, A., Friedman, N. P., Emerson, M. J., Witzki, A. H., Howerter, A., & Wager, T. D. (2000).** The unity and diversity of executive functions and their contributions to complex "frontal lobe" tasks: A latent variable analysis. *Cognitive Psychology, 41*, 49–100. — The landmark latent variable study that fractionated executive functions into shifting, updating, and inhibition, providing a principled decomposition of Baddeley's central executive.

- **Sweller, J. (1988)**: **Sweller, J. (1988).** Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. *Cognitive Science, 12*, 257–285. — The founding paper of [[Cognitive-Load-Theory]], explicitly drawing on Baddeley's working memory architecture to explain why problem-solving is often an inefficient instructional method compared to worked examples.

- **Mayer, R. E. (2009)**: **Mayer, R. E. (2009).** *Multimedia learning* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press. — The comprehensive statement of the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning with its twelve design principles, evidence base, moderating variables, and connections to Baddeley's working memory architecture.

- **Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980)**: **Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980).** Individual differences in working memory and reading. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19*, 450–466. — The introduction of the Reading Span task and the first demonstration of the strong predictive relationship between working memory capacity and reading comprehension, launching the individual differences research programme.

- **Gathercole, S. E., & Alloway, T. P. (2008)**: **Gathercole, S. E., & Alloway, T. P. (2008).** *Working memory and learning: A practical guide for teachers*. SAGE. — Applied translation of working memory research for educational practitioners, covering working memory assessment, implications for children with learning difficulties, and classroom strategies for working memory support.

- **Melby-Lervåg, M., et al. (2013)**: **Melby-Lervåg, M., & Hulme, C. (2013).** Is working memory training effective? A meta-analytic review. *Developmental Psychology, 49*(2), 270–291. — The most comprehensive meta-analysis of working memory training effects, finding robust near-transfer but no reliable far-transfer, significantly tempering earlier optimism about training-based cognitive enhancement.

- **Logie, R. H. (1995)**: **Logie, R. H. (1995).** *Visuo-spatial working memory*. Erlbaum. — The primary statement of the distinction between visual cache and inner scribe within the visuospatial sketchpad, providing theoretical refinement and neuropsychological evidence for the sketchpad's internal architecture.

- **Norman, D. A., & Shallice, T. (1986)**: **Norman, D. A., & Shallice, T. (1986).** Attention to action: Willed and automatic control of behavior. In R. J. Davidson, G. E. Schwartz, & D. Shapiro (Eds.), *Consciousness and self-regulation* (Vol. 4, pp. 1–18). Plenum. — The foundational paper for the Supervisory Attentional System (SAS), which Baddeley adopted as the theoretical model of the central executive.

- **Engle, R. W., et al. (1999)**: **Engle, R. W., Tuholski, S. W., Laughlin, J. E., & Conway, A. R. A. (1999).** Working memory, short-term memory, and general fluid intelligence: A latent-variable approach. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 128*(3), 309–331. — The latent variable study demonstrating that complex span (working memory capacity) and simple span are separable constructs, and that working memory capacity uniquely predicts fluid intelligence beyond short-term memory.

- **Kintsch, W., & van Dijk, T. A. (1978). Toward a model of text comprehension and production. *Psychological Review, 85*(5), 363–394. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.85.5.363**: **Annotation:** The foundational paper introducing the propositional theory of text comprehension that became the CI model. Introduces the textbase concept and the analysis of macro-structure construction. This report's theoretical core.
**Recommended section:** Entire paper for foundations; Section 2 on macro-structure most directly relevant to academic reading.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 163–182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.95.2.163**: **Annotation:** The paper introducing the Construction-Integration model's two-phase cycle. Essential reading for understanding the spreading activation and constraint satisfaction mechanisms discussed throughout this report.

- **Palincsar, A. S., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction, 1*(2), 117–175.**: **Annotation:** The original reciprocal teaching study, reporting both the theoretical rationale and the first experimental evidence. Effect sizes were large; this paper launched three decades of reciprocal teaching research and replication.

- **Nation, I. S. P. (2001). *Learning vocabulary in another language*. Cambridge University Press.**: **Annotation:** The definitive reference on vocabulary acquisition for reading comprehension, including the coverage threshold research establishing 98% as the functional minimum for adequate comprehension. Directly informs the vocabulary section of this report.

- **Beck, I. L., McKeown, M. G., & Kucan, L. (2013). *Bringing words to life: Robust vocabulary instruction* (2nd ed.). Guilford Press.**: **Annotation:** The primary reference for the Tier 1/2/3 vocabulary framework used throughout this report. Provides both theoretical framework and practical instructional guidance for academic vocabulary development.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M. H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: **Annotation:** The foundational study demonstrating large effects of self-explanation during text reading on comprehension and learning. The mechanism is identified as forced situation model construction through inference generation. Directly informs Section 6.

- **Stanovich, K. E. (1986). Matthew effects in reading: Some consequences of individual differences in the acquisition of literacy. *Reading Research Quarterly, 21*(4), 360–407.**: **Annotation:** The seminal theoretical account of cumulative advantage and disadvantage in reading development. The Matthew Effect metaphor (from Matthew 25:29) is introduced here. This paper's influence on reading research has been enormous and continues to shape intervention priorities.

- **Flavell, J. H. (1979). Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry. *American Psychologist, 34*(10), 906–911.**: **Annotation:** Short theoretical paper introducing the metacognition construct in its mature form. Defines metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive regulation in terms that remain standard. Critical background for this report's metacognition sections.

- **Zwaan, R. A., Langston, M. C., & Graesser, A. C. (1995). The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension: An event-indexing model. *Psychological Science, 6*(5), 292–297.**: **Annotation:** Introduces the five-dimensional Event-Indexing Model of situation model construction. Compact paper with large empirical and theoretical impact. Informs Section 5 on inference generation and situation model dimensions.

- **Willingham, D. T. (2006). How knowledge helps. *American Educator, 30*(1), 30–37.**: **Annotation:** Accessible and elegant account of why background knowledge is the most powerful lever in reading comprehension development. Argues that reading comprehension "skill" is substantially a knowledge issue. Widely assigned in teacher education; directly relevant to the knowledge-building debate (Section 7).

- **Rumelhart, D. E. (1980). Schemata: The building blocks of cognition. In R. J. Spiro, B. C. Bruce, & W. F. Brewer (Eds.), *Theoretical issues in reading comprehension* (pp. 33–58). Erlbaum.**: **Annotation:** The key theoretical chapter developing modern schema theory as a computational-cognitive framework. Defines schemas, explains their activation and inheritance properties, and articulates the schema theory account of reading comprehension. Essential background for Section 4.

- **Brown, A. L. (1987). Metacognition, executive control, self-regulation, and other more mysterious mechanisms. In F. E. Weinert & R. H. Kluwe (Eds.), *Metacognition, motivation, and understanding* (pp. 65–116). Erlbaum.**: **Annotation:** Comprehensive synthesis of Ann Brown's metacognitive monitoring research in the context of reading comprehension. Key reference for the comprehension monitoring and self-regulation sections.

- **Graesser, A. C., Singer, M., & Trabasso, T. (1994). Constructing inferences during narrative text comprehension. *Psychological Review, 101*(3), 371–395.**: **Annotation:** The constructionist theory paper distinguishing coherence from elaborative inferences and characterising the conditions under which each is generated. Informs Section 5's inference generation analysis.

- **Anderson, R.C. & Pearson, P.D. (1984). A schema-theoretic view of basic processes in reading comprehension. In P.D. Pearson (Ed.), *Handbook of Reading Research* (Vol. 1, pp. 255-291). Longman.**: *Annotation:* The foundational review establishing schema theory as the dominant framework for reading comprehension research. Demonstrates comprehensively the relationship between prior knowledge and comprehension quality. Central framework for Section 6.

- **Bartlett, F.C. (1932). *Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology*. Cambridge University Press.**: *Annotation:* The foundational empirical demonstration that memory and comprehension are schema-driven and constructive, not reproductive. His cross-cultural folk tale experiments remain compelling evidence for schema-driven comprehension distortion.

- **Chi, M.T.H., Bassok, M., Lewis, M.W., Reimann, P., & Glaser, R. (1989). Self-explanations: How students study and use examples in learning to solve problems. *Cognitive Science, 13*(2), 145-182.**: *Annotation:* The landmark study establishing the self-explanation effect. Documented that students who spontaneously self-explained during learning dramatically outperformed those who did not, launching a productive research program on elaborative learning strategies. Central to Section 5.3.

- **Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K.A., Marsh, E.J., Nathan, M.J., & Willingham, D.T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14*(1), 4-58.**: *Annotation:* The most authoritative systematic review of the evidence base for learning strategies, classifying 10 techniques by utility based on literature review. Establishes retrieval practice and elaborative interrogation as high-utility strategies; re-reading and highlighting as low-utility. Essential practical reference for Section 5.

- **Flavell, J.H. (1979). Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry. *American Psychologist, 34*(10), 906-911.**: *Annotation:* The definitive statement of the metacognition framework introducing the distinction between metacognitive knowledge and metacognitive experiences, and identifying metacognitive monitoring as a critical self-regulatory process. Foundational for Section 3.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 163-182.**: *Annotation:* Kintsch's landmark theoretical paper articulating the Construction-Integration model and establishing the theoretical distinction between textbase and situation model construction. The foundational text for the entire multi-level comprehension framework discussed in Section 1.

- **Nelson, T.O. & Narens, L. (1990). Metamemory: A theoretical framework and new findings. *The Psychology of Learning and Motivation, 26*, 125-173.**: *Annotation:* Establishes the monitoring-control framework that provides the formal computational model for metacognitive processes during reading and learning. Essential theoretical infrastructure for Section 3.2.

- **Palincsar, A.S. & Brown, A.L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction, 1*(2), 117-175.**: *Annotation:* The founding paper of Reciprocal Teaching, documenting the design rationale and initial research evidence for the four-strategy collaborative reading protocol. The most frequently cited paper in reading comprehension instruction research. Essential for Section 7.2.

- **Roediger, H.L. & Karpicke, J.D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249-255.**: *Annotation:* Landmark experimental demonstration of the testing effect showing that retrieval practice dramatically outperforms re-study for long-term retention, even when initial learning is equated. Central evidence for the strategy hierarchy in Section 5.4.

- **Zimmerman, B.J. (2000). Attaining self-regulation: A social-cognitive perspective. In M. Boekaerts, P. Pintrich, & M. Zeidner (Eds.), *Handbook of Self-Regulation* (pp. 13-39). Academic Press.**: *Annotation:* Establishes the three-phase self-regulated learning model (forethought, performance, self-reflection) that frames the metacognitive architecture of self-directed academic reading in Section 7.4.

- **McDaniel, M. A., & Donnelly, C. M. (1996). Learning with analogy and elaborative interrogation. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 88*(3), 508–519.**: The foundational mechanistic analysis of elaborative interrogation, distinguishing EI from analogical encoding and specifying the conditions under which each produces learning advantages. Establishes the accuracy constraint and the distinctiveness hypothesis as central mechanisms. Essential primary source for Phase IV's mechanism analysis.

**Recommended Sections:** The discussion section provides the most theoretically precise mechanistic account; the results section documents the prior knowledge moderation effect.

- **Pressley, M., McDaniel, M. A., Turnure, J. E., Wood, E., & Ahmad, M. (1987). Generation and precision of elaboration: Effects on intentional and incidental learning. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition, 13*(2), 291–300.**: One of the foundational studies establishing the EI effect for factual propositions. Documents the generation advantage (self-generated elaborations > read elaborations) and provides the initial framework for EI as a learnable study strategy.

**Recommended Sections:** Experiment 2 provides the most direct test of the generation component; the general discussion situates EI within the elaborative strategies literature.

- **Woloshyn, V. E., Pressley, M., & Schneider, W. (1992). Elaborative-interrogation and prior-knowledge effects on learning of facts. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 84*(1), 115–124.**: Directly addresses the prior knowledge moderator using cross-cultural comparisons (Canadian and German students studying German history and geography). Establishes that prior knowledge availability is the primary determinant of EI effectiveness, not learner age or general strategy knowledge.

**Recommended Sections:** The cross-cultural comparisons in Experiment 3 are particularly illuminating for the prior knowledge moderator; the discussion provides the clearest statement of the prior knowledge threshold problem.

- **Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. *Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14*(1), 4–58.**: The most comprehensive meta-analytic evaluation of ten major learning strategies, rating EI as "moderate utility." Provides the comparative framework situating EI relative to retrieval practice, distributed practice, self-explanation, and lower-utility strategies. Essential reading for understanding EI's position in the full strategy landscape.

**Recommended Sections:** Section 5 (Elaborative Interrogation) provides the core analysis; the general comparison across all strategies (Section 11) contextualises EI's moderate utility rating.

- **Craik, F. I. M., & Lockhart, R. S. (1972). Levels of processing: A framework for memory research. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 11*(6), 671–684.**: The foundational levels-of-processing paper providing the primary theoretical framework for EI. Required background reading for understanding why why-question answering produces superior encoding compared to re-reading or shallow study strategies.

**Recommended Sections:** The theoretical framework sections; the discussion of elaboration as encoding depth determinant (distinct from pure "depth").

- **Wittrock, M. C. (1990). Generative processes of comprehension. *Educational Psychologist, 24*(4), 345–376.**: Wittrock's mature statement of generative learning theory, situating EI within the broader framework of generative comprehension processes. Provides the theoretical home for EI as one among several generative strategies that should be cultivated in educational contexts.

**Recommended Sections:** The taxonomy of generative strategies (Section 3) contextualises EI's specific design; the instructional implications section has direct practical relevance.

- **Slamecka, N. J., & Graf, P. (1978). The generation effect: Delineation of a phenomenon. *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Learning and Memory, 4*(6), 592–604.**: The foundational paper documenting the generation effect. Required background for understanding EI's generation component and distinguishing EI's mechanism from simple generation effects.

- **Chi, M. T. H., & Wylie, R. (2014). The ICAP framework: Linking cognitive engagement to active learning outcomes. *Educational Psychologist, 49*(4), 219–243.**: Presents the ICAP framework classifying learning activities along a passive–active–constructive–interactive continuum. Positions EI within the constructive category and predicts its efficacy through the constructive engagement hypothesis.

**Recommended Sections:** The framework description and the empirical predictions for constructive vs. active learning (Sections 2-4).

- **van Dijk, T. A., & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies of discourse comprehension*. Academic Press.**: The foundational textbase/situation model framework for text comprehension. Provides the theoretical grounding for understanding how EI contributes to situation model construction by enriching the causal dimension of mental text representation.

- **Reder, L. M. (1980). The role of elaboration in the comprehension and retention of prose. *Review of Educational Research, 50*(1), 5–53.**: A comprehensive early review of elaboration research that provides important historical context for EI's development and situates it within the broader elaboration literature.

- **Pressley, M., Symons, S., McDaniel, M. A., Snyder, B. L., & Turnure, J. E. (1988). Elaborative interrogation facilitates acquisition of confusing facts. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 80*(3), 268–278.**: Documents EI's specific advantage for confusing or easily-confused factual content — an important finding for understanding EI's ecological validity in academic reading contexts where confusion and interference are common.

- **Willoughby, T., Wood, E., & Kraftcheck, E. R. (1990). Elaborative interrogation effects at different levels of learning. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 82*(1), 90–95.**: Examines whether EI effectiveness varies with learning criterion level; documents EI advantages specifically for inference-demanding outcomes (what this report calls "deep comprehension" measures).

- **Ozgungor, S., & Guthrie, J. T. (2004). Interactions among elaborative interrogation, knowledge, and interest in the process of constructing knowledge from text. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 96*(3), 437–443.**: Examines the three-way interaction between EI, prior knowledge, and topic interest; documents that motivation moderates EI effectiveness and that interest partially compensates for knowledge limitations in EI deployment.

- **Rawson, K. A., & Dunlosky, J. (2012). When is practice testing most effective for improving the durability and efficiency of student learning? *Educational Psychology Review, 24*, 419–435.**: Addresses the combination of retrieval practice and EI, providing evidence on the comparative effectiveness of EI and testing schedules for durable learning. Directly relevant to PKB practice combining EI encoding with spaced retrieval review.

- **Johnson-Laird, P.N. (1983). *Mental Models: Towards a Cognitive Science of Language, Inference, and Consciousness*. Harvard University Press.**: The foundational monograph. Establishes the theoretical framework, the contrast with rule-based theories, the empirical program, and the connection to model-theoretic semantics. Essential reading — but note that subsequent work has substantially revised the theory.

- **Johnson-Laird, P.N. & Byrne, R.M.J. (1991). *Deduction*. Erlbaum.**: The major empirical program. Systematic investigation of syllogistic, propositional, and relational reasoning from the mental models perspective. Contains the most complete presentation of the model-number predictions.

- **Rips, L.J. (1994). *The Psychology of Proof: Deductive Reasoning in Human Thinking*. MIT Press.**: The primary theoretical alternative. Develops the mental logic account (PSYCOP) in detail. Essential for understanding what mental models theory is *contrasted against*; also contains important methodological critiques.

- **Evans, J.St.B.T., Newstead, S.E., & Byrne, R.M.J. (1993). *Human Reasoning: The Psychology of Deduction*. Erlbaum.**: Comprehensive review of the empirical literature. Remains a standard reference for the difficulty effects, belief-bias findings, and comparative performance of models and rules.

- **Cheng, P.W. & Holyoak, K.J. (1985). Pragmatic reasoning schemas. *Cognitive Psychology, 17*, 391–416.**: Introduces pragmatic reasoning schemas — the main alternative that accommodates content effects within a rule-based framework. Directly challenges the interpretation of facilitation effects as evidence for mental models.

- **Oaksford, M. & Chater, N. (1994). A rational analysis of the selection task as optimal data selection. *Psychological Review, 101*, 608–631.**: Establishes the probabilistic rational analysis framework for the Wason selection task. Argues that human performance is near-optimal under realistic probabilistic assumptions — the most important challenge to both mental models and mental logic accounts.

- **Pylyshyn, Z.W. (1981). The imagery debate: Analogue media versus tacit knowledge. *Psychological Review, 88*, 16–45.**: The canonical argument that apparent analog properties of mental imagery could be artifacts of tacit knowledge rather than evidence of a genuinely analog representational format. Applies directly to the analogical status of mental models.

- **Van Dijk, T.A. & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies of Discourse Comprehension*. Academic Press.**: Develops the situation model framework in discourse comprehension — the closest empirical tradition to mental models theory with stronger methodological development and broader empirical coverage.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N. (1983). *Mental Models: Towards a Cognitive Science of Language, Inference, and Consciousness*. Cambridge University Press.**: The foundational text establishing [[Mental-Models-Theory|Mental Models Theory]] in its comprehensive form. Johnson-Laird develops the distinction between propositional representations, mental models, and mental images; proposes the three-stage inference cycle; demonstrates the model-multiplicity account of syllogistic reasoning difficulty; and extends the framework to spatial, relational, and modal reasoning. Essential primary reading for any serious engagement with the theory. Readers approaching without background in logic or cognitive science should be prepared for technical density in chapters 3–6.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N., & Byrne, R. M. J. (1991). *Deduction*. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.**: Comprehensive experimental and theoretical treatment of deductive reasoning from the mental models perspective. Reports the systematic studies of all 64 syllogistic figures, proposes the principle of truth, and develops the computational model in detail. A key reference for the empirical evidence supporting MMT over mental logic alternatives.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N., & Byrne, R. M. J. (2002). Conditionals: A theory of meaning, pragmatics, and inference. *Psychological Review*, 109(4), 646–678.**: Develops the application of the principle of truth to conditional ("if-then") reasoning — one of the most contested domains in the reasoning literature. The paper demonstrates how the principle predicts specific error patterns in conditional inference and engages directly with mental logic alternatives. Supports the Phase III discussion of the theoretical landscape and the Principle of Truth.

- **Byrne, R. M. J. (2005). *The Rational Imagination: How People Create Alternatives to Reality*. MIT Press.**: Extends MMT to counterfactual reasoning, developing the claim that people represent both the actual and the imagined alternative when thinking counterfactually. Contains extensive empirical support for the dual-model account of counterfactual cognition. Important for the Phase IV discussion of counterfactual mechanisms and for the planned expansion node on [[Counterfactual-Reasoning|Counterfactual Reasoning]].

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review*, 95(2), 163–182.**: Proposes the Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension and introduces the situation model as the deepest level of text representation. Foundational for the extension of MMT to comprehension and for the planned expansion node on [[Situation-Models-in-Text-Comprehension|Situation Models in Text Comprehension]]. Kintsch's distinction among surface form, text-base, and situation model has become standard in discourse psychology.

- **Zwaan, R. A., Langston, M. C., & Graesser, A. C. (1995). The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension: An event-indexing model. *Psychological Science*, 6(5), 292–297.**: Introduces the Event Indexing Model, specifying the five dimensions (space, time, causality, intentionality, protagonist) along which situation models are tracked during narrative comprehension. Reports reading-time studies showing that discontinuities along these dimensions slow comprehension — strong evidence that readers actively maintain and update multidimensional situation models.

- **Vosniadou, S., & Brewer, W. F. (1992). Mental models of the earth: A study of conceptual change in childhood. *Cognitive Psychology*, 24(4), 535–585.**: Reports the classic study documenting children's synthetic mental models of the Earth's shape and how these models combine naive perceptual beliefs with partially absorbed scientific information. Essential for the Phase V discussion of science education applications. Demonstrates the coherence and persistence of misconception-as-model and the inadequacy of simple information presentation as a remediation strategy.

- **Mayer, R. E. (2009). *Multimedia Learning* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.**: The most comprehensive treatment of [[Multimedia-Learning|Multimedia Learning Theory]], integrating three decades of experimental research on instructional design. Mayer's theory is explicitly grounded in the mental model framework: his "generative theory of multimedia learning" proposes that learners build verbal models, pictorial models, and an integrated mental model, and that effective instruction supports this construction without overloading working memory channels. Directly relevant to Phase V applications.

- **Hegarty, M., & Just, M. A. (1993). Constructing mental models of machines from text and diagrams. *Journal of Memory and Language*, 32(6), 717–742.**: Key empirical study demonstrating that mechanical reasoning depends on the construction and mental animation of spatial mental models. Readers who received only text were less able to reason about the mechanism than those receiving diagrams — not because the text was inadequate propositionally, but because the text made model construction more effortful. Supports the Phase IV discussion of spatial mental models and mental simulation.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N. (1983). *Mental Models: Towards a Cognitive Science of Language, Inference, and Consciousness*. Cambridge University Press.**: The foundational text establishing [[Mental-Models-Theory|Mental Models Theory]] in its comprehensive form. Johnson-Laird develops the distinction between propositional representations, mental models, and mental images; proposes the three-stage inference cycle; demonstrates the model-multiplicity account of syllogistic reasoning difficulty; and extends the framework to spatial, relational, and modal reasoning. Essential primary reading for any serious engagement with the theory. Readers approaching without background in logic or cognitive science should be prepared for technical density in chapters 3–6.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N., & Byrne, R. M. J. (1991). *Deduction*. Lawrence Erlbaum Associates.**: Comprehensive experimental and theoretical treatment of deductive reasoning from the mental models perspective. Reports the systematic studies of all 64 syllogistic figures, proposes the principle of truth, and develops the computational model in detail. A key reference for the empirical evidence supporting MMT over mental logic alternatives.

- **Johnson-Laird, P. N., & Byrne, R. M. J. (2002). Conditionals: A theory of meaning, pragmatics, and inference. *Psychological Review*, 109(4), 646–678.**: Develops the application of the principle of truth to conditional ("if-then") reasoning — one of the most contested domains in the reasoning literature. The paper demonstrates how the principle predicts specific error patterns in conditional inference and engages directly with mental logic alternatives. Supports the Phase III discussion of the theoretical landscape and the Principle of Truth.

- **Byrne, R. M. J. (2005). *The Rational Imagination: How People Create Alternatives to Reality*. MIT Press.**: Extends MMT to counterfactual reasoning, developing the claim that people represent both the actual and the imagined alternative when thinking counterfactually. Contains extensive empirical support for the dual-model account of counterfactual cognition. Important for the Phase IV discussion of counterfactual mechanisms and for the planned expansion node on [[Counterfactual-Reasoning|Counterfactual Reasoning]].

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review*, 95(2), 163–182.**: Proposes the Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension and introduces the situation model as the deepest level of text representation. Foundational for the extension of MMT to comprehension and for the planned expansion node on [[Situation-Models-in-Text-Comprehension|Situation Models in Text Comprehension]]. Kintsch's distinction among surface form, text-base, and situation model has become standard in discourse psychology.

- **Zwaan, R. A., Langston, M. C., & Graesser, A. C. (1995). The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension: An event-indexing model. *Psychological Science*, 6(5), 292–297.**: Introduces the Event Indexing Model, specifying the five dimensions (space, time, causality, intentionality, protagonist) along which situation models are tracked during narrative comprehension. Reports reading-time studies showing that discontinuities along these dimensions slow comprehension — strong evidence that readers actively maintain and update multidimensional situation models.

- **Vosniadou, S., & Brewer, W. F. (1992). Mental models of the earth: A study of conceptual change in childhood. *Cognitive Psychology*, 24(4), 535–585.**: Reports the classic study documenting children's synthetic mental models of the Earth's shape and how these models combine naive perceptual beliefs with partially absorbed scientific information. Essential for the Phase V discussion of science education applications. Demonstrates the coherence and persistence of misconception-as-model and the inadequacy of simple information presentation as a remediation strategy.

- **Mayer, R. E. (2009). *Multimedia Learning* (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press.**: The most comprehensive treatment of [[Multimedia-Learning|Multimedia Learning Theory]], integrating three decades of experimental research on instructional design. Mayer's theory is explicitly grounded in the mental model framework: his "generative theory of multimedia learning" proposes that learners build verbal models, pictorial models, and an integrated mental model, and that effective instruction supports this construction without overloading working memory channels. Directly relevant to Phase V applications.

- **Hegarty, M., & Just, M. A. (1993). Constructing mental models of machines from text and diagrams. *Journal of Memory and Language*, 32(6), 717–742.**: Key empirical study demonstrating that mechanical reasoning depends on the construction and mental animation of spatial mental models. Readers who received only text were less able to reason about the mechanism than those receiving diagrams — not because the text was inadequate propositionally, but because the text made model construction more effortful. Supports the Phase IV discussion of spatial mental models and mental simulation.

- **Flavell, J. H. (1979). Metacognition and cognitive monitoring: A new area of cognitive-developmental inquiry. *American Psychologist*, 34(10), 906–911. https://doi.org/10.1037/0003-066X.34.10.906**: The foundational paper for the entire field. Flavell introduces the term "metacognition," provides the tripartite taxonomy of metacognitive knowledge, experiences, and regulation, and outlines the research program that would follow. Essential reading for understanding the conceptual origins of all metacognitive reading research.

**Recommended Sections:** Full text; particularly pp. 906–909 for the taxonomy.

- **Baker, L., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Metacognitive skills and reading. In P. D. Pearson (Ed.), *Handbook of reading research* (pp. 353–394). Longman.**: The defining synthesis of metacognitive principles applied to reading comprehension. Baker and Brown articulate comprehension monitoring, its evaluation standards, and the fix-up strategy repertoire with a precision that subsequent research has not substantially superseded. Essential for Phases III and IV of this report.

**Recommended Sections:** Sections on evaluation standards (pp. 359–368) and regulatory responses (pp. 368–382).

- **Nelson, T. O., & Narens, L. (1990). Metamemory: A theoretical framework and new findings. *Psychology of Learning and Motivation*, 26, 125–173. https://doi.org/10.1016/S0079-7421(08)60053-5**: Establishes the object-level/meta-level architecture and the monitoring-control framework that provides the formal computational backbone for the field. Indispensable for the mechanistic analysis in Phase IV; the monitoring-control coupling concept derives directly from this framework.

**Recommended Sections:** Sections 2 and 3 on the formal framework; the empirical work on JoL and FoK.

- **Palincsar, A. S., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction*, 1(2), 117–175. https://doi.org/10.1207/s1532690xci0102_1**: The original reciprocal teaching paper. Documents the development, theoretical rationale, and initial empirical evaluation of the intervention. Required reading for Section 5.1 of this report; provides the most important single example of metacognitive reading theory instantiated in pedagogical practice.

**Recommended Sections:** The theoretical rationale section (pp. 117–124); the transcript examples throughout.

- **Schraw, G., & Moshman, D. (1995). Metacognitive theories. *Educational Psychology Review*, 7(4), 351–371. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02212307**: Provides the bipartite knowledge-regulation taxonomy and the Metacognitive Awareness Inventory. The most widely cited single account of metacognitive structure in educational psychology.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review*, 95(2), 163–182. https://doi.org/10.1037/0033-295X.95.2.163**: Establishes the Construction-Integration model of discourse comprehension, including the textbase/situation model distinction that anchors the conceptual framework in Phase II.

- **Pressley, M., & Afflerbach, P. (1995). *Verbal protocols of reading: The nature of constructively responsive reading*. Erlbaum.**: The most comprehensive empirical account of skilled reading using think-aloud protocols; documents the metacognitive strategies that expert readers actually deploy, as distinct from what they report deploying. Essential for Section 4 and for understanding the gap between self-report and behavioral evidence.

- **Gough, P. B., & Tunmer, W. E. (1986). Decoding, reading, and reading disability. *Remedial and Special Education*, 7(1), 6–10. https://doi.org/10.1177/074193258600700104**: Original paper establishing the Simple View of Reading; the foundation for Section 2.2's account of the decoding-comprehension architecture.

- **Zimmerman, B. J. (2000). Attaining self-regulation: A social-cognitive perspective. In M. Boekaerts, P. R. Pintrich, & M. Zeidner (Eds.), *Handbook of self-regulation* (pp. 13–39). Academic Press.**: Zimmerman's systematization of his cyclic SRL model; the theoretical source for Phase III.4's treatment of self-regulated reading within the SRL framework.

- **Paris, S. G., Lipson, M. Y., & Wixson, K. K. (1983). Becoming a strategic reader. *Contemporary Educational Psychology*, 8(3), 293–316. https://doi.org/10.1016/0361-476X(83)90018-8**: Introduces the declarative/procedural/conditional trichotomy in the reading strategy context; the theoretical foundation for Phase III.3's treatment of the Schraw-Moshman framework.

- **Perfetti, C. A. (1985). *Reading ability*. Oxford University Press.**: The foundational text for Verbal Efficiency Theory; establishes the decoding-efficiency mechanism by which fluency constrains comprehension resources.

- **van Dijk, T. A., & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies of discourse comprehension*. Academic Press.**: Original source for the situation model construct; provides the full three-level text representation architecture (surface code, textbase, situation model).

- **Duffy, G. G., Roehler, L. R., Sivan, E., Rackliffe, G., Book, C., Meloth, M. S., ... & Bassiri, D. (1987). Effects of explaining the reasoning associated with using reading strategies. *Reading Research Quarterly*, 22(3), 347–368.**: Empirical evaluation of explicit reasoning instruction for reading strategies; demonstrates that explaining *why* strategies work (conditional knowledge) is critical for transfer — a key finding for Section 5.2.

- **Rosenshine, B., & Meister, C. (1994). Reciprocal teaching: A review of the research. *Review of Educational Research*, 64(4), 479–530. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543064004479**: Comprehensive meta-analysis of reciprocal teaching research; the primary empirical source for Section 5.1's efficacy claims.

- **Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2017). *Self-Determination Theory: Basic Psychological Needs in Motivation, Development, and Wellness*. Guilford Press.**: The comprehensive theoretical statement of SDT across domains. Directly relevant to this report's entire motivational architecture analysis (Section 4 and Tier 3 strategies). Chapters on academic motivation and internalization provide the primary empirical and theoretical basis for the regulatory quality framework and basic needs analysis in reading contexts. Recommended reading: Chapters 6 (academic motivation), 8 (internalization), and 14 (self-regulation).

- **Kintsch, W. (1998). *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*. Cambridge University Press.**: The definitive theoretical statement of the construction-integration model and the three-level text representation framework. Foundational to this report's cognitive architecture analysis (Section 2). Provides the theoretical basis for the distinction between textbase and situation model processing that underlies the entire comprehension-oriented strategy analysis.

- **Zimmerman, B. J., & Schunk, D. H. (Eds.) (2011). *Handbook of Self-Regulation of Learning and Performance*. Routledge.**: Comprehensive reference on self-regulated learning across domains. Relevant to this report's Section 7 and metacognitive self-regulation analysis. Provides extensive empirical grounding for the cyclical SRL model applied to reading and academic work. Key chapters: Zimmerman on self-regulation of learning, Pintrich on goal orientation and self-regulation.

- **Wigfield, A., & Guthrie, J. T. (1997). Relations of children's motivation for reading to the amount and breadth of their reading. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 89*(3), 420–432.**: Seminal empirical study establishing the Motivations for Reading Questionnaire (MRQ) and documenting the multidimensional structure of reading motivation. Foundation for the Section 3 treatment of reading motivation's multidimensional nature. Demonstrated that different motivational dimensions (challenge, curiosity, involvement, importance, recognition, grades, competition, social, compliance, efficacy) predict reading behavior independently.

- **Hidi, S., & Renninger, K. A. (2006). The four-phase model of interest development. *Educational Psychologist, 41*(2), 111–127.**: Primary source for the four-phase interest development model. Directly foundational to the Section 3 treatment of interest theory and the Tier 3 interest-building reading program strategy. Provides the theoretical basis for distinguishing situational from individual interest and specifying the developmental transitions between phases.

- **Bjork, R. A. (1994). Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings. In J. Metcalfe & A. Shimamura (Eds.), *Metacognition: Knowing about knowing* (pp. 185–205). MIT Press.**: Primary source for the desirable difficulties framework. Foundational to the Tier 2 strategy analysis, particularly spaced repetition, retrieval practice, and the cognitive load calibration analysis. Provides the theoretical basis for recommending effortful learning conditions despite their short-term costs.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M. H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: Seminal empirical demonstration of self-explanation effects on comprehension and learning. Foundational to the Tier 2 self-explanation strategy recommendation. Demonstrated that students who self-explained during learning achieved significantly higher comprehension than those who re-read the same material.

- **Elliot, A. J., & McGregor, H. A. (2001). A 2×2 achievement goal framework. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80*(3), 501–519.**: Primary source for the 2×2 achievement goal framework. Foundational to this report's Section 5 analysis. Demonstrates the distinct motivational and performance patterns associated with mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals.

- **Palincsar, A. S., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction, 1*(2), 117–175.**: Primary source and original empirical validation of the reciprocal teaching method. Foundational to this report's Section 7 treatment of social metacognition and collaborative reading. Demonstrated significant comprehension improvements from reciprocal teaching in comparison conditions.

- **Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249–255.**: Foundational empirical demonstration of the testing effect (retrieval practice advantage over re-reading). Directly foundational to the Tier 2 retrieval practice strategy recommendation and the calibration training analysis in Section 7.

- **Ryan, R. M., & Deci, E. L. (2017). *Self-Determination Theory: Basic Psychological Needs in Motivation, Development, and Wellness*. Guilford Press.**: The comprehensive theoretical statement of SDT across domains. Directly relevant to this report's entire motivational architecture analysis (Section 4 and Tier 3 strategies). Chapters on academic motivation and internalization provide the primary empirical and theoretical basis for the regulatory quality framework and basic needs analysis in reading contexts. Recommended reading: Chapters 6 (academic motivation), 8 (internalization), and 14 (self-regulation).

- **Kintsch, W. (1998). *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*. Cambridge University Press.**: The definitive theoretical statement of the construction-integration model and the three-level text representation framework. Foundational to this report's cognitive architecture analysis (Section 2). Provides the theoretical basis for the distinction between textbase and situation model processing that underlies the entire comprehension-oriented strategy analysis.

- **Zimmerman, B. J., & Schunk, D. H. (Eds.) (2011). *Handbook of Self-Regulation of Learning and Performance*. Routledge.**: Comprehensive reference on self-regulated learning across domains. Relevant to this report's Section 7 and metacognitive self-regulation analysis. Provides extensive empirical grounding for the cyclical SRL model applied to reading and academic work. Key chapters: Zimmerman on self-regulation of learning, Pintrich on goal orientation and self-regulation.

- **Wigfield, A., & Guthrie, J. T. (1997). Relations of children's motivation for reading to the amount and breadth of their reading. *Journal of Educational Psychology, 89*(3), 420–432.**: Seminal empirical study establishing the Motivations for Reading Questionnaire (MRQ) and documenting the multidimensional structure of reading motivation. Foundation for the Section 3 treatment of reading motivation's multidimensional nature. Demonstrated that different motivational dimensions (challenge, curiosity, involvement, importance, recognition, grades, competition, social, compliance, efficacy) predict reading behavior independently.

- **Hidi, S., & Renninger, K. A. (2006). The four-phase model of interest development. *Educational Psychologist, 41*(2), 111–127.**: Primary source for the four-phase interest development model. Directly foundational to the Section 3 treatment of interest theory and the Tier 3 interest-building reading program strategy. Provides the theoretical basis for distinguishing situational from individual interest and specifying the developmental transitions between phases.

- **Bjork, R. A. (1994). Memory and metamemory considerations in the training of human beings. In J. Metcalfe & A. Shimamura (Eds.), *Metacognition: Knowing about knowing* (pp. 185–205). MIT Press.**: Primary source for the desirable difficulties framework. Foundational to the Tier 2 strategy analysis, particularly spaced repetition, retrieval practice, and the cognitive load calibration analysis. Provides the theoretical basis for recommending effortful learning conditions despite their short-term costs.

Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: Seminal empirical demonstration of self-explanation effects on comprehension and learning. Foundational to the Tier 2 self-explanation strategy recommendation. Demonstrated that students who self-explained during learning achieved significantly higher comprehension than those who re-read the same material.

- **Elliot, A. J., & McGregor, H. A. (2001). A 2×2 achievement goal framework. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 80*(3), 501–519.**: Primary source for the 2×2 achievement goal framework. Foundational to this report's Section 5 analysis. Demonstrates the distinct motivational and performance patterns associated with mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals.

- **Palincsar, A. S., & Brown, A. L. (1984). Reciprocal teaching of comprehension-fostering and comprehension-monitoring activities. *Cognition and Instruction, 1*(2), 117–175.**: Primary source and original empirical validation of the reciprocal teaching method. Foundational to this report's Section 7 treatment of social metacognition and collaborative reading. Demonstrated significant comprehension improvements from reciprocal teaching in comparison conditions.

- **Roediger, H. L., & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. *Psychological Science, 17*(3), 249–255.**: Foundational empirical demonstration of the testing effect (retrieval practice advantage over re-reading). Directly foundational to the Tier 2 retrieval practice strategy recommendation and the calibration training analysis in Section 7.

- **van Dijk, T. A., & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies in Discourse Comprehension*. Academic Press.**: The founding monograph of the situation model framework. Introduces the three-level representation architecture, the textbase-situation model distinction, macrostructure, and the local/global coherence distinction. Required primary reading for anyone working in discourse comprehension.

**Recommended Sections:** Chapters 2 (propositional analysis), 5 (situation models), 8 (comprehension strategies).

- **Kintsch, W. (1998). *Comprehension: A Paradigm for Cognition*. Cambridge University Press.**: Kintsch's comprehensive synthesis of 30 years of research on text comprehension, integrating propositional analysis, the Construction-Integration model, and extensions to learning from text and problem solving. The definitive C-I model account.

**Recommended Sections:** Chapters 1 (overview), 4 (C-I model), 6 (situation models and knowledge), 10 (learning from text).

- **Zwaan, R. A., Langston, M. C., & Graesser, A. C. (1995). The construction of situation models in narrative comprehension: An event-indexing model. *Psychological Science, 6*(5), 292–297.**: The original Event Indexing Model paper. Concise but theoretically dense; provides the structural specification of situation model content across five dimensions.

- **Zwaan, R. A., & Radvansky, G. A. (1998). Situation models in language comprehension and memory. *Psychological Bulletin, 123*(2), 162–185.**: Comprehensive review of the situation model literature through the late 1990s. The most accessible survey of the empirical evidence base for the situation model as a distinct level of representation.

- **Kintsch, W. (1988). The role of knowledge in discourse comprehension: A construction-integration model. *Psychological Review, 95*(2), 163–182.**: The original formal presentation of the C-I model. More accessible than the 1998 book; the clearest statement of the two-phase architecture and its psychological motivations.

- **Gernsbacher, M. A. (1990). *Language Comprehension as Structure Building*. Erlbaum.**: Presents the Structure Building Framework with empirical support, including the suppression mechanism and individual differences evidence. The most direct treatment of why comprehension skill is partly determined by inhibitory capacity.

- **Graesser, A. C., Singer, M., & Trabasso, T. (1994). Constructing inferences during narrative text comprehension. *Psychological Review, 101*(3), 371–395.**: The definitive statement of Constructionist Theory. Specifies which inference types are generated automatically (causal antecedents, goal-motives) versus selectively (predictive, elaborative).

- **Daneman, M., & Carpenter, P. A. (1980). Individual differences in working memory and reading. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 19*(4), 450–466.**: Foundational study establishing the correlation between reading span (WMC measure) and reading comprehension. First rigorous demonstration that WMC constraints affect situation model construction quality.

- **Chi, M. T. H., de Leeuw, N., Chiu, M.-H., & LaVancher, C. (1994). Eliciting self-explanations improves understanding. *Cognitive Science, 18*(3), 439–477.**: The seminal self-explanation study. Demonstrates that prompting readers to explain content produces substantially better comprehension (including more inference questions answered correctly) than re-reading. Primary empirical support for self-explanation as a situation model construction strategy.

- **van den Broek, P., Risden, K., & Husebye-Hartmann, E. (1995). The role of readers' standards for coherence in the generation of inferences during reading. In R. F. Lorch & E. J. O'Brien (Eds.), *Sources of coherence in reading* (pp. 353–373). Erlbaum.**: Presents the Landscape Model and the standards of coherence concept. Explains how individual differences in coherence standards produce different rates of inference generation and different situation model qualities.

- **Trabasso, T., & van den Broek, P. (1985). Causal thinking and the representation of narrative events. *Journal of Memory and Language, 24*(5), 612–630.**: Foundational study demonstrating that causal connectivity — the number of causal connections a text event has — is the primary predictor of recall probability, more predictive than serial position. The empirical basis for the primacy of causal structure in situation model construction.

- **McNamara, D. S., & Kintsch, W. (1996). Learning from texts: Effects of prior knowledge and text coherence. *Discourse Processes, 22*(3), 247–288.**: Counterintuitive finding: high-knowledge readers learn more from low-coherence texts (they must generate more inferences, producing deeper processing); low-knowledge readers learn more from high-coherence texts (explicit coherence compensates for absent prior knowledge). Demonstrates the interaction between domain knowledge and text coherence in situation model construction.

- **Bransford, J. D., & Johnson, M. K. (1972). Contextual prerequisites for understanding: Some investigations of comprehension and recall. *Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior, 11*(6), 717–726.**: Classic demonstration of prior knowledge dependence in comprehension. The "washing clothes" passage: incomprehensible without context; highly comprehensible with it. Among the most elegant demonstrations of the schema-dependence of situation model construction.

- **Kintsch, W., & van Dijk, T. A. (1978). Toward a model of text comprehension and production. *Psychological Review, 85*(5), 363–394.**: Introduces the propositional analysis methodology and the macrostructure model. Essential historical context for understanding how the situation model framework emerged from the propositional tradition.

- **van Dijk, T. A., & Kintsch, W. (1983). *Strategies in Discourse Comprehension*. Academic Press.**: The founding monograph of the situation model framework. Introduces the three-level representation architecture, the textbase-situation model distinction, macrostructure, and the local/global coherence distinction. Required primary reading for anyone working in discourse comprehension.

**Recommended Sections:** Chapters 2 (propositional analysis), 5 (situation models), 8 (comprehension strategies).

The definitive C-I model account.

More accessible than the 1998 book; the clearest statement of the two-phase architecture and its psychological motivations.

- **Gernsbacher, M. A. (1990). *Language Comprehension as Structure Building*. The empirical basis for the primacy of causal structure in situation model construction.

- **McNamara, D. S., & Kintsch, W. (1996).
